output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Important Correction to the Starting Premise

Before diving into the records, one significant correction is needed: Massachusetts *did* have civil vital registration before 1841. Town-level recording was ordered as early as **1639**, though not all towns complied uniformly. The landmark **1841 act** created a *statewide* registry — the first in any U.S. state — layered on top of the existing town-clerk series. This means:

- **1820–1840:** Town vital records *may* exist, depending on that town's compliance with the 1639 mandate. Gaps are real, but absence should be confirmed rather than assumed.
- **1841–1850:** Two parallel civil series exist — the town book *and* the state registry.

Church registers and cemetery inscriptions are genuine and important sources for this period, but they supplement the civil series rather than replace it.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761, from Hampshire County
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Location:** Westernmost county in Massachusetts; coordinates ~42.37°N, 73.21°W
- **Neighboring state lines:** New York to the west, Vermont to the north
- **Key border towns** (near both state lines): Williamstown, Adams, North Adams, Clarksburg, Florida

No internal boundary changes within Berkshire County during 1820–1850 were identified.

---

## Available Record Types

### 1. Vital Records — Town-Level Civil Registration *(Primary source)*

**Registration history:**
- **1639 mandate:** Town clerks were ordered to record births, marriages, and deaths. Compliance varied.
- **1841 statewide act:** Created a second, state-level registry running in parallel with town books.

**FamilySearch collections:**
| Collection | ID | Coverage | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 | [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) | 1820–1850 ✓ | **Indexed + images** — name-searchable |
| Town Clerk Vital and Town Records (Berkshire Co., 1761–1850) | Vol. 004500891 (512 images) | 1820–1850 ✓ | **Browse-only** — page-by-page only |

**Printed "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series:** Published compilations covering over 200 Massachusetts towns through 1850, transcribing the town-clerk vital records. Held at NEHGS and many public libraries; some volumes digitized. A critical finding aid for the pre-1841 years.

**Note on marriage intentions:** Under Massachusetts law, intentions were filed in multiple towns — often the bride's town, the groom's town, and their current residence. For a border family, check all relevant town clerks.

---

### 2. Church Records *(Critical for 1820–1840 gaps)*

**What exists:** Baptismal registers, marriage registers, and burial registers. When a specific town has a gap in its civil series — especially 1820–1840 — church registers may be the only dated documentary evidence. They often contain richer detail (sponsors, witnesses, parents' occupations).

**FamilySearch collections:**
| Collection | ID | Coverage | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 | [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) | 1820–1850 ✓ | **Indexed + images** |
| Church Records (Congregational), Pittsfield, 1791–1850 | Vol. 004500892 (274 images) | Pittsfield only | **Browse-only** — page-by-page only |

**Caveat:** Volume 004500892 covers *one congregation in one town*. Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and other denomination registers are **not** represented in the returned results. Seek other volumes through the FamilySearch Catalog by individual town name, NEHGS, and the Congregational Library and Archives (Boston).

**Where originals are held:** Surviving local congregations; denominational archives (Congregational Library & Archives, Boston; Methodist conference archives; Episcopal Diocese); or NEHGS.

---

### 3. Cemetery Records *(Death evidence, especially pre-1841)*

**What exists:** Headstone inscriptions record death dates and often birth dates and family relationships. For the pre-1841 years when town-book compliance was uneven, cemetery inscriptions may be the only death evidence available.

**Important limitation:** Inscriptions document *deaths* only. They do not record births and rarely record marriages; they cannot substitute for a full vital records search.

**Online:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) — coverage is uneven for rural hill towns; search what exists and look for gaps.

**Physical:** Sexton records and burial registers (where they survive) are at the town or congregation. The **Berkshire Athenaeum** (Pittsfield Public Library) holds transcription projects for some Berkshire cemeteries.

---

### 4. Federal Census Records

| Census | Format | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1820 | Head of household only; others counted by age/sex bracket | Establishes household existence and approximate ages |
| 1830 | Same as 1820 | — |
| 1840 | Same as 1820 | — |
| **1850** | **Names every household member** — age, sex, birthplace, occupation | **Best snapshot for family reconstruction at the end of the period** |
| 1850 Mortality Schedule | Deaths June 1849–June 1850 | Name, age, sex, cause of death, birthplace |

All are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

### 5. Probate Records *(Substitute when vital records are absent)*

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (id 1678901, [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901))
- Estate files name the decedent, spouse, and **all heirs** — key for establishing family structure when vital records are missing.
- Check both testate (will + inventory) and intestate (administration file naming next of kin) series.
- **Physical:** Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield.

---

### 6. Land Records

- Massachusetts is a state-land (metes-and-bounds) state; county-level deed series survive "in remarkably complete runs" from the 1630s.
- **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield** — note there are **northern and southern registry divisions**: a family in Adams, North Adams, Williamstown, or Clarksburg falls under the *northern* registry.
- Heirs' deeds following a death can establish family structure when probate records are sparse.

---

### 7. Military Records

- **War of 1812** pensioners were active throughout 1820–1850: pension files are at NARA and available via [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Mexican-American War, 1846–1848:** service records at NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)).

---

### 8. Newspapers

- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — Berkshire County had local papers by the 1820s (e.g., *Pittsfield Sun*). Obituaries, marriage notices, and estate administrator legal notices appeared regularly and can date events when no civil or church record survives.
- Microfilm of Berkshire papers is held at the **Berkshire Athenaeum**.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Town Vital Records (id 2061550), Church Records (id 1921657), Probate (id 1678901), 2 browse-only volumes | Free |
| **Ancestry** (ancestry.com) | Federal censuses | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions and photographs | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Berkshire County newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal records, pension files | Free to visit; some online |
| **AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS)** | Printed "Vital Records to 1850" series, manuscript church registers, Massachusetts collections | Subscription |
| **Berkshire Athenaeum, Pittsfield** | Local history, newspaper microfilm, cemetery transcription projects | In-person |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Original colony and state records | In-person |
| **Congregational Library & Archives, Boston** | Congregational church registers statewide | In-person; some microfilm at FamilySearch |
| **Town clerks (individual Berkshire towns)** | Original vital records from 1639 onward | Contact each town separately |
| **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds** | Deeds from 1761; northern division for border towns | In-person; some online |

---

## Records Not Yet Online

- Pre-1841 town vital records for Berkshire towns beyond what volume 004500891 captured — search the FamilySearch Catalog by individual town name for additional microfilmed town-clerk volumes.
- Non-Congregational church registers (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal) for Berkshire towns — physical originals only.
- Sexton records and burial registers for individual cemeteries.
- The full "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" printed series (not all volumes digitized).
- New York and Vermont church registers for border events (see below).

---

## Critical Research Tips for a Border-County Family

1. **Search the indexed collection first, then browse the volume.** Collection 2061550 is name-indexed; volume 004500891 is not. Start with the index, then page through the browse volume for events that don't appear in it.

2. **For 1841–1850, check both the town book and the state series.** Two parallel civil series overlap for these years; an event may appear in one but not the other.

3. **Cross-border research is essential.** For a family near both the New York and Vermont lines, births, marriages, or deaths may have been recorded on the other side of the state line.
   - **New York:** No statewide civil registration until 1880 — NY church records are critical for any cross-border event 1820–1850. Consult the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society and the relevant NY county clerk.
   - **Vermont:** Town clerks have recorded vital events since before statehood (1791). Vermont town records may capture cross-border events. A separate locality survey for the adjoining Vermont county (Bennington County) is recommended.

4. **The 1850 census is the anchor record.** It names every family member with age, birthplace, and occupation — use it to build out the family unit, then work backward with vital, church, and probate records.

5. **Probate files substitute when vital records are absent.** An estate file names all heirs and establishes death date and family relationships — search "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (id 1678901) for every family member.

6. **NEHGS is the specialist repository.** The largest genealogical library in the region holds the complete printed "Vital Records to 1850" series, manuscript church registers, and much more. Their AmericanAncestors.org platform provides online access.

---

**Recommended next step:** Run companion locality surveys for the adjoining New York county (Columbia or Rensselaer County, depending on which Berkshire border town the family lived in) and Bennington County, Vermont — then build a unified research plan across all three jurisdictions.

**Testate vs. intestate:** A decedent who left a will (testate) generates a will file and inventory; one who died without a will (intestate) generates an administration file naming the administrator and the next of kin. Search both series for the 1820–1850 window.

### Land records

**Coverage:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) reports that county-level deeds survive "in remarkably complete runs" from the 1630s. Massachusetts is a state-land (metes-and-bounds) state; no federal patent process applies.

**Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield. Note that Berkshire County has a northern and a southern registry division; a family in a northern border town (Adams, North Adams, Williamstown, Clarksburg) should check the northern registry.

**Value for vital research:** Deeds name grantors and grantees with relationships; heirs' deeds following a death can establish family structure when probate records are sparse.

### Military records

**Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (pensioners active throughout 1820–1850); Mexican-American War 1846–1848. War of 1812 pension files are at NARA and are available via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/), returned by `external_links_search`. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was also returned.

### Newspapers

**Coverage:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) was returned by `external_links_search`. Berkshire County had local papers by the 1820s (the Pittsfield Sun is an early example). Obituaries, marriage notices, and estate administrator legal notices appeared regularly and can date events for which no town record or church register has survived. Microfilm of Berkshire papers is held at the Berkshire Athenaeum.

### Immigration and emigration records

**Relevance:** A border-county family near both NY and VT lines generated no international immigration records in this period in the ordinary course; however, passenger lists and naturalization papers are relevant if ancestors arrived from Europe. "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (id 1784312) and "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (id 1459213) were both returned by `collections_search`. Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record including Berkshire County courts.

## Research tips

1. **Start with the indexed collection, not the browse-only volume.** The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (id 2061550) is name-indexed; the browse-only volume 004500891 is not. Search the indexed collection first, then browse the volume for events that do not appear in the index.

2. **Search at the town level, not the county level.** Vital records and church registers in Massachusetts are created and held at the town level (Massachusetts Vital Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records). Know the specific Berkshire town before searching; a county-wide search in a tool may miss a town-filed entry.

3. **For 1841–1850, two civil series overlap.** The 1841 statewide act created a second series running in parallel with the town books. Check both. The statewide series for these years is captured in the "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" collection; the original town book is at the town clerk (Massachusetts Vital Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).

4. **Marriage intentions were filed in multiple towns.** The Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) states: "There were marriage intentions commonly recorded in the bride's home town and additional recordings may be found in the groom's home town and their current residence." For a border family whose parties may have been from different towns — or from New York or Vermont — this means checking multiple town clerks.

5. **Volume 004500892 is Pittsfield Congregational only.** Despite being the only church-records volume returned for the county, it covers one congregation in one town. Do not treat it as representative of Berkshire County church records broadly. Seek other town and denomination registers through the FamilySearch Catalog, NEHGS, and the Congregational Library and Archives.

6. **Cross-border research is essential for a family near both state lines.** Events — especially births and marriages — may have been recorded on the New York or Vermont side. The Berkshire County Genealogy wiki page returned only generic content, so the Neighboring Counties table was not available from tool results; consult the page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Berkshire_County,_Massachusetts_Genealogy for the current table. For the New York side: New York State did not have statewide civil registration until 1880, making NY church records critical for events across that border in 1820–1850. For Vermont: Vermont town clerks have recorded vital events since before statehood (1791), so cross-border events may appear in Vermont town records. Search both sides rather than assuming events were recorded only in Massachusetts.

7. **The 1850 federal census names every family member.** The 1820, 1830, and 1840 censuses name only the household head and count others by age and sex brackets. The 1850 census names every person, with age, birthplace, and occupation — the single best snapshot for reconstructing family structure at the end of the target period. The 1850 mortality schedule adds deaths from June 1849 through June 1850.

8. **Probate records substitute when vital records are absent.** Berkshire County estate files name decedents, spouses, and heirs and establish death dates, family relationships, and residence. "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (id 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) covers the period.

9. **The printed "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series is a first-line resource.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) reports that this published series covers over 200 Massachusetts towns and transcribes town-clerk records through 1850. NEHGS holds the full set; many volumes are at state and county libraries. These transcriptions are faster to work through than the browse-only digitized volumes.

10. **NEHGS is the key specialist repository.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military) identifies NEHGS as "the largest genealogical library in the region." Their AmericanAncestors.org platform provides subscription online access to Massachusetts-specific collections not available on FamilySearch, including early church registers and transcribed vital records.

11. **Most wiki pages for this place returned only generic content.** All four `wiki_place_page` sections for Berkshire and Massachusetts, plus the wiki_read calls for Massachusetts Church Records, Massachusetts Cemetery Records, and Massachusetts Naming Customs, returned the generic guide page rather than Massachusetts-specific pages. The researcher should visit those FamilySearch Wiki articles directly and should not treat the absence of specific data in this guide as confirmation that the pages lack it.

---

This guide covered Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850). The three neighboring jurisdictions whose records this family likely also generated — the two New York border counties to the west and Bennington County, Vermont to the north — each warrant their own locality survey.

Berkshire County, Massachusetts sits along the New York and Vermont state lines; it has kept town-level civil vital records since colonial times, and many of those records have been indexed online, though the church registers and some town-clerk volumes are digitized only as browse-only images requiring page-by-page review. The most important caution is that the family's town is close to two state lines, which means births, marriages, or deaths may have been recorded in New York or Vermont rather than in Massachusetts.

The next step is to run a locality survey for the specific New York and Vermont border counties adjoining the family's town, then build a research plan across all three jurisdictions.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Baronies:** Partly in Carey; chiefly in Lower Dunluce
- **County:** Antrim, Ulster
- **Poor Law Union:** Coleraine
- **Main settlement:** Bushmills
- **Church of Ireland ecclesiastical union:** Formerly united with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride
- **Roman Catholic district:** Coleraine
- **Nonconformist congregations confirmed:** Presbyterian (General Assembly), Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterian), and Wesleyan Methodist

---

## Boundary & Jurisdictional Notes

The civil-parish boundary of Billy was stable across 1780–1870. The Poor Law Union of Coleraine was created under the 1838 Poor Law Act, so workhouse and out-relief records are only available post-1838. Congregational boundaries do **not** align with civil-parish boundaries — a family in an outlying townland of Billy may have worshipped in a congregation seated in a neighboring parish such as Dunluce.

---

## Record Types Available

### Church Records *(most important class for 1780–1864)*

Ireland had no civil registration before 1864, so church registers are the backbone of research for this entire period.

**Presbyterian registers — which congregation?**
A "Presbyterian" family in Billy parish could belong to one of at least two separate traditions, each with its own register series:

1. **Bushmills Presbyterian congregation** (General Assembly) — the main mainstream congregation serving the post town. Registers are on microfilm at PRONI in the MIC 1P series. Look up the specific film number in PRONI's eCatalogue under "Bushmills."
2. **Covenanters / Reformed Presbyterian congregation** — a separate body with its own meeting house confirmed within the parish. This is a *different register series* at PRONI from the General Assembly registers. Search PRONI's eCatalogue under "Reformed Presbyterian" or "Covenanters, County Antrim."
3. **Neighboring congregations** — depending on the townland, the family may have attended a congregation seated in Dunluce or another adjacent parish.

**Church of Ireland:** Registers for the Billy ecclesiastical union are at PRONI. The Representative Church Body Library (Dublin) also holds some Church of Ireland registers.

**Roman Catholic:** The RC parish covering Billy is under Coleraine. PRONI holds microfilm copies of many County Antrim Catholic registers.

**Where to find church registers:**
- PRONI, Belfast — MIC 1P series (microfilm); search the [PRONI eCatalogue](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-proni-ecatalogue)
- FamilySearch — search the Catalog for "County Antrim" + "Presbyterian" or the congregation name; many PRONI MIC 1P reels have been filmed
- Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland (Belfast) — congregational histories, session records
- Local congregations may still hold some originals

> ⚠️ **The church records section of the Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch wiki page was empty stubs** — no PRONI film numbers or start dates for Billy's congregations were listed. The PRONI eCatalogue must be checked directly for current references.

---

### Civil Registration

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths in Ireland began **1 January 1864** (Protestant marriages were registrable from 1 April 1845). These records are outside the 1780–1864 window for births and deaths, making church registers essential for the target period. Civil records are searchable free at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie).

---

### Census Substitutes *(original pre-1900 census returns largely destroyed)*

- **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** Lists householders subject to tithe, by townland. Free and name-searchable at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) and on Ancestry.
- **Griffith's Valuation (c. 1847–1864):** The primary land-valuation survey; covers every property holder by name and townland. Free name-search at [AskAboutIreland](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and at IrishGenealogyToolkit; also on Ancestry.
- **1766 Religious Census (partial):** Some Antrim parishes have a return of householders by religion. Held at the Representative Church Body Library and PRONI.

> The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns were almost entirely destroyed (pre-1922 destruction and the Four Courts fire of 1922). The 1901 and 1911 returns survive fully and are free online at [census.nationalarchives.ie](https://census.nationalarchives.ie), but those are outside this period.

---

### Land Records

- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Memorials of registered property transactions; many Antrim tenant farmers appear here. Microfilmed by FamilySearch (search Catalog for "Registry of Deeds Ireland").
- **Tithe Applotment Books:** See above.
- **Griffith's Valuation:** See above. Accompanying field books and house books (with greater detail) are at the Valuation Office, Dublin.
- **Estate papers:** Much of north Antrim was tenanted. Landlord estate records (rentals, tenant lists, correspondence) are held at PRONI.

> **Key practice:** Identify the **townland** first. All Irish records are filed by townland, not by post town or street. Use Griffith's Valuation or the Tithe Applotment Books to pin the family to a specific townland before searching other record sets.

---

### Probate Records

Pre-1858 probate was handled by church courts (Prerogative Court of Armagh; Consistorial Court of Connor for County Antrim). The vast majority of these records were destroyed in the Four Courts fire, 1922. Surviving abstracts and indexes are at the National Archives of Ireland (NAI) and PRONI. Post-1858 civil probate records survive better; searchable at [willsindex.nationalarchives.ie](https://willsindex.nationalarchives.ie).

**When wills are missing, look for:** Registry of Deeds memorials (often state family relationships), Griffith's Valuation (shows who inherited a holding), newspaper death notices.

---

### Military Records

- **British Army service records:** Many Antrim men served in the British Army and militia. Pre-1913 records are at The National Archives (Kew, UK), and are searchable at Ancestry and Findmypast.
- **Antrim militia and yeomanry:** At PRONI and The National Archives (Kew).
- **1798 rebellion:** Lists of persons swearing loyalty oaths, and some rebel lists, survive at PRONI.

---

### Newspapers

- **Coleraine Chronicle** (from 1844) and **Coleraine Constitution** cover the Bushmills area.
- **Belfast News-Letter** (from 1737) published notices from across Ulster — death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices. Searchable online at Findmypast and the British Newspaper Archive.

---

### Other Valuable Sources

- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (c. 1835):** Detailed social surveys of each Antrim parish, including congregation histories and approximate membership. Published by Queen's University Belfast's Institute of Irish Studies. Can identify which congregation a family likely attended before registers begin.
- **School registers (from 1832):** National school registers at the NAI name pupils, ages, parents' names, and religion.
- **Poor law workhouse records (from 1838):** Coleraine Union records at PRONI — admissions, deaths, by name and townland.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Church register microfilms (MIC 1P), estate papers, poor law, land, court | In-person + eCatalogue online |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** | Civil registration, Tithe Applotment, Griffith's, school registers, post-1858 probate | In-person + [nationalarchives.ie](https://www.nationalarchives.ie) |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Civil registration; Tithe Applotment Books; some church registers | Free — [irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) |
| **AskAboutIreland** | Griffith's Valuation, name-searchable by townland | Free — [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) |
| **FamilySearch** | PRONI microfilm catalog; some indexed Irish collections | Free — [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland** | Congregational records, session books | In-person — Belfast |
| **Representative Church Body Library, Dublin** | Church of Ireland registers; 1766 religious census fragments | In-person |
| **Registry of Deeds, Dublin** | Original deed memorials from 1708 | In-person — [prai.ie](https://www.prai.ie) |
| **The National Archives, Kew** | British Army service records; militia muster rolls | In-person + Ancestry/Findmypast |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation** | Ulster Presbyterian surname indexes, Ancestor Network database | Belfast; subscription |

---

## Key Research Tips for a Presbyterian Family in Billy, c. 1825

1. **Check both Presbyterian register series** — General Assembly (Bushmills congregation) and Covenanters — at PRONI. They are separate films. If the family is not in one, search the other.
2. **Identify the townland first** — search Griffith's Valuation (free online) by surname in County Antrim to place the family in a specific townland, then use that townland to navigate church and land records.
3. **The Ordnance Survey Memoirs for the Billy/Bushmills area (c. 1835)** describe the local Presbyterian and Covenanters congregations in detail — this can identify the congregation before registers survive.
4. **North Antrim was a major source of Ulster-Scots emigration** — if the family moved to North America, arrival manifests and naturalization records may give county or parish of origin.
5. **Check the PRONI eCatalogue** for the specific MIC 1P film numbers for Bushmills, and note whether those reels have been digitized on FamilySearch — this is the single most important next step.
6. **Naming patterns in Ulster-Scots families** often placed the paternal grandfather's name on the first son and the maternal grandfather's on the second — useful for working back a generation, but verify for each individual family.

### Census records

**Note on Irish census losses:** No tool returned the Ireland Census wiki page. What is well established in the field — though no tool confirmed it — is that the 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns for Ireland were almost entirely destroyed: the 1821 and 1831 returns were largely destroyed before 1922; the 1841 and 1851 returns were deliberately pulped during World War I; the Four Courts fire of 1922 destroyed surviving fragments. **Census substitutes that apply to County Antrim and Billy parish:**
- **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** Cover townlands and list householders subject to tithe. Billy parish will have entries. Digitized and searchable at Ancestry (subscription) and also at the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Griffith's Valuation (c. 1847–1864):** The primary-valuation survey of all property holders in Ireland. Billy parish entries were surveyed in this period. Digitized and name-searchable for free at AskAboutIreland (www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and at IrishGenealogyToolkit; also on Ancestry.
- **1766 Religious Census (partial):** A return of householders by religion for some parishes in Antrim survives. Coverage is incomplete. Held at the Representative Church Body Library and PRONI.
- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s) and Muster Rolls (1630s):** Pre-period but useful for earlier family presence in the area. Available for some Antrim townlands at PRONI and online via various indexes.

### Probate and court records

The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ireland Probate Records was not returned by tools (redirected to a generic page). No PRONI references or National Archives of Ireland collection data were returned.

- **Pre-1858:** Probate was handled by church courts — the Prerogative Court of Armagh (for estates over a threshold) and the Consistorial Court of Connor (the diocese covering County Antrim) for smaller estates. The vast majority of these records were destroyed in the Four Courts fire of 1922. Surviving indexes and abstracts (including Sir William Betham's genealogical abstracts of prerogative wills) are at the National Archives of Ireland, PRONI, and the Royal Irish Academy.
- **Post-1858:** Civil probate began 1 January 1858 under the Principal Registry (later the Public Record Office). Original wills filed 1858–1900 were also largely destroyed in 1922, but the grant books and will books (abstracts) often survive. The National Archives of Ireland holds the surviving post-1858 records.
- **Where to search:** Indexes to surviving wills and administrations are searchable at the National Archives of Ireland (willsindex.nationalarchives.ie) and at PRONI for estates in what is now Northern Ireland.

### Land records

- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Memorials of deeds (transcripts or abstracts) registered in Dublin. Covers major property transactions; not every deed was registered, but many tenant farmers in Antrim appear here. Searchable by grantor index at the Registry of Deeds, Dublin. Microfilmed by FamilySearch (search FamilySearch Catalog for "Registry of Deeds Ireland").
- **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** See Census section above.
- **Griffith's Valuation (c. 1847–1864):** See Census section above. The accompanying field books and house books (giving greater detail) are held at the Valuation Office, Dublin.
- **Estate papers:** Much of north Antrim was tenanted. The Antrim estates of the Antrim family (MacDonnell, Earl of Antrim) and other landlords generated estate maps, rentals, and tenancy records. PRONI holds many private estate collections for County Antrim.
- **Survey system:** Ireland used a metes-and-bounds/townland system, not the rectangular survey. The townland is the fundamental unit; every event record in Billy parish will be filed under a townland name. Identify the correct townland before searching.

No tool returned land records specific to Billy parish.

### Military records

The Ireland Military Records wiki page was not returned by tools. For 1780–1870, the relevant records are:

- **British Army service records:** Many men from County Antrim served in the British Army and militia. Pre-1913 records are held at The National Archives (Kew, UK) — many are online at Ancestry and Findmypast under "British Army service records."
- **Muster rolls and militia lists:** Antrim militia and yeomanry records are at PRONI and at The National Archives (Kew).
- **1798 rebellion:** Lists of persons who took the oath of allegiance, and some rebel lists, survive. PRONI holds relevant County Antrim material.
- **Pensioners:** Chelsea and Greenwich pension records (at The National Archives, Kew) can place a soldier and often give his county of origin. The 1841 and 1851 census schedules listed pensioners (originals destroyed, but some abstracts survive).

### Probate substitutes when wills are missing

Given the near-total destruction of pre-1922 probate records, look for:
- Church records naming executors or witnesses
- Registry of Deeds memorials (often contain family-relationship statements)
- Griffith's Valuation showing who inherited a holding after a death
- Newspaper death notices and obituaries

### Cemetery records

- **Billy parish burial ground:** The Church of Ireland ecclesiastical parish included a burial ground. Records may be in the church register or a separate sexton's book.
- **Nonconformist burial grounds:** Presbyterian and Covenanters' congregations maintained separate burial grounds. Inquire at PRONI.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have some County Antrim cemeteries, but rural north Antrim coverage is uneven. The Irish Genealogical Research Society and local historical societies have done some transcription work.

- **Coleraine Chronicle** (from 1844) and the **Coleraine Constitution** cover the Bushmills area. Earlier, the **Belfast News-Letter** (from 1737, one of Ireland's oldest papers) published notices from across Ulster including Antrim.
- Death notices, marriage announcements, and legal notices appear in these papers.
- **Where held:** Belfast Central Library; British Newspaper Archive (online subscription); some volumes at PRONI. The Belfast News-Letter is searchable online at www.findmypast.com and through the British Newspaper Archive.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Emigration:** North Antrim was a major source of Ulster-Scots emigration to North America, especially to the American colonies (pre-1783) and Canada (post-1783). Presbyterian families are well represented in passenger lists.
- **Passenger lists:** Arrival manifests at US ports are held at NARA and are searchable at Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Findmypast. Canadian arrivals at Quebec appear in the Library and Archives Canada database (https://www.bac-lac.gc.ca).
- **Pre-1820 emigration:** Lists are fragmentary. The Famine-era and post-Famine (1845–1870) emigration generated more systematic manifests.
- **Naturalization records:** US declarations of intention and naturalizations, pre-1906, were filed in any court of record. Many immigrants from Billy parish settled in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and the Carolinas.
- Note: Passenger lists (arrival manifests) name every person on board, including infants and young children. When researching a family group, examine the full manifest page, not just the entry for the head of household.

It was a predominantly Presbyterian and Church of Ireland area, with Covenanting and Methodist congregations also confirmed. # Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Baronies:** Lower Dunluce (chiefly) and Carey — the parish straddles both, so some land and administrative records may be filed under either barony name
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **Post town:** Bushmills (within the parish)
- **Ecclesiastical union (Church of Ireland):** Billy was formerly head of a union comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride — earlier CoI records may reference linked parishes
- **Roman Catholic:** Billy falls within the **Coleraine district**; there is no standalone Catholic parish register for Billy itself

**Denominations confirmed as having a meeting house in Billy parish:** Presbyterian (General Assembly), Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian), Wesleyan Methodist, and Church of Ireland.

---

## Record Types Available

### Church Records *(most critical for a Presbyterian family)*

Two distinct Presbyterian bodies had meeting houses in Billy parish:
1. **Mainstream (General Assembly) Presbyterian** — registers held at PRONI (MIC 1P/\* microfilm series); many also filmed by FamilySearch
2. **Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian)** — a separate denomination with its own registers; do not assume General Assembly registers cover Covenanter members

**Access routes:**
- **PRONI eCatalogue** (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) — search by congregation name for the exact MIC reference and availability
- **Ulster Historical Foundation / Ancestry Ireland** (https://www.ancestryireland.com) — indexed many County Antrim Presbyterian registers; often the fastest route to a specific baptism or marriage entry (subscription)
- **FamilySearch Catalog** (https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) — search "Billy" + "Antrim" for any microfilmed registers available online or at the FHL

### Census Substitutes *(census originals for 1821–1851 were destroyed in 1922)*

| Source | Date range | Coverage | Online? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | c. 1823–1837 | Land occupiers (head of household only) | Free — https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie |
| **Griffith's Primary Valuation** | c. 1847–1864 | All property occupiers and landlords | Free — https://www.askaboutireland.ie |
| **1901/1911 Census** | Post-period | Full households | Free — https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie |

Both Tithe Books and Griffith's name the occupier only — use them to confirm where in the parish the family lived, then cross to church registers for family reconstruction.

### Civil Registration

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in Ireland during the 1860s (non-Catholic marriages somewhat earlier). For most of the 1780–1870 window, **church registers are the only vital record source.** Surviving civil records are searchable at the General Register Office via https://www.irishgenealogy.ie.

### Land Records

- **Tithe Applotment Books** — National Archives of Ireland; free online (see above)
- **Griffith's Valuation** — Valuation Office, Dublin, and PRONI; free online (see above)
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin** — deed memorials from 1708 onward; name-indexed
- **PRONI estate papers** — leases, rent rolls, and maps deposited by landlords; physical at PRONI, searchable via eCatalogue

### Probate Records

Wills and administrations before 1858 were proved before the ecclesiastical Diocese of Connor. The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most originals. Surviving abstracts and calendars are at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland. Post-1858 records are in the civil District Probate Registry.

### Military Records

British Army service and pension records for soldiers from County Antrim are at The National Archives (UK), Kew; partially indexed on Ancestry and Findmypast.

### Newspapers

- *Coleraine Chronicle* (founded 1844) and *Ballymoney Free Press* are the most relevant local titles
- **British Newspaper Archive** (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription)
- Linen Hall Library, Belfast holds physical and microfilm runs of many Ulster titles

### Ordnance Survey Memoirs (c. 1833–1837)

The OS Memoirs for Billy parish describe each townland, the Presbyterian and other congregations, population, and economy in the 1830s — directly overlapping with a c. 1825 birth. Published by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast; held at the Royal Irish Academy, Dublin, and available in major genealogical libraries. **An essential step before searching registers.**

### Other Notable Sources

- **Flaxseed Premium Returns (1796):** Lists County Antrim householders who received a grant for planting flax; transcribed by the Ulster Historical Foundation; physical at PRONI
- **National Schools records (from 1831):** Some school registers survive at PRONI
- **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com) has some County Antrim cemetery entries

---

## Key Record Losses

- **1922 Four Courts fire (Dublin):** Destroyed the great majority of original pre-1858 probate records and the census originals for 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851
- The **Griffith's Valuation and Tithe Applotment Books** are the primary census substitutes that survived

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Presbyterian and other church register microfilm (MIC 1P/\*); estate papers; Grand Jury records; school records; Valuation records | In-person; eCatalogue at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** | Tithe Applotment Books; some will abstracts; civil registration records | In-person + many records free online |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation** | Indexed Presbyterian registers for County Antrim | Subscription at https://www.ancestryireland.com |
| **FamilySearch** | Microfilm of many church registers; Catalog search | Free at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog |
| **General Register Office** | Civil registration (births/marriages/deaths, 1860s onward) | https://www.irishgenealogy.ie |
| **The National Archives (UK), Kew** | British Army service records | In-person; Ancestry/Findmypast |
| **Royal Irish Academy, Dublin** | Ordnance Survey Memoirs for Ulster | In-person; published volumes widely available |
| **Registry of Deeds, Dublin** | Deed memorials from 1708 | In-person; indexes partially online |

---

## Priority Next Steps for a Presbyterian Family Born c. 1825

1. **Check the Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page directly** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy — the church records section lists congregation names and register start dates that are essential before searching
2. **Identify the congregation** — mainstream Presbyterian or Covenanter? These are separate denominations with separate registers; the answer changes where you search
3. **Search PRONI's eCatalogue** for the congregation name to get the MIC 1P/\* reference and confirm whether images are available online or reading-room-only
4. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books** (free online) to place the family in a specific townland c. 1823–1837
5. **Search Griffith's Valuation** (free online) for the same family c. 1847–1864 — townland placement is essential for narrowing a church search
6. **Consult the Ordnance Survey Memoirs for Billy parish** for 1830s context on congregation names and townland layout
7. **Try the Ulster Historical Foundation** database for an indexed Presbyterian baptism or marriage entry if the PRONI register hasn't been digitized with online images

## Tool-coverage note

The FamilySearch `place_search`, `collections_search`, `volume_search`, `wiki_place_page`, and `wiki_read` tools returned no Ireland-specific data in this session — each resolved to a generic placeholder page or an empty result set. ---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy

- **Ecclesiastical history (Church of Ireland):** Billy parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union that comprised the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. Earlier Church of Ireland records may reference any of those linked parishes.
- **Roman Catholic ecclesiastical division:** Billy forms part of the **district of Coleraine** in the Roman Catholic hierarchy — it is not a standalone Catholic parish. Catholic registers must be sought through the Coleraine district.
- **Religious denominations confirmed by tool results:** Presbyterian meeting house, Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) meeting house, Wesleyan Methodist meeting house. (Source: Billy Civil Parish page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)

The `place_search` and `place_population` tools returned no data for Irish places in this session. Population figures and economic context cannot be confirmed from tool output.

## Boundary changes

Billy parish was stable as a civil parish within County Antrim across 1780–1870. The key jurisdictional split to know is that the parish straddles two baronies (Lower Dunluce and Carey), so land valuation and some Grand Jury records may be filed under either barony heading. After 1921 the county came within Northern Ireland; records generated after that date are held under Northern Ireland jurisdiction, but this falls outside the 1780–1870 survey period.

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch wiki tools did not return the Ireland Vital Records page in this session. The start date for civil registration cannot be confirmed from tool output. ### Church records

This is the **most critical record class** for a Presbyterian family in Billy parish in 1780–1870.

3. **Wesleyan Methodist** — a Methodist meeting house was present.

4. **Church of Ireland** — the civil parish of Billy has a Church of Ireland parish church. The former ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride means earlier Church of Ireland registers may be interleaved or held under a linked parish.

5. **Roman Catholic** — Roman Catholics in Billy parish are part of the Coleraine district; Catholic registers should be sought through Coleraine-district records, not a dedicated Billy Catholic register.

**Access:** PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland), Belfast, holds microfilm copies of most surviving Presbyterian and other denominational registers for County Antrim under their MIC 1P/\* series. The eCatalogue at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni allows searching by congregation name. Many registers have also been filmed by FamilySearch and are available at the FamilySearch Library or online; check the FamilySearch Catalog at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog by searching for "Billy" and "Antrim." ### Census records

- **Critical known gap (widely documented in genealogical reference literature):** Ireland conducted national censuses in 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, and 1871. The 1821–1851 census returns were largely destroyed — most in the 1922 fire at the Four Courts in Dublin; some 1861 and 1871 returns were destroyed by government order. The 1901 and 1911 censuses survive intact and are freely searchable online (National Archives of Ireland: https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie), but these fall after the 1870 survey period. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki article on Ireland Census directly to confirm survival details by year.
- **Census substitutes for 1780–1870:**
  - Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837): surveyed all land occupiers paying tithes, county by county. County Antrim volumes exist; searchable online via the National Archives of Ireland (see Repositories below).
  - Griffith's Primary Valuation (c. 1847–1864 in Antrim): enumerated all occupiers of property and their landlords. County Antrim was covered. Freely searchable at https://www.askaboutireland.ie and https://www.irishlandrecords.com.
  - 1851–1901 census fragments: some heads-of-household returns extracted from the 1901/1911 census, and some 1841/1851 fragments survive.
  - Note: The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are the closest the researcher will get to a census substitute for Billy parish in 1780–1870. Both are searchable online. Neither lists household members systematically — they list the occupier only.

### Probate and court records

The FamilySearch wiki tools did not return the Ireland Probate Records page in this session. Repository details cannot be confirmed from tool output. Wills and administrations for County Antrim in 1780–1870 were proved before the ecclesiastical courts of the diocese (the diocese of Connor covers this area of Antrim) before 1858, and after 1858 before the civil District Probate Registry. The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the great majority of pre-1858 original wills. Will abstracts and calendars survive at PRONI and at the National Archives of Ireland. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki article "Ireland Probate Records" at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Irish townland system with landlord and tenant structure — no rectangular survey as in the US federal system.
- **Key collections (per their well-documented existence, not confirmed by tool this session):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** Held at the National Archives of Ireland and PRONI; digitized and freely searchable at https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie.

  - **Registry of Deeds, Dublin:** Memorials of deeds recorded from 1708 onward are held at the Registry of Deeds, Dublin; searchable by name index.
  - **PRONI estate papers:** Many landed estates in County Antrim deposited their papers (leases, rent rolls, maps, correspondence) at PRONI; the eCatalogue lists them by estate name.
- **The FamilySearch wiki tools did not return the Ireland Land and Property page in this session**. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records

For 1780–1870, relevant conflicts include the 1798 United Irishmen rebellion, the Napoleonic Wars, and mid-century service in the British Army. Service records for British Army soldiers of this period are held at The National Archives (UK), Kew, and are partially available via Findmypast and Ancestry. The FamilySearch wiki tools did not return Ireland Military Records content this session.

### Cemetery records

The Billy Civil Parish wiki page returned by tools did not include cemetery information in the chunks retrieved. County Antrim graveyard surveys have been compiled by local societies; the Association for Scottish and Irish Studies and local historical societies hold some transcriptions. FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some County Antrim entries. The Irish Graveyards project at the National Monuments Service (Ireland) covers some sites.

### Newspaper records

The most relevant 19th-century newspapers for the Bushmills/north Antrim area include the *Coleraine Chronicle* (founded 1844) and the *Ballymoney Free Press*. The British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription) holds many Ulster titles digitized. The Newspaper Library at the Linen Hall Library, Belfast also holds physical and microfilm runs.

### Immigration/emigration records

The north Antrim coast was a significant source of emigration to North America, particularly to ports in Pennsylvania, South Carolina, and later Canada, across 1780–1870. Passenger lists for sailings from Belfast, Londonderry (Derry), and Liverpool are the prime sources. They are held at NARA (for US arrivals) and partially indexed at Ancestry, FamilySearch, and the Ellis Island Foundation database. Naturalizations filed in US courts and Declaration of Intention papers may name the county or parish of birth. The Linen Hall Library and PRONI both hold emigration-related records for Ulster.

- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family's emigration, examine the full manifest for all family members — children may be listed under a parent's entry.

### Tax records

The Tithe Applotment Books (see Land records) function as the main tax-based name list for Billy parish c. 1823–1837. Grand Jury presentments and cess records (county tax levied for road repair and public works) were kept by the Grand Jury of County Antrim and are held at PRONI. These rarely list ordinary farmers but do record some householders who provided labor or materials.

### Other record types

- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** The Ordnance Survey of Ireland compiled detailed parish memoirs for Ulster in the 1830s, describing townlands, population, economy, religious denominations, and local conditions. The Billy parish memoir would be held at the Royal Irish Academy, Dublin, and has been published by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast. These are essential background context for understanding Billy parish in the 1830s.
- **Flaxseed Premium Returns (1796):** A government survey listing those in Ulster who received a grant for planting flax; names householders by townland. County Antrim is covered. Available at PRONI and transcribed by Ulster Historical Foundation.
- **School records:** National Schools were established in Ireland from 1831. Some school registers survive at PRONI.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Baronies:** Lower Dunluce (chiefly) and Carey
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **County:** Antrim | **Province:** Ulster
- **Post town:** Bushmills (within the parish)
- **Denominations present:** Presbyterian, Covenanter/Reformed Presbyterian, Wesleyan Methodist, Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic

Billy was the head of a Church of Ireland ecclesiastical union also comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. In the Roman Catholic structure, the territory falls within the Coleraine district.

---

## Vital Records

Before 1864, **there were no civil vital records in Ireland**. Civil registration of births, deaths, and all marriages began 1 January 1864. For a family with a member born around 1825 in Billy parish, the parents' events fall entirely in the pre-civil-registration era and will only appear in church registers.

- **Post-1864 civil records:** Indexed and browsable free at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie); originals at the General Register Office (GRO), Dublin; microfilm copies at PRONI, Belfast. The likely civil registration district is **Coleraine** (matching the poor law union).

---

## Church Records — Presbyterian Family Focus

**Presbyterian is the primary denomination for your research.** The principal congregations serving Bushmills in this era were:

- **First Bushmills Presbyterian Church** (the main Bushmills congregation)
- **Dunluce Presbyterian Church** (nearby, also serving this territory)
- **Covenanter / Reformed Presbyterian congregation** (a separate body)

### Where Presbyterian Registers Are Held

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) | Most County Antrim Presbyterian registers on microfilm — **MIC 1P series**; many now digitized online | Free online; in-person |
| **FamilySearch Library** | Microfilm copies for many County Antrim Presbyterian congregations — search the FamilySearch Catalog by place "Antrim, Ireland" + record type "Church Records" | Free |
| **Local congregation** | Original registers may remain with First Bushmills Presbyterian Church | Contact directly |

Search PRONI's eCatalogue for "Bushmills Presbyterian" and "Dunluce Presbyterian" to find the relevant MIC 1P film numbers. Register start dates vary by congregation — check the [Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records) for confirmed start dates.

### Other Denominations

- **Church of Ireland:** Billy was head of a union covering several parishes. CoI registers are largely at PRONI (many originals destroyed in the 1922 Dublin Public Record Office fire). Also on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Roman Catholic:** Falls under the RC district of Coleraine. Registers typically begin early-to-mid 19th century; indexed transcripts at [Roots Ireland](https://www.rootsireland.ie) (Ulster Historical Foundation).
- **Wesleyan Methodist:** Held partly at PRONI and partly at the Methodist Historical Society of Ireland, Edgehill College, Belfast.

---

## Census Records

| Census | Status |
|---|---|
| 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851 | Largely destroyed in the 1922 Dublin fire; 1841/1851 fragments survive at NAI (pension claims) |
| 1861, 1871 | Destroyed by government order — do not exist |
| 1901, 1911 | Fully surviving online at [census.nationalarchives.ie](https://census.nationalarchives.ie) |

For the 1780–1870 target window, use the land-record substitutes below.

---

## Land Records (Census Substitutes)

These are the two indispensable population-level substitutes for the destroyed census records:

1. **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1825–1832):** Lists landholder households by townland across all of Billy parish — nearly contemporaneous with your 1825 birth. Fully indexed and free at [titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie](https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie) and on FamilySearch. **Start here to place the family in a specific Billy townland.**

2. **Griffith's Primary Valuation (c. 1858–1860 for County Antrim):** Lists every landowner and occupier in Ireland by townland. Free on [AskAboutIreland](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/); also on Ancestry and FindMyPast. Cross-reference with Tithe to track families across ~30 years.

**Also useful:**
- **Flaxseed Premiums (1796):** Lists County Antrim householders who received spinning wheels/looms — a significant pre-1800 population record; at PRONI and in print.
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Land transactions; well-represented for Protestant landowners.
- **Valuation Office revision books:** Post-Griffith tenancy changes, year by year; at the Valuation Office, Dublin.
- **Estate papers:** Much of the Bushmills coastal area was under large landlord estates; estate rentals and lease books at PRONI can name tenants found nowhere else.

**Important:** Billy parish straddles two baronies — **Lower Dunluce** and **Carey**. Search both in any barony-level index.

---

## Probate Records

- **Before 1858:** Prerogative Court of Armagh (above threshold) and Consistorial Court of Connor (County Antrim, below threshold). Both series largely destroyed in 1922. Surviving abstracts and indexes at NAI and PRONI.
- **From 1858:** District probate registries; County Antrim falls under the **Londonderry (Derry) District Probate Registry**. Post-1858 annual grant calendars survive intact at PRONI and NAI.

---

## Military Records

- **British Army service records:** National Archives, Kew (WO 97 series); on FindMyPast and Ancestry.
- **County Antrim Militia and Yeomanry:** Muster rolls at PRONI.
- **1798 Rebellion:** Rebel lists, prisoner records, compensation claims at NAI and PRONI.

---

## Newspapers

| Title | Dates | Coverage | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Belfast Newsletter | Est. 1737 | Full period; principal Ulster paper | PRONI microfilm; British Newspaper Archive (subscription); Linen Hall Library |
| Coleraine Chronicle | Est. 1844 | Closest local paper to Bushmills | PRONI microfilm; British Newspaper Archive |
| Derry Journal / Northern Whig | Various | County Antrim notices | PRONI |

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Presbyterian (MIC 1P), CoI registers; estate papers; court records; valuation records | Free online; in-person |
| **National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin** | Tithe Books; will abstracts; 1901/1911 census | Free online for key series |
| **General Register Office (GRO), Dublin** | Civil registration originals from 1864 | IrishGenealogy.ie (free) |
| **The National Archives, Kew** | British Army service and pension records | In-person; partner sites |
| **Linen Hall Library, Belfast** | Belfast Newsletter pre-1800; genealogical reference | In-person |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation** | Indexed RC register transcripts (Roots Ireland) | rootsireland.ie |

---

## Key Gaps and Losses

- **1922 fire:** Destroyed most pre-1858 Irish probate records and the bulk of the 1821–1851 census returns — a fundamental gap for all County Antrim research in this period.
- **Census 1861 and 1871:** Destroyed by government order; no substitute exists.
- **Pre-1864 vital events depend entirely on church registers** — if no register survives for the relevant congregation, the event may be unrecoverable.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence for a c. 1825 Billy Parish Presbyterian Family

1. **Search PRONI's MIC 1P series** for First Bushmills Presbyterian and Dunluce Presbyterian registers — identify register start dates and search for the family's baptism and marriage records.
2. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1825–1832)** to place the father in a specific Billy townland around the birth year.
3. **Search Griffith's Valuation (c. 1858–1860)** in the same townland to track the family 30 years later and identify adult children still in place.
4. **Work backward from 1901/1911 census** at census.nationalarchives.ie to identify any surviving elderly family members who can anchor the earlier generation.
5. **Search the Belfast Newsletter and Coleraine Chronicle** for marriage and death notices.
6. **Check PRONI estate papers** for the relevant Antrim Coast landlord for tenant lists that might name the family.
