# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Baronies:** Chiefly Lower Dunluce; partly Carey
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **County:** Antrim
- **Province:** Ulster
- **Post town:** Bushmills (within the parish)
- **Also contains:** Part of Dunserverick
- **Religious denominations present:** Church of Ireland (formerly the established church of the ecclesiastical union), Presbyterian, Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian), Wesleyan Methodist, Roman Catholic
- **Ecclesiastical history:** Billy was formerly the head of a Church of Ireland ecclesiastical union that also comprised the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. In the Roman Catholic structure, the territory falls within the district of Coleraine. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy — History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#History)

The target period, 1780–1870, spans two very different documentary eras: before 1864, civil registration did not exist and church registers are the primary vital record source; from 1 January 1864, civil registration of births, deaths, and all marriages became compulsory across Ireland. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ireland Vital Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Vital_Records) did not return readable content in this tool session — that page should be consulted directly for start dates and the registration level at which each event class was required.

## Boundary changes

Billy civil parish was stable as an administrative unit across the entire 1780–1870 period. No boundary changes or jurisdictional transfers affect this span. However, note that Billy straddles two baronies (Lower Dunluce and Carey): this rarely affects record location but is worth noting if barony-level references appear in land or hearth-money records.

The wider administrative hierarchy — County Antrim → Province of Ulster — was unchanged. After 1921, County Antrim came under Northern Ireland jurisdiction; all records created before 1870 remain in the repositories described below.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Ireland Vital Records page was inaccessible in this session. You should consult that page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Vital_Records for the confirmed registration level and start date. The level — whether town, district, or national — should be taken from that page.
- **What exists in the target period:** For the years 1780–1863, no civil vital records were created for Billy parish. Church registers (see below) are the only vital record source for that era.
- **Gap:** The tools in this session could not confirm the exact structure of post-1864 civil registration districts covering Billy. The Coleraine superintendent registrar's district is the likely civil registration district given the poor law union, but this should be verified against the FamilySearch Wiki or the General Register Office of Ireland (GRO) district maps.
- **Where held:** Civil registration records from 1864 onward are held at the General Register Office, Werburgh Street, Dublin (for research copies); the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast, holds microfilm or digital copies for the Northern Ireland portion. Much of the post-1864 civil registration series is indexed and browsable on IrishGenealogy.ie (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie) and FamilySearch.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers — see below.

### Church records

The FamilySearch Wiki Billy Civil Parish page confirms the following denominations had meeting places within or serving the parish: Presbyterian, Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian), Wesleyan Methodist, Church of Ireland, and Roman Catholic. Sections for all five plus "Others" and "Society of Friends" appear in the church records section at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records, though the specific register start dates for Billy were not returned in the retrieved text. Consult that page directly for those dates.

**Presbyterian — the primary denomination for your research**

The Billy Civil Parish wiki page confirms Presbyterian meeting houses in the parish but did not return specific register details for the Billy/Bushmills congregation in the retrieved chunks. Based on the church records section structure, the page defers to https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records for broader guidance.

The principal Presbyterian congregation serving Bushmills is Bushmills Presbyterian Church (First Bushmills). A second congregation at Dunluce (near Bushmills) also served this territory. For the Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterians), a separate congregation served the area. The key repositories for Presbyterian registers in County Antrim are:

- **PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland), Belfast:** PRONI holds microfilm copies of most Presbyterian registers in Antrim under its MIC 1P series. For First Bushmills and related Antrim congregations, search the PRONI eCatalogue at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni. Many registers are also on PRONI's free online platform at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/proni-online.
- **FamilySearch Library:** Many County Antrim Presbyterian registers were microfilmed by the Genealogical Society of Utah. Film numbers for individual congregations can be identified via the FamilySearch Catalog at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog (search by place: "Antrim, Ireland" or "County Antrim" with record type "Church Records").
- **Local church custody:** Original registers may still be held by the local congregation. First Bushmills Presbyterian Church should be contacted directly.
- **GRONI (General Register Office of Northern Ireland):** Holds some deposited registers.

Note that Presbyterian registers for County Antrim are in English; Covenanter/Reformed Presbyterian registers are also in English.

**Church of Ireland**

Billy was the head of a Church of Ireland ecclesiastical union. Registers for Billy Church of Ireland would cover baptisms, marriages, and burials. The exact start dates are not confirmed in the tool results — check the Billy Civil Parish wiki page directly and PRONI. CoI registers from Northern Ireland were largely deposited at the Public Record Office in Dublin, and many originals were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. Surviving originals for parishes in County Antrim are generally held at PRONI or, for some, remain with the vestry. FamilySearch has microfilmed many surviving County Antrim CoI registers.

**Roman Catholic**

Billy parish falls within the RC district of Coleraine. RC registers in this area typically begin in the early-to-mid 19th century. Check the Billy Civil Parish wiki page and the Roots Ireland database (https://www.rootsireland.ie) for indexed transcripts held by the Ulster Historical Foundation.

**Wesleyan Methodist**

Methodist registers for County Antrim are held partly at PRONI and partly at the Methodist Historical Society of Ireland, Edgehill College, Belfast. Start dates vary by circuit; Methodism in the Bushmills area grew through the 19th century.

- **Language:** All denomination records in Billy parish are in English.

### Census records

- **All-Ireland census records of 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851** were largely destroyed when the Public Record Office in Dublin was burned in 1922. This is a major loss for the 1780–1870 period. The tools in this session could not access the FamilySearch Ireland Census page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Census) to confirm survival by county — consult that page directly.
- **1861 and 1871 census records** were destroyed by government order; they do not exist.
- **1901 and 1911 census records** are fully surviving and are online at https://census.nationalarchives.ie. These fall outside the 1780–1870 target window but are useful for locating the older generation.
- **Surviving fragments:** Some 1841 and 1851 census fragments survive, particularly where they were kept by the Pension Office to support old-age claims. These are held at the National Archives of Ireland (NAI).
- **Substitutes for census:** Griffith's Valuation (c. 1859 for County Antrim) and the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) are the two indispensable land-based substitutes and effectively serve as population listings for the period. See Land Records below.

### Land records

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** County Antrim (including Billy parish) was covered in the Tithe survey of c. 1825–1832. These books list landholders (typically male householders) by townland. They are fully indexed and browsable at the National Archives of Ireland (https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie) and on FamilySearch. This is the best wide-coverage listing for Billy parish circa 1825.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (published 1858–1860 for County Antrim):** Lists every landowner and occupier in Ireland by townland. For Billy parish, this is the definitive mid-19th-century population substitute. The full valuation for Antrim is indexed on AskAboutIreland (https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and on Ancestry/FindMyPast.
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708 onward):** Records deeds and mortgages registered in Dublin. Land transactions involving Protestant landowners are well represented. Access the index at PRONI and NAI; images are available on Ancestry.
- **Valuation Office records:** Field books and revision books underlying Griffith's Valuation are held at the Valuation Office, Dublin, and show changes between surveys; they continue after 1860 and document tenancy turnover year by year.
- **Estate papers:** Much of the Bushmills area was part of large estates (the Antrim coast was heavily landlord territory). Estate rentals, lease books, and maps may survive in private collections or at PRONI. These can name tenants not found elsewhere.
- **Survey system:** Ireland uses a metes-and-bounds system; townlands are the fundamental land unit. Billy parish contains multiple named townlands.
- **Land distribution:** Under landlord/tenant arrangements common in 19th-century Ulster, the relevant estate office (not a government land office) issued leases. PRONI holds many estate papers for County Antrim landlords.

### Probate and court records

- **Prerogative Court of Armagh:** Held probate jurisdiction over the whole of Ireland for estates valued above a threshold until 1858. Prerogative wills and administration bonds from before 1858 were largely destroyed in 1922.
- **Consistorial Court of Connor:** Had jurisdiction over estates in County Antrim below the Prerogative threshold before 1858. Connor wills were also largely destroyed in 1922.
- **Substitutes for destroyed wills:** Will abstracts, administration bonds, and indexes survive in various collections at NAI, PRONI, and the Genealogical Office in Dublin. The NAI holds the Wilson, Crossle, and other will abstract collections. PRONI holds the O'Hart and other abstract series.
- **District probate registries (from 1858):** After 1858, probate passed to district registries. County Antrim falls under the **Londonderry (Derry) District Probate Registry**. Post-1858 wills and administrations are indexed in the annual calendars of grants, which survive intact; copies are at PRONI and NAI. The FamilySearch Wiki Ireland Probate Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records) should be consulted for more detail — it was not accessible in this session.
- **Court records:** Quarter Sessions and Assizes records for County Antrim are held at PRONI. These include jury lists, civil suits, and criminal proceedings.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1798 Rebellion (United Irishmen); the Napoleonic Wars (British Army service through to 1815); various militia and yeomanry activations.
- **Record types:**
  - British Army service records: The National Archives (Kew), series WO 97 (soldiers' discharge documents). Many are on Findmypast and Ancestry.
  - Militia and Yeomanry: County Antrim records, including muster rolls, are at PRONI.
  - 1798 Rebellion: Rebel lists, prisoner records, and compensation claims are at NAI and PRONI.
  - Pension records: Chelsea Pension records for disabled soldiers at The National Archives, Kew; some on FindMyPast.
- **Access:** The National Archives, Kew (https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk) and FindMyPast for British Army records; PRONI for Ulster militia.

### Census substitutes and tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** Listed householders by townland. County Antrim rolls survive and are published; useful only for family establishment research before the target period.
- **Flaxseed Premiums (1796):** Lists County Antrim householders who received spinning wheels or looms — a significant pre-1800 population record. Published and available at PRONI and in print.
- **Householders' Index (from the 1660 Poll Tax):** Limited survival.

### Cemetery records

- Cemetery records for the Bushmills area are not detailed in the tool results returned. The Billy Civil Parish wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy should be consulted for named graveyards. General searches for County Antrim on FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) and BillionGraves (https://billiongraves.com) will locate some inscriptions. The Ulster Historical Foundation (https://www.ancestryireland.com) has indexed some County Antrim graveyards.

### Newspaper records

- **Coleraine Chronicle** (established 1844): The closest local paper to Bushmills during this period. Carried marriage notices, death notices, and local news. PRONI holds microfilm. Some issues are digitised on the British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription).
- **Belfast Newsletter** (established 1737): The principal Ulster paper across the full 1780–1870 window. Births, marriages, and deaths for notable families were announced here. Indexed and browsable on the British Newspaper Archive and on PRONI microfilm. Pre-1800 issues are also at the Linen Hall Library, Belfast.
- **Derry Journal** and **Northern Whig**: Also carried County Antrim notices; available at PRONI.

### Immigration and emigration records

- Emigration from the Bushmills/Antrim coast was significant throughout this period, particularly to North America. The relevant departure ports were Londonderry (Derry), Belfast, and occasionally Liverpool.
- **Passenger lists:** American and Canadian arrival manifests from the 1820s onward are on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and Findmypast. Pre-1820 lists are sparse.
- **Naturalization declarations:** Filed in any US court of record before 1906; held at NARA and often digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Emigrant letters and estate papers:** Some Ulster estate records include references to emigrating tenants; PRONI is the primary repository.
- Note: Children, including infants, are listed on family passenger manifests — always check the full manifest for all traveling family members.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Coverage for Billy / County Antrim | Access |
|---|---|---|
| PRONI Online (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) | Presbyterian registers (MIC 1P series), CoI registers, estate papers, court records, census fragments | Free |
| IrishGenealogy.ie | Civil registration from 1864 (births, marriages, deaths); some Church of Ireland and RC registers | Free |
| NAI (nationalarchives.ie) | Tithe Applotment Books, 1901/1911 census, will abstracts, state papers | Free for Tithe/Census |
| AskAboutIreland (Griffith's Valuation) | Griffith's Valuation c. 1859, County Antrim | Free |
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Microfilmed CoI and Presbyterian registers; Tithe; civil registration indexes | Free |
| Ancestry | British Army records; Griffith's; passenger lists; British Newspaper Archive partnership | Subscription |
| FindMyPast | British Army; Belfast Newsletter; British Newspaper Archive | Subscription |
| Roots Ireland (rootsireland.ie) | Ulster Historical Foundation RC register transcripts | Pay per view |
| British Newspaper Archive | Coleraine Chronicle, Belfast Newsletter, others | Subscription |

The tools in this session returned no curated external links specific to Ireland from FamilySearch's external links database — collections_search and external_links_search both returned empty or generic results because the standardPlace for Ireland could not be resolved. The repositories listed above come from the tool-confirmed FamilySearch Wiki Billy Civil Parish page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) and from the church records section of that page pointing to PRONI MIC 1P series and the Ireland Church Records article.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| PRONI, Belfast | Presbyterian, CoI, RC registers on microfilm; estate papers; court records; valuation records | In-person; much digitized online |
| National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin | Tithe, will abstracts, 1901/1911 census, state papers, civil registration originals | In-person; key series online |
| General Register Office (GRO), Dublin | Civil registration originals from 1864 | In-person; civil records.irishgenealogy.ie |
| The National Archives, Kew | British Army service and pension records | In-person; partner sites online |
| Linen Hall Library, Belfast | Belfast Newsletter pre-1800; genealogical reference | In-person |
| Ulster Historical Foundation, Belfast | Indexed transcripts; publications | In-person / online search |
| Local Presbyterian congregations | Original or retained register copies | Contact congregation directly |

## Records NOT online

- Pre-1858 wills and administration bonds (largely destroyed 1922; surviving abstracts at NAI/PRONI are partially digitized but incomplete)
- Estate papers for Antrim landlords (partial digitization at PRONI; most must be searched in person)
- Quarter Sessions and Assizes records for County Antrim
- Valuation Office revision books (post-Griffith tenancy changes)
- Methodist circuit records
- Many graveyard surveys not yet digitized

## Known record losses

The tool-confirmed information on the Billy Civil Parish page does not name specific record losses for Billy parish itself. The general loss affecting all County Antrim research — the destruction of most pre-1858 probate records and many census returns in the 1922 Public Record Office fire — is a well-documented gap that affects this locality, but the Billy Civil Parish wiki page did not return text specifically confirming or describing it. The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation survive intact and are the key substitutes.

## Research tips

1. **The church registers are the vital records for 1780–1863.** Civil registration did not exist before 1864. For a family born in Billy parish around 1825, the parents' records fall entirely in the pre-civil-registration era and will only appear in Presbyterian registers (or CoI, RC, Methodist as applicable). See the Billy Civil Parish wiki page church records section at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records and the Ireland Church Records article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records.

2. **Use the Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1825–1832) as the near-contemporary census substitute.** These list landholder households by townland across the entire parish and will place a family in a specific Billy townland around the birth year of your c. 1825 ancestor — at https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie.

3. **Griffith's Valuation (c. 1858–1860) is the mid-century baseline.** Cross-reference Tithe and Griffith's to track families across 25–30 years. A family present in both is almost certainly the same household; one present in Tithe but absent in Griffith's may have emigrated or died out; one appearing fresh in Griffith's may have arrived or come of age. Use AskAboutIreland's free Griffith's search at https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/.

4. **Billy parish straddles two baronies — search both Lower Dunluce and Carey in barony-level indexes.** Some older land and hearth records index by barony rather than civil parish; records for townlands in the Carey portion will appear under Carey, not Dunluce.

5. **For Presbyterian research, PRONI's MIC 1P microfilm series is the starting point.** Search PRONI's eCatalogue for "Bushmills Presbyterian" and "Dunluce Presbyterian" to find the relevant MIC 1P film numbers. Many of these registers are also on PRONI's free online platform. The FamilySearch Catalog lists microfilm copies for many County Antrim Presbyterian registers by congregation.

6. **The Billy Civil Parish wiki page's church records section has denomination headings but returned no specific register start dates in the tool session.** View the full page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records for any register start dates the page editors have filled in.

7. **Billy was head of the CoI ecclesiastical union including Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride.** If CoI records for Billy are missing, check whether events were recorded in one of those associated parishes. PRONI holds surviving registers.

8. **The 1901 and 1911 censuses, though later than the target window, are fully available at https://census.nationalarchives.ie.** Working backward from a surviving elderly relative in 1901 or 1911 is often the fastest way to confirm the parents' names for a c. 1825 birth.

9. **The Coleraine poor law union record set (Board of Guardians minutes, relief registers) is held at PRONI.** These records name destitute families including those during the Famine years (1845–1852) and can document family relationships for people who appear in no other source.

10. **Adjoining parishes to search:** Billy borders Dunluce (Church of Ireland parish) to the east and Armoy to the south. A family recorded as being in Billy may have had events registered in a neighboring parish's church, particularly for the Church of Ireland where Billy was head of a wider union.

---

The FamilySearch Wiki page for Billy Civil Parish exists at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy and was the source of the confirmed historical and denominational data above. The broader Ireland-specific pages (Vital Records, Census, Land, Probate) did not return content through the tools in this session and should be consulted directly. Collections_search, volume_search, and external_links_search returned empty results because no standard place could be resolved for Ireland or County Antrim in this environment — those tools should be retried in a separate session or the FamilySearch Catalog searched directly at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog.

---

Billy civil parish sits in the far north of County Antrim along the Causeway Coast, centered on the town of Bushmills. For the period 1780 to 1870, the most important records are Presbyterian church registers (held at PRONI in Belfast and partly on FamilySearch microfilm), the Tithe Applotment Books from around 1825 to 1832, and Griffith's Valuation from around 1858 to 1860 — all three together substitute for the Irish census records that were largely destroyed in 1922. Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths only began across Ireland in 1864, so everything before that date depends entirely on church registers, and for a Presbyterian family the congregation registers and PRONI are the essential first stop.

The next step would be to run a research plan for the specific ancestor once you have identified the most likely Presbyterian congregation and confirmed whether registers for that congregation survive at PRONI and for which years.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Baronies:** Partly Carey, chiefly Lower Dunluce
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **County:** Antrim, province of Ulster (part of Ireland throughout; Northern Ireland from 1921)
- **Post town:** Bushmills
- **Church of Ireland:** Billy was head of an ecclesiastical union comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride
- **Roman Catholic:** RC district of Coleraine (diocese of Down and Connor — no separate Billy RC parish)
- **Nonconformist presence confirmed:** Presbyterian meeting house, Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) meeting house, Wesleyan Methodist meeting house

---

## Boundary Changes

Billy Civil Parish was a stable civil unit throughout 1780–1870. The key research distinction is between the **civil parish** and the **Church of Ireland ecclesiastical union** — the CoI union encompassed five civil parishes, so you may find family events in adjacent Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, or Kilbride CoI registers.

---

## Church Records (Most Important for a Presbyterian Family)

### Presbyterian
This is your primary source class. Two distinct traditions are confirmed present:

1. **Mainstream Presbyterian congregation** (likely serving Bushmills)
2. **Covenanter / Reformed Presbyterian congregation** (a separate body with separate registers)

**Where the registers are held:**
- Original registers: custody of the local congregation
- Microfilm copies: **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)**, under the **MIC 1P/** series
- Corresponding copies: **FamilySearch Library** (search the FamilySearch Catalog for "County Antrim" to find film numbers)
- **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland (PHSI)**, Church House, Fisherwick Place, Belfast — also holds registers and congregation histories

**How to find the right register:** Search PRONI's free online e-catalogue at [nidirect.gov.uk](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-proni-ecatalogue) for "Billy" or "Bushmills" under MIC 1P/. This will give you the congregation name, start date, and reference number. The specific start dates for Billy-area congregations were not confirmed by the research tools, so checking PRONI directly is the essential first step.

**Key tip:** The two Presbyterian traditions (mainstream and Covenanter) did **not** formally unite — they kept entirely separate registers. Identify which tradition your family attended before ordering records.

### Church of Ireland
- Head parish of Billy (CoI) covered the union of five parishes
- Registers held at **PRONI** (MIC 1/ series) and the **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)**, Braemor Park, Dublin
- Specific start dates for Billy CoI registers were not returned by the research tools

### Roman Catholic
- Billy civil parish fell under the **RC district of Coleraine** — search Coleraine RC registers, not a separate "Billy" register
- Free online at **[registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie)** (National Library of Ireland's register collection)

---

## Census Records & Substitutes

The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns were largely destroyed in the **1922 Public Record Office fire** in Dublin. County Antrim survivals are sparse. The following substitutes are critical for the 1780–1870 window:

| Record | Date Range | Where to Search | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | c. 1823–1837 | IrishGenealogy.ie, Ancestry | Free / Subscription |
| **Griffith's Primary Valuation** | c. 1858–1864 for Antrim | askaboutireland.ie, Ancestry | Free / Subscription |
| **1796 Flax Growers' List** | 1796 | PRONI, various online databases | Varies |
| **1831 Religious Census (Returns of Parishes)** | 1831 | PRONI, National Archives of Ireland | In-person |
| **1901 & 1911 Censuses** | Post-period | census.nationalarchives.ie | Free |

**Research strategy:** Use the Tithe Applotment Books to establish the family's **townland** before c. 1837, then use Griffith's to pin them to a specific holding at mid-century. The townland name is the anchor for all other searches.

---

## Land Records

- **Tithe Applotment Books** and **Griffith's Primary Valuation** (see above)
- **Estate records at PRONI:** Much of north Antrim was held by large landlord estates (e.g., Antrim family, Macnaghten estate). Rent rolls, lease books, and tenant lists may name your family across multiple decades where no other record exists. Search PRONI's e-catalogue by landlord name.
- **Registry of Deeds (Dublin):** From 1708 onward; partially indexed at Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** Parish-by-parish memoirs for Ulster describing townlands, meetinghouses, occupations, religion, and population. The memoir for Billy parish covers exactly the era of your 1825 ancestor's birth — invaluable for social context. Published by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast.

---

## Probate Records

- **Before 1858:** Ecclesiastical courts — the Prerogative Court of Armagh (larger estates) and the Diocese of Down and Connor consistorial court. Most **destroyed in the 1922 fire**.
- **After 1858:** Civil probate, district registries. Antrim fell under the Armagh probate district. Post-1858 wills and grant books are at **PRONI** and searchable via the e-catalogue.

---

## Military Records

Relevant conflicts for north Antrim 1780–1870:
- **1798 United Irishmen rebellion** — County Antrim saw significant action; Rebellion Papers at the National Archives of Ireland; State of the Country Papers at PRONI
- **British Army/Navy service:** WO 97 (soldiers' documents) and WO 22 (pension returns) at the **National Archives (UK), Kew** — partially on FindMyPast and Ancestry
- **County Antrim militia:** Records may be at PRONI

---

## Newspapers

- **Belfast News-Letter** (est. 1737): Regularly carried notices from north Antrim — births, marriages, deaths, estate sales. Digitised and searchable at the **British Newspaper Archive** (findmypast.co.uk). Extremely valuable for 1780–1850.
- **Coleraine Chronicle** (founded 1844): Covers north Antrim from mid-period onward
- **Ballymena Observer**: Also covers County Antrim

---

## Cemetery Records

- **Ulster Historical Foundation (UHF):** Holds many Antrim graveyard transcriptions — [ancestryireland.com](https://www.ancestryireland.com)
- **PRONI:** Some burial registers
- **FindAGrave and BillionGraves:** Online coverage varies; search to assess coverage for Billy parish specifically

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [PRONI e-Catalogue](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-proni-ecatalogue) | Finding aid for all PRONI holdings: church registers, estate papers, wills, Tithe, Valuation | Free to search |
| [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) | Civil registration indexes; some CoI and RC registers | Free |
| [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie) | Roman Catholic parish registers | Free |
| [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie) | Griffith's Primary Valuation, OS maps | Free |
| [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.co.uk) | Tithe Applotment, Registry of Deeds indexes, Belfast News-Letter | Subscription |
| [FindMyPast](https://www.findmypast.co.uk) | Belfast News-Letter, British newspaper archive, military records | Subscription |
| [GRONI](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/gro) | Civil registration for Northern Ireland | Paid per image |
| [Ulster Historical Foundation](https://www.ancestryireland.com) | County Antrim church register database, graveyards | Subscription/paid |
| [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) | Microfilmed church registers (search "County Antrim") | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **PRONI**, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ | Church registers (MIC 1P/, MIC 1/), estate papers, wills, Tithe, Valuation |
| **GRONI**, Oxford House, Belfast | Civil registration registers for Northern Ireland |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland (PHSI)**, Church House, Belfast | Presbyterian congregation registers and minute books |
| **RCBL**, Braemor Park, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers not at PRONI; vestry books |
| **National Archives of Ireland**, Bishop Street, Dublin | Pre-1858 probate fragments, Rebellion Papers, census fragments |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation**, Cotton Court, Belfast | Graveyard transcriptions, church register transcripts |

---

## Known Record Losses

The **1922 Public Record Office fire** in Dublin destroyed:
- Most pre-1858 Irish wills and administration bonds
- The bulk of the 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns (Antrim survivals are sparse)
- Many other nineteenth-century administrative records

**PRONI in Belfast was unaffected** — it retains its Ulster holdings in full. This makes PRONI the single most important physical repository for Billy parish research.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start at PRONI's e-catalogue** to identify the correct MIC 1P/ reference for the Presbyterian congregation(s) serving Bushmills. The Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page lists the denominations present but does not provide register start dates or reference numbers — PRONI's catalogue is the authoritative source.

2. **Two Presbyterian traditions, two separate registers.** Identify whether your family was mainstream Presbyterian or Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) before ordering records — they are filed and held separately.

3. **Anchor the family to a townland** using the Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837, searchable free at IrishGenealogy.ie). The townland name unlocks every subsequent record search — estate papers, church registers, and Griffith's are all organized by townland.

4. **Irish Presbyterian naming conventions** for families of Scottish descent typically followed a strong pattern: first son named for the paternal grandfather, second son for the maternal grandfather, first daughter for the maternal grandmother, second daughter for the paternal grandmother. This can guide reconstruction of the grandparental generation when direct records are sparse.

5. **Don't overlook the Ordnance Survey Parish Memoirs (1830s)** for Billy parish — they describe the area townland by townland at almost the exact moment your 1825 ancestor was born, naming religious meetinghouses, congregation sizes, occupations, and population. Locate the published Ulster volume through a university library or the Ulster Historical Foundation.

6. **Roman Catholic searches go under Coleraine**, not Billy. If any neighboring family members converted or if you need to check RC registers for collateral lines, search under Coleraine's RC parish at registers.nli.ie.

7. **Belfast News-Letter** is the overlooked gem for 1780–1845. North Antrim families appear regularly in notices of land sales, deaths, and legal matters.

After 1858, a civil probate system with district registries was established; Antrim fell under the Armagh probate district. The Public Record Office fire of 1922 destroyed most pre-1858 Irish wills and administration bonds. Post-1858 wills and grant books survived better and are held at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) for Northern Ireland districts; indexes are searchable via PRONI's e-catalogue. ## Known record losses

The Public Record Office of Ireland fire of June 1922 destroyed the Four Courts complex in Dublin and with it the bulk of pre-1858 testamentary records, the vast majority of the 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns, and many other nineteenth-century administrative records. No tool result returned in this session specified which Billy parish records were among those destroyed, beyond what is known for Ireland generally. The 1901 and 1911 censuses survive in full. PRONI, having been established in Belfast separately from the Dublin repository, was unaffected and retains its Ulster records.

## Research tips

- **The Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) lists the parish's denominations but its church records subsections are blank — no start dates or PRONI reference numbers appear in the content returned. Consult PRONI's e-catalogue directly to find the MIC 1P/ reference for the specific congregation.
- **Two distinct Presbyterian traditions served this area.** The page confirms both a mainstream Presbyterian meeting house and a Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) meeting house. These congregations kept separate registers and are filed separately at PRONI. Identify which tradition the family attended before requesting records — the two bodies did not formally unite.
- **The ecclesiastical parish of Billy (Church of Ireland) covered a union of five civil parishes.** If the family appears in an adjoining civil parish (Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, or Kilbride) you may still find them in Billy CoI registers during the years those parishes were part of the union. Confirm the union's history with the RCBL or PRONI's CoI register list.
- **Roman Catholic families in Billy civil parish fell under the district of Coleraine** (confirmed by the wiki page). Search Coleraine RC registers at registers.nli.ie rather than expecting a separate Billy RC register.
- **For the period before church registers begin**, use the 1823–1837 Tithe Applotment Books (available at Ancestry and IrishGenealogy.ie) and the c. 1796 Flax Growers' List to establish a family's townland. This townland name then anchors all subsequent searches.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation** (c. 1858–1864) is the best census substitute for the mid-century generation. Once the townland is established, the Valuation pins the family to a specific holding and may list multiple related households.
- **Neighbouring counties and parishes:** Billy parish borders include parts of the barony of Carey to the north and northeast, and the barony of Lower Dunluce runs along the coast. Adjacent civil parishes include Ballintoy, Ramoan, and Armoy to the north and east. A family near the parish boundary may have generated records in an adjoining parish. The FamilySearch Wiki Neighboring Parishes table for Billy was not available in the tool results; consult the Billy wiki page directly.
- **Irish naming conventions:** Irish Presbyterian families of Scottish descent in this period typically followed a strong naming pattern: the first son named for the paternal grandfather, the second son for the maternal grandfather, the first daughter for the maternal grandmother, the second daughter for the paternal grandmother. This pattern is not confirmed for Billy parish by any tool result fetched in this session, but it is well-established for Ulster Presbyterian families and can guide reconstruction of the grandparental generation. Do not reverse the pattern: the first son names the paternal grandfather, not the maternal.
- **The Ordnance Survey Memoirs of the 1830s** for Billy parish are a uniquely valuable source for understanding the physical and social landscape at exactly the birth date of your 1825 ancestor. They describe townland by townland, note religious meetinghouses and their congregations, and give population and economic data. Locate the published volume for this barony through a university library or the Ulster Historical Foundation.

---

For a Presbyterian family in this period, the most important surviving records are the congregation registers held on microfilm at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland in Belfast — but the FamilySearch Wiki page for this specific parish did not list which congregations or when their registers begin, so the first step is to look up the relevant MIC 1P/ reference in PRONI's free online catalogue. output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

County Cork is the largest county in Ireland, located in the Province of Munster. During the 1830s–1840s, it was part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland under the Act of Union (1800). The county seat is Cork City, a significant port. The economy was primarily agricultural — grain, dairy, livestock, and fishing — with butter export through Cork City being economically central. The population was predominantly Roman Catholic. Key events affecting records include the Tithe War (1831–1836) and the onset of the Great Famine (1845–1852), which drove mass emigration through Cobh (then Queenstown).

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No civil vital records exist for the 1830s–1840s.** Civil registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did not begin until **1 January 1864**. Non-Catholic marriages were registered from **1845**.
- **Use church registers as the substitute** (see below).

---

### Church Records *(Backbone of research for this period)*
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (vast majority), Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Quakers.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (primary surviving series), marriages, and occasionally burials/confirmations.
- **Where held:**
  - **Roman Catholic registers** — National Library of Ireland (NLI); images freely viewable online at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie). Many Cork RC parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s, though survival varies.
  - **Church of Ireland registers** — Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin; some indexed online.
  - **Quaker registers** — Religious Society of Friends Historical Library, Dublin (in-person by appointment).
- **Language note:** RC registers from this period are often in Latin. A Latin glossary is essential for reading the columns.
- **Critical caveat:** The Catholic *civil parish* (used in land records) and the Catholic *ecclesiastical parish* (whose register you need) often have different names and boundaries. You must match your ancestor's **townland** to the correct ecclesiastical parish before searching registers.

---

### Census Records
- **Almost entirely destroyed** in the 1922 Four Courts fire in Dublin. The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns are largely gone; only fragments survive.
- **Census substitutes — ESSENTIAL:**
  1. **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists occupiers of tithe-liable land, organized by barony and civil parish. *Note: landless labourers and town dwellers were often excluded.* Indexed and free online at IrishGenealogy.ie and FindMyPast.
  2. **Griffith's Primary Valuation (early 1850s for Cork):** Lists every householder with their land/property, valuation, and landlord name. Fully indexed and free at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie).

---

### Probate and Court Records
- Pre-1858 probate was handled by ecclesiastical courts (Diocese of Cork and Ross). Most wills proved before 1858 were **destroyed in the 1922 fire**.
- **Substitutes:** Will abstracts and calendars (name indexes) survive and note parties and dates even when the will text is lost.
- The Probate Act 1857 transferred jurisdiction to civil District Probate Registries effective 1858.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin.

---

### Land Records
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Tax record and census substitute. Indexed and online.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (early 1850s):** Names every householder with property description, landlord, and valuation. Free at askaboutireland.ie.
- **Estate papers:** Landlord rent rolls, leases, and tenant lists — held at the NAI and NLI; access varies by estate.
- **Registry of Deeds:** Deeds, mortgages, and conveyances from 1708. Indexes partially microfilmed; deed texts physical only at the Registry of Deeds, Dublin.

---

### Military Records
- Ireland was part of the UK, so service was in the **British Army or Royal Navy** — records held at The National Archives (Kew), London; many series on Findmypast and Ancestry.
- **Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC, formed 1836):** Service records are an underused source for tracing working-class men. Held at the NAI; some microfilm at FamilySearch.

---

### Poor Law Records *(Underused — especially valuable for 1838 onward)*
- The Irish Poor Law Act (1838) established workhouses throughout Cork. **Workhouse admission registers, indoor relief registers, and outdoor relief lists** name individuals — including the poor who appear in no other surviving record.
- Especially important for the Famine period (1845–1852).
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland; some local archive copies. Not systematically indexed online.

---

### Immigration/Emigration Records
- Cork ports — primarily **Cobh (Queenstown)** — were among the busiest emigration ports in the British Isles.
- **US arrival manifests:** Indexed and imaged at Ancestry and FamilySearch (NARA series). Famine-era manifests list complete family groups including infants.
- **UK Board of Trade departure lists:** Held at TNA Kew; some on Findmypast. Less comprehensively indexed.
- **Naturalisation records:** Filed at US federal, state, or local courts — not centralized.
- *Tip:* From the late 1840s, some manifests and naturalisation records state the county or parish of origin.

---

### Newspaper Records
- **Key papers:** *Cork Examiner* (founded 1841), *Cork Constitution*, *Southern Reporter*.
- **Content:** Obituaries, marriage notices (more common for Protestant families), legal notices, estate sales, and shipping news listing departures from Cobh.
- **Where held:** Irish Newspaper Archives and British Newspaper Archive (subscription); microfilm at NLI.

---

### Cemetery Records
- Catholic churchyards, Church of Ireland churchyards, and some municipal cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave has some transcribed headstones, but rural Cork coverage for this period is uneven.
- Headstones from the 1830s–1840s are often absent or illegible. Separate burial registers are rare in Catholic parishes for this period.

---

## Known Record Losses

The **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed:
- Nearly all pre-1901 Irish census returns (1821, 1831, 1841, 1851)
- Most pre-1858 probate records (wills and administrations)
- Various government administrative records

Do not assume failure to find a census record means no ancestor was recorded — the records themselves are gone.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland (nli.ie) | RC parish register images to 1880 | Free online |
| IrishGenealogy.ie | RC & CoI register images; Tithe indexes | Free |
| Askaboutireland.ie | Griffith's Valuation (indexed + images) | Free |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Census fragments; probate; Poor Law; estate papers; RIC records | In-person; some online |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers | In-person; some indexes online |
| Registry of Deeds, Dublin | Land conveyances from 1708 | In-person; indexes microfilmed |
| Cork City and County Archives | Local government and estate records | In-person |
| The National Archives (Kew), London | British Army; UK departure passenger lists | In-person; Findmypast/Ancestry |
| NARA (archives.gov) | US immigration and naturalisation records | Free to search; Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| FindMyPast (subscription) | Tithe Applotment Books; RIC records; UK passenger lists | Subscription |
| Ancestry (subscription) | US arrival manifests; some Irish collections | Subscription |

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Search Griffith's Valuation** (free at askaboutireland.ie) to place the family in a specific **townland** in the early 1850s.
2. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books** (free at IrishGenealogy.ie or FindMyPast) for the same townland in the 1820s–1830s.
3. **Identify the Catholic ecclesiastical parish** for that townland (using Lewis's *Topographical Dictionary of Ireland*, 1837, or NLI parish maps), then search the NLI/IrishGenealogy.ie register images for baptisms and marriages.
4. **For emigration**, search US arrival manifests at Ancestry or FamilySearch; look at full manifest pages for all family members.
5. **For probate and land conveyances**, consult the National Archives of Ireland and Registry of Deeds.
6. **For 1838 onward**, check Poor Law workhouse records at the NAI for labourers and poorer families.

---

**Bottom line:** Church records (freely online via the NLI) combined with the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are the three pillars of 1830s–1840s County Cork research. The 1922 fire means there are no usable census records. Pinning down the **townland** is the essential first step — everything else flows from it.

The external_links_search tool returned a standardPlace of "" (empty) in its query output, indicating it could not resolve County Cork or Ireland to a curated FamilySearch link set — only six generic links were returned (U.S. Census, NARA, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, Archives.gov). No population data was returned by place_population. Step 6 does not run — there is no research.json in the working directory. The full guide follows.

---

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** County Cork was established as an administrative county under the Irish county system formalised in 1606, making it one of Ireland's oldest counties. It is the largest county in Ireland by area.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Cork City (also called Cork)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Munster, Ireland. During this period, Ireland was part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland under the Act of Union (1800).
- **Population during period:** No population figure was returned by the place_population tool for this query. County Cork was one of the most populous counties in Ireland; it suffered catastrophic population loss during the Great Famine (1845–1852), which began just at the close of this survey window.
- **Economy:** Primarily agricultural — grain, dairy, and livestock farming. Cork City was a significant port and market town. Fishing communities along the coastline. Butter export through Cork City was economically central.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Irish Catholic population. A Protestant Ascendancy landowning class (Church of Ireland) held much of the land under the landlord-tenant system. Small Quaker and Methodist communities in commercial centres.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant majority), Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian, Methodist, Society of Friends (Quakers). The parish structure for record purposes runs in two parallel hierarchies — Catholic civil parishes (the unit for Tithe and Griffith's records) and Catholic ecclesiastical parishes (the unit for church registers), which do not always align with civil parish boundaries.
- **Key historical events:** The 1798 rebellion and its aftermath; the Tithe War (1831–1836), during which Catholic tenants resisted paying tithes to the Church of Ireland — Tithe Applotment records date from this same period. The Great Famine (1845–1852) struck immediately after this survey window and drove mass emigration from Cork ports, particularly Cobh (then called Queenstown). These events directly shaped which records were created and who appears in them.

## Boundary changes

County Cork's boundaries were stable throughout the 1830s–1840s. It was divided internally into baronies (a subdivision used in Tithe and Griffith's records) and then civil parishes, which are the key units for locating records. Baronies matter: both the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are organised by barony then civil parish, so knowing your ancestor's barony is the key to navigating those sources. The county has not been split or merged with another county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Civil registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did not begin until **1 January 1864** (national level). Non-Catholic marriages were registered from **1845** (national level). The FamilySearch Wiki states this explicitly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy
- **What exists for 1830s–1840s:** None. There are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the target period. The wiki states plainly: "No civil vital records exist for the 1830s–1840s — use church registers instead."
- **Where held:** General Register Office, Dublin (post-1864 records). Not applicable for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1830s–1840s is a gap in civil vital records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below) are the essential substitute for this period.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (the overwhelming majority of the population); Church of Ireland; Presbyterian; Methodist; Society of Friends (Quakers).
- **Record types:** For Roman Catholic parishes: baptisms (the primary surviving series), marriages, and occasionally burials. Confirmations were also recorded and can supply a date years after baptism. For Church of Ireland: baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **Where held:** The National Library of Ireland (NLI) holds microfilm and digital images of Roman Catholic parish registers up to 1880, available free online. Many Cork RC parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s, though survival varies by parish — some parishes have gaps or late starts. Church of Ireland registers are held at the Representative Church Body Library (RCBL) in Dublin and in some local custody. The RCBL holdings are partially indexed.
- **Critical access note:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) confirms the NLI provides free online images of Catholic registers. To locate the right register, you must know which Catholic civil parish — and which ecclesiastical parish — covered the townland where your ancestor lived. These do not always match; a townland can sit in one civil parish and a different Catholic ecclesiastical parish.
- **Language:** Latin was used in Roman Catholic registers through much of this period, particularly for baptismal and marriage entries. A Latin glossary is essential for reading the columns.

### Census records

- **National census:** National censuses were taken in Ireland in 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851. The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed almost all returns from these enumerations. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy), "most pre-1901 census returns… were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire." Fragments survive for some areas.
- **Census substitutes — CRITICAL:** Because the censuses are gone, two substitute records carry the weight of census research for this period:
  1. **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists occupiers of tithe-liable land throughout Ireland, including County Cork. Organised by barony and civil parish. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies this as "a key census substitute for the 1830s." Available online and indexed.
  2. **Griffith's Primary Valuation (early 1850s for Cork):** Lists every householder in Ireland with the land or property they occupied. Published for Cork in the early 1850s. The wiki calls it "the major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses." Fully indexed and available online at askaboutireland.ie and other repositories.
- **Access:** Both the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are indexed and searchable online. Digitization level: indexed + images.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate estates), and testamentary bonds.
- **Holding jurisdiction:** The Prerogative Court of Armagh handled wills of those with property in more than one diocese. The Consistorial Court of Cork and Ross handled local probate.
- **Record loss:** The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the Principal Registry's copies of most wills proved before 1900. Will books and grant books for the Diocese of Cork and Ross prior to 1858 were among the losses. **Substitute:** Will abstracts and calendars (indexes) survive and name parties and dates even when the will text is lost. The National Archives of Ireland holds surviving fragments and the post-1858 probate records from District Probate Registries.
- **Probate reform:** The Probate Act 1857 transferred testamentary jurisdiction from ecclesiastical courts to civil District Probate Registries effective 1858. Records from the 1830s–1840s were under the ecclesiastical system.
- **Access:** Largely physical only or microfilm for pre-1858 records; some calendars have been digitised and indexed.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds combined with the Irish townland system. The townland is the fundamental unit of Irish land description — knowing your ancestor's townland is essential.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under the landlord-tenant system, most Catholic farmers held land as tenants from Protestant landowners (often absentee). The Landed Estates Court (post-1849) and estate papers held at the National Archives of Ireland are relevant when a landlord's estate was sold.
- **Types available:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Name land occupiers liable for tithe. Organised by barony and civil parish. Indexed and online.
  - **Griffith's Primary Valuation (early 1850s):** Names every householder, with description of land and buildings, valuation, and landlord. Indexed and online.
  - **Estate papers:** Many landlord estate records (leases, rent rolls, tenant lists) survive in the National Archives of Ireland and the National Library of Ireland collections, though access varies by estate.
  - **Registry of Deeds:** Deeds, mortgages, and land conveyances were registered in Dublin from 1708 onward. Indexes are available at the Registry of Deeds, Dublin; some are microfilmed.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland; National Library of Ireland; Registry of Deeds, Dublin.

### Military records

- **Relevant service:** Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, so military service was in the British Army or Royal Navy. Some Irishmen served in the East India Company's forces. Pension records, muster rolls, and service records are held at The National Archives (Kew), London (TNA/Kew).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension records, militia lists, and muster books. The 1820s–1840s saw no major conflict in which Irish forces were heavily engaged, but the British Army maintained garrisons throughout Ireland.
- **Irish Constabulary:** The Peace Preservation Force and later the Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC, formed 1836) kept service records of constables. These are at the National Archives of Ireland and are an underused source for tracing working-class men not easily found elsewhere.
- **Access:** TNA Kew (British Army): many series available via Findmypast and Ancestry. RIC records: National Archives of Ireland (some microfilm at FamilySearch).

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic churchyards (most common), Church of Ireland churchyards, and by the 1840s, some municipal cemeteries. Cork City's St. Finbarr's Cemetery opened 1869 (after the target period). Many rural burials were in churchyard ground adjacent to ruined pre-Reformation churches.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) carries many transcribed headstones, but coverage for 1830s–1840s rural Cork is uneven. The Irish Graveyards project and local historical societies have transcribed some churchyards.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held locally at parish or diocesan level. Many churchyard records for this period were never formally kept.
- **Caveat:** Headstones for this period are often not present or are illegible due to age. Burial registers separate from the baptismal register are rare in Catholic parishes for this period.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Cork Examiner (founded 1841, still publishing as the Irish Examiner) is the most significant paper for the later part of this period. The Cork Constitution and the Southern Reporter also published during the 1830s–1840s.
- **Content value:** Obituaries (more common for middle and upper classes), marriage notices (Church of Ireland families more routinely; Catholic notices are less common for this period), legal notices, estate sales, and shipping news listing departures from Cobh.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive and Irish Newspaper Archives hold digitised runs; some are available on subscription. The National Library of Ireland holds microfilm runs.
- **Access:** Subscription services (Irish Newspaper Archives; British Newspaper Archive). Some browsable at NLI.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Critical for this period:** The 1830s saw pre-Famine emigration; the late 1840s saw mass Famine emigration. Cork ports — primarily Cobh (Queenstown) — were among the busiest emigration ports in the British Isles.
- **Relevant ports:** Cobh/Queenstown (Cork Harbour); Liverpool (many Cork emigrants transited through Liverpool before crossing the Atlantic); New York, Boston, Quebec, and Liverpool were primary destinations.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests (arrival manifests at US ports); UK Board of Trade passenger lists (departures from British ports, held at TNA Kew); naturalisation records filed at US courts (declarations of intention, petitions for naturalisation).
- **Content note (per FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):** Famine-era passenger manifests "list complete family groups including infants, not just heads of household." Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family — children including infants are listed alongside parents.
- **Where held:** US arrival manifests (pre-1891): National Archives and Records Administration (NARA); indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. UK departure records: TNA Kew (some on Findmypast). Naturalisation records: NARA, and filed in whatever federal, state, or local court the immigrant chose — not just one court.
- **Access:** Indexed + images for most US arrival series via Ancestry and FamilySearch. UK departure records are less comprehensively indexed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) function as a tax record and census substitute simultaneously — they list tithe-liable occupiers of agricultural land. Note that landless labourers (cottiers) and those in towns were often excluded.
- **County cess and grand jury presentments:** The grand jury system levied local rates for road maintenance and public works. Grand jury records are at the National Archives of Ireland but are not indexed for individual names and are rarely digitised.
- **Hearth Money Rolls (earlier period):** Pre-date this survey window but can establish earlier family presence in a townland.
- **Access:** Tithe Applotment Books — indexed and online. Grand jury records — physical only at National Archives of Ireland.

### Other record types

- **Poor Law records:** The Irish Poor Law Act (1838) established Poor Law Unions and workhouses throughout Ireland, including in County Cork. Workhouse admission registers, indoor relief registers, and outdoor relief lists name individuals. Many survive at county level and are held by the National Archives of Ireland or local archives. For the late 1840s and Famine period, these are essential records.
- **Quaker records:** The Religious Society of Friends kept meticulous registers of births, marriages, and burials. Cork had a Quaker community. Quaker records are centralised at the Religious Society of Friends Historical Library, Dublin.
- **Estate and landlord records:** Lists of tenants, rent rolls, and eviction notices from landlord estate papers name individuals not otherwise recorded. These are at the National Library of Ireland and the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories (e.g., Samuel Lewis's _A Topographical Dictionary of Ireland_, 1837) describe parishes, townlands, churches, and local institutions and can help identify which parishes and denominations served a particular area.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland (www.nli.ie) | Catholic parish register images up to 1880; digitised online free | Free |
| IrishGenealogy.ie | RC and Church of Ireland register images and some indexing for Cork | Free |
| Askaboutireland.ie | Griffith's Valuation fully indexed and imaged | Free |
| FindMyPast (findmypast.com) | Tithe Applotment Books index; UK passenger lists; RIC records | Subscription |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | US arrival manifests indexed; some Irish collections | Subscription |
| The National Archives (UK) (discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk) | British Army service records; UK departure passenger lists | Free to search; some images fee |
| NARA (archives.gov) | US immigration and naturalisation records | Free to search; some online via Ancestry/FamilySearch |

**Note on external_links_search:** The tool did not resolve County Cork or Ireland to a curated FamilySearch link set for the 1830–1850 window and returned only six generic links (FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, Ancestry census collection, NARA, FamilySearch Wiki category). None were Ireland-specific. The repositories named above come from the FamilySearch Wiki page content returned, not from a curated external-links list.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Census fragments; probate records; Poor Law records; estate papers; grand jury records; RIC records | In-person; some records online via NAI website |
| National Library of Ireland, Dublin | RC parish register microfilm/originals; estate and landlord papers; maps; newspapers | In-person; many register images free online |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | In-person; some indexes online at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| The National Archives (Kew), London | British Army records; UK departure passenger lists | In-person; Findmypast/Ancestry for many series |
| Registry of Deeds, Dublin | Land conveyances and mortgages from 1708 | In-person; indexes microfilmed |
| Cork City and County Archives, Cork | Local government records; estate papers; Cork-specific collections | In-person; contact for access |
| Religious Society of Friends Historical Library, Dublin | Quaker birth, marriage, and burial registers | In-person by appointment |

## Records NOT online

- Grand jury presentments and county cess records (physical only at National Archives of Ireland)
- Most estate and landlord papers (physical only at NLI or NAI; a few digitised)
- Poor Law workhouse admission registers (physical at NAI; some local archive copies; not systematically indexed online)
- Registry of Deeds deeds (indexes partially microfilmed; deed texts physical only)
- Church of Ireland burial registers for many rural Cork parishes (physical at RCBL or local custody)
- Cork newspaper runs (partial coverage online on subscription; comprehensive runs on microfilm at NLI)

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) states that the **1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1901 census returns and many wills and government records**. For County Cork this means:

- The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns are almost entirely destroyed. Only fragments survive (the 1821 census has some surviving returns for parts of Ireland, but survival for Cork is minimal and must be verified against the National Archives of Ireland's known holdings).
- Pre-1858 probate records (wills, administrations) proved in the Consistorial Courts, including the Diocese of Cork and Ross, were largely lost. Will calendars (name indexes without the full text) survive for many.
- Some government administrative records are also lost.

**Substitute sources:** Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, church registers, estate papers, and newspaper notices partially compensate for the census and probate losses. Researchers should not assume that failure to find an ancestor in a census index means no census record existed — the records themselves are gone.

## Research tips

- **Church records are the backbone of 1830s–1840s research** in County Cork. Civil registration does not exist for this period; the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) is explicit that for the 1830s–1840s you must use church registers. Determine your ancestor's religion — almost certainly Catholic — before searching.
- **Identify the townland first.** Irish records are organised at the townland level, not by street address. The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are indexed by townland. Without the townland, navigating Catholic register series (each of which covers a specific group of townlands) is very difficult.
- **Match the Catholic civil parish to the ecclesiastical parish.** The civil parish (used in Tithe and Griffith's records) and the Catholic ecclesiastical parish (whose register you need) do not always have the same name or boundaries. Lewis's _Topographical Dictionary of Ireland_ (1837) and the NLI's parish maps can help match them.
- **The Tithe Applotment Books cover 1823–1837 and are often the earliest surviving record placing a specific person in a specific townland** in Cork. Note that landless labourers are often absent — the books list only those who occupied tithe-liable land.
- **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s for Cork) is the baseline census substitute.** It is the most comprehensive name-indexed source for the county and is often used to anchor a family to a townland even when the target period is the 1830s–1840s.
- **Naming conventions in Irish Catholic families** were highly regularised: the first son was typically named after the paternal grandfather, the second son after the maternal grandfather, the first daughter after the paternal grandmother, the second daughter after the maternal grandmother. Repeating given names across siblings (especially when a child died young) are common. The FamilySearch Wiki note on this applies to Ireland broadly; the tool returned this information as part of the Ireland Genealogy page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy.
- **Emigration records can name the origin townland.** From the late 1840s onward, some passenger manifests and naturalisation records state the county or parish of origin. Earlier manifests typically say only "Ireland." If your ancestor emigrated in the 1840s, check the full manifest — all family members including infants were listed, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Poor Law records (from 1838) are underused.** Workhouse registers and outdoor relief lists from the Famine period (1845–1852) name individuals who often appear in no other surviving record, including labourers and the very poor excluded from the Tithe books.
- **Efficient research sequence for this jurisdiction:**
  1. Search Griffith's Valuation (free at askaboutireland.ie) to place the family in a townland in the early 1850s.
  2. Search the Tithe Applotment Books (free on FindMyPast and IrishGenealogy.ie) for the same townland in the 1820s–1830s.
  3. Identify the Catholic ecclesiastical parish for that townland; search the NLI/IrishGenealogy.ie register images for baptisms and marriages.
  4. For emigration, search US arrival manifests at Ancestry or FamilySearch.
  5. For probate and land conveyances, consult the National Archives of Ireland and Registry of Deeds.

---

County Cork in the 1830s and 1840s was a predominantly Catholic, agricultural county where almost no government-issued birth, marriage, or death records were kept — those did not begin until 1864. The records that survive for this period are Catholic church registers (baptisms and marriages, now freely viewable online through the National Library of Ireland), the Tithe Applotment Books listing land occupiers from the 1820s-1830s, and Griffith's Valuation from the early 1850s. The single most important warning is that the 1922 fire in Dublin destroyed virtually all Irish census records for this period, so researchers cannot rely on census searches the way they would for other countries. A second warning: the parish that your ancestor worshipped in and the civil parish named in land records often have different names and boundaries, so you need to match them using a townland before searching church registers.

The recommended next step is to build a research plan targeting your ancestor specifically — starting with Griffith's Valuation to pin down their townland, then working backward through the Tithe Applotment Books and Catholic parish registers for the 1830s-1840s events in County Cork.

# Locality Guide: Javorje, Škofja Loko, Slovenia (1812)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Javorje nad Škofjo Loko is a small village in the Škofja Loka area. In 1812, it was known under the German administrative name *Bischoflack* (for the town of Škofja Loka), within the **Duchy of Carniola (Krain), Habsburg Austria**. Notably, from 1809 to 1813 the area was briefly governed as part of Napoleon's **Illyrian Provinces** — meaning your 1812 marriage falls squarely in this French-administered period.

Ecclesiastically, the area fell within the **Diocese of Ljubljana (Labacensis)**.

---

## Primary Record: Catholic Parish Marriage Register

The routine record of an 1812 marriage would be the **Liber Matrimoniorum** (Latin marriage register) kept by the local Catholic parish priest.

- **Format:** Tabular format adopted in 1770/1784 by Habsburg decree; entries in Latin, possibly with German annotations.
- **Duplicate copies:** Did **not** exist yet — duplicate registers for civil authorities were not required for Roman Catholic records until 1835. In 1812 there was only one register kept at the parish.
- **Key step first:** Identify which parish served Javorje. The Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana (Archdiocesan Archive) can confirm this.

---

## Secondary Record: French Civil Registration (État-Civil)

Because 1812 falls within the **Illyrian Provinces period (1809–1813)**, the French introduced civil registration modeled on the Code Civil. A **parallel civil marriage record** may exist alongside the church register entry.

- **Where held:** Archive of Slovenia (Arhiv Republike Slovenije), Ljubljana — www.arhiv.gov.si

---

## Where to Look Online

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Matricula Online** (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/) | Slovenia Catholic parish register *images*, browseable by diocese and parish | Free |
| **FamilySearch Catalog** (search "Škofja Loka, Slovenia") | 36 catalog items for Škofja Loka; some available online | Free |

> **Important note:** No FamilySearch indexed collections or digitized volumes were found for Škofja Loka in the 1790–1830 window. This is a digitization/indexing gap — it does **not** mean the records don't exist. Matricula Online is your best online starting point.

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana** (Archdiocesan Archive) | Earlier originals and transcripts of Catholic parish registers for the Diocese of Ljubljana | arhiv.lj@rkc.si |
| **Arhiv Republike Slovenije** (Archive of Slovenia), Ljubljana | Civil registration from French Illyrian Provinces period (1809–1813) | www.arhiv.gov.si |
| **FamilySearch Library**, Salt Lake City | Some Škofja Loka catalog items (on-site only) | familysearch.org |

## Research Tips

1. **Identify the serving parish first.** Javorje is a village; you must confirm which parish covered it before searching any register. The archdiocesan archive (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) can answer this, and a published inventory of all Slovenian parish registers (1972–1974) is a key finding aid.
