## Records NOT online
- Full deed book series (county courthouse) — only selective records may be online; the complete series requires courthouse or KDLA access.
- Original court order books — not confirmed as fully digitized.
- Most individual church congregation records — the Pulaski County Historical Society holds the most comprehensive local collection; many congregations still hold their own records and are not online.
- County school records — not confirmed online for 1840–1880.
- Original estate inventories and administration files beyond the digitized will books.

## Known record losses
- The FamilySearch Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page states: "A disaster destroyed some records in 1838 and again in 1871." Source: [Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). The 1871 loss falls within the target period. No tool result specifies which record series or volumes were destroyed. Verify with the Pulaski County Courthouse and KDLA which specific volumes survive before treating a negative search result as final. Church records, tax lists, and newspaper notices are the primary substitutes.

## Research tips
- **Vital records gap strategy:** For 1840–1852 and 1863–1873 — the two longest gaps in county-level birth/death registration — prioritize church registers, federal census mortality schedules, and cemetery transcriptions. The Pulaski County Historical Society's church record and obituary files are the most concentrated local source. Source: [Kentucky Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records)
- **Marriage strategy:** Marriage bonds and licenses exist at the county courthouse from 1799 and are digitized on FamilySearch through 1871. The bond (signed by the groom and a surety, often a relative) can identify a father or older brother. The consent form, when present, names the parent or guardian of an underage bride.
- **Land records as vital record substitutes:** Kentucky deeds commonly name a wife (releasing dower rights) and sometimes list heirs in partition deeds. These are especially valuable when no civil birth or death record exists. Always search deed books for the years before and after a known death. Source: [Kentucky Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property)
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Kentucky county tax lists run annually and can trace a person's presence in the county in the years between censuses (1841–1849, 1851–1859, 1861–1869, 1871–1879). Absence from the list may signal death or migration.
- **Record loss awareness:** The 1871 courthouse disaster means records filed around 1870–1871 may be incomplete. Cross-reference any negative results in marriage, deed, or probate books with KDLA to determine whether the volume survived.
- **Civil War records — search both sides:** Kentucky's border-state status means family members may have served Union and Confederate forces simultaneously. Union pension files (NARA) are more complete; Confederate records at NARA cover service records but pension files are sparser.
- **Pulaski County Historical Society:** This repository holds surname vertical files for every Pulaski County family name and the most comprehensive local church record and obituary collection. Contact them before making a courthouse trip — they may have already compiled relevant records.
- **Neighboring counties:** The wiki page for Pulaski County did not return a Neighboring Counties table in this session. Geographically, Pulaski County borders Casey, Lincoln, Rockcastle, Laurel, McCreary, Wayne, Russell, and Adair counties. Families near county lines likely generated records in adjacent counties — search those deed and probate series as well, particularly Lincoln County (one of Pulaski's parent counties, from which records predate 1798).
- **Pre-formation records:** Any Pulaski County events before December 10, 1798 will be in Lincoln County or Green County records, the two parent counties.

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001** in the project. Here is the full guidance:

---

Researching an ancestor in the Alabama area around 1800 means working with **Mississippi Territory** records, not Alabama state records, since Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction until 1819. The territory was sparsely settled, and no system of civil birth, marriage, or death registration existed at all for that period.

### Key Record Types and Repositories

**Territorial & County Court Records**
- Washington County (organized 1800) covered nearly all of settled present-day Alabama — its deed books and court minutes are the primary civil records for this period.

**Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery)**
- Holds territorial militia muster rolls and tax lists for the Mississippi Territory period.

**Territorial Censuses**
- Census substitutes were taken in **1801, 1805, and 1808** for the Mississippi Territory — these are invaluable since no federal census covered the area before 1810.

**Catholic Sacramental Registers (Mobile area)**
- Mobile was under Spanish control until 1813, so church registers from that period are held in **Seville, Spain** (Archivo General de Indias) and microfilmed copies are at the **Library of Congress**.

**FamilySearch Digitized Volumes**
- Three digitized volumes cover this period, but all three are **browse-only with no name index** — you'd need to page through them manually.

**BLM General Land Office (GLO) Records**
- If your ancestor owned land, federal land patents (after the territory opened for sale) are searchable at the GLO website.

---

**Recommended next step:** Build a research plan targeting the territorial census substitutes and Washington County court records first, then land records at the GLO if land ownership can be confirmed.

The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Alabama-specific vital records page; the FamilySearch Wiki does not state a statewide registration date for Alabama from any page returned in this survey. County-level marriage registration appears in some Alabama collections beginning 1809 (FamilySearch collection 1598408, Alabama County Marriages, begins 1809). Statewide vital registration in Alabama did not begin until the late 19th/early 20th century — the FamilySearch Wiki did not return the specific date.
- **What exists for 1800:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records created as a government system at this date. Individual counties kept marriage bonds/licenses once organized after 1809.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (for post-1809 county marriages); Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, for state-era records
- **Gaps:** Complete gap for civil vital registration in the 1780–1809 window
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (Catholic sacramental registers in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist church minute books); land records naming family members; probate/estate records; census enumerations

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, continuous from French period); Baptist and Methodist (arriving with Anglo-American settlers ca. 1800–1810)
- **Record types:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); Protestant church minute books (membership, discipline, occasional vital data)
- **Where held:**

- **Language:** Catholic registers in the colonial/territorial period are in French or Spanish; Latin for sacramental formulas

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1800 federal census nominally covered the Mississippi Territory, but coverage of the Alabama area was extremely limited (Washington County district only). The 1810 federal census is the first to enumerate Alabama Territory residents in reasonable numbers. FamilySearch collection 2016756 (Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890) begins in 1810; it is name-indexed with no images.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory took unofficial censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery — per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). FamilySearch collection 1927171 (Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890) covers the territory starting 1792.
- **Access:** The Alabama compiled index (collection 2016756) is name-indexed but has no images online (imageCount: 0). The Mississippi compiled census collection (1927171) similarly has no images.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court minutes and petitions
- **Date range:** Washington County, Alabama, organized 1800; earliest deed and probate records date from 1803. FamilySearch collection 1537764 (Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985) begins 1809.
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch volume 004512890 contains 96 browse-only images of Washington County, Alabama deed and probate records, 1803–1820 (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). - **Where held:** Washington County Courthouse, Chatom, Alabama (originals); ADAH, Montgomery; FamilySearch (browse-only images listed above)

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Alabama is a **federal-land state** — land was distributed by the U.S. federal government, not by the state or territory. The rectangular survey (township and range) system applies.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office (GLO) issued patents for land in Alabama. Original land patents are searchable at the BLM General Land Office website: https://glorecords.blm.gov. FamilySearch collection 1919694 (Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907) covers territorial-era patents and grants beginning 1798.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish land grants (Mobile area, pre-1813), British land grants (pre-1780), deed transfers, territorial court land records
- **Date range:** Federal land sales in Alabama began ca. 1803–1808 as the territory was surveyed. Spanish-era land grants predate this.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents); ADAH (territorial records); Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Spanish grants); county courthouses (deed transfers after organization)
- **Digitized:** Volume 004512889 (214 browse-only images, Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819); volume 004498712 (143 browse-only images, Mississippi Territory territorial records, 1799–1817). Both are 0% indexed and not full-text searchable.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Quasi-War/frontier militia (ca. 1798–1800); Creek War 1813–1814 (just after the core period); War of 1812
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; War of 1812 service records and bounty land warrants; pension files
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C., and Southeast Region (Atlanta) — NARA holds federal military records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized many War of 1812 records. ADAH holds state militia records.
- **Note:** Militia and territorial muster rolls for the Mississippi Territory period are among the most useful records for placing a person in a specific community around 1800, as they name adult male residents of record.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries (Catholic, Baptist) and family burial grounds; formal municipal cemeteries did not exist in most of Alabama in 1800
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Alabama cemetery records, though coverage for pre-1820 burials is thin
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely survive for this period; transcriptions by the Daughters of the American Revolution and local genealogical societies are the main secondary source

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Alabama area in 1800. The first Alabama newspaper, the *Mobile Centinel*, appeared ca. 1811.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Alabama Department of Archives and History microfilm collection
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices began appearing after 1811; not a source for 1800 events

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf of Mexico port; Spanish-controlled until 1813); New Orleans (for river traffic)
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial passenger and residency lists (Mobile District); later federal passenger manifests at Mobile and New Orleans
- **Where held:** Spanish colonial lists: Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress copies. Federal manifests (post-1820): NARA; Ancestry.com

- **Inland declarations:** Naturalization petitions from the territorial period were filed in territorial/county courts; these exist even inland, far from Mobile.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; county property and poll tax lists once counties organized

- **Where held:** ADAH; county courthouses; partially covered by the compiled census substitutes collections (FamilySearch 2016756 for Alabama, 1927171 for Mississippi/Territory)

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Alabama, County Marriages 1809-1950 (collection 1598408); Alabama, Probate Records 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (1927171); 3 browse-only digitized volumes (IGNs 004512889, 004512890, 004498712) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1800, 1810 | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military records including War of 1812 | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Federal records, military, naturalization | Free/Fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes under the Alabama standardPlace and 1 under the Mississippi Territory standardPlace for this period — all 3 are detailed above. This represents the complete page of results (no nextPageToken returned); however, additional volumes may be catalogued under county-level place names not searched here.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses 1801-1810, state records, county records on microfilm, published histories | In-person; some finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| Washington County Courthouse, Chatom, AL | Original deed, probate, and court records from 1800 | In-person or mail request |
| NARA, Southeast Region, Atlanta, GA | Federal land records, military records, naturalizations | In-person or online request |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records: padrones, church registers, land grants (Mobile District) | In-person; some microfilm copies at Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records for the Mobile area | In-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records pre-1763 | In-person |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records | In-person |
| Diocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic sacramental registers | Contact the diocese |

## Records NOT online

- Territorial militia muster rolls for 1798–1817 (held at ADAH; not digitized online)
- Washington County court minute books from 1800 (partially in browse-only FamilySearch volume 004512890, but no name index)
- Spanish colonial padrones and residency lists for the Mobile District (held at Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress has some copies on microfilm, not fully digitized)
- French colonial church registers pre-1763 (held at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Early Baptist and Methodist church minute books (held by local churches and historical societies; not systematically digitized)
- County tax lists pre-1810 (held at ADAH and county courthouses)

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this survey states that a specific Alabama record set was destroyed for this period. Washington County records beginning 1800 appear to survive and are partially captured in FamilySearch volume 004512890. Where a search returns zero results, treat the result as a coverage gap (the record may not be digitized or indexed), not as evidence the record does not exist. Confirm the status of any specific record set with ADAH before concluding it is lost.

## Research tips

- **Search both Alabama and Mississippi-scoped collections.** Pre-statehood Alabama records were created under the Mississippi Territory and are often catalogued under Mississippi rather than Alabama at FamilySearch. Run searches in both the Alabama and Mississippi collections listed above.
- **Identify the correct county for the date of the event.** In 1800, Washington County covered virtually all of settled present-day Alabama. Madison County was not organized until 1808. Using modern county boundaries for a 1800 event will send you to the wrong repository.
- **Territorial censuses are the primary substitute for the 1800 federal census gap.** The 1800 federal census covered Mississippi Territory only partially; the territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808 at ADAH are often more complete for the Alabama portion — per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Alabama is a federal-land state — go to the BLM GLO, not a state land office.** Land patents for Alabama are at https://glorecords.blm.gov. Territorial-era land records are also in FamilySearch collection 1919694.
- **For the Mobile area in 1800, the controlling sovereign was Spain.** The Mobile District remained Spanish territory until 1813. - **The three digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period are browse-only.** Volumes 004512889, 004512890, and 004498712 are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. There is no name search; you must browse each image in sequence.
- **Militia muster rolls name adult male residents.** For a period when census coverage is thin and vital records do not exist, territorial militia rolls at ADAH are among the most reliable ways to establish that a person was present in the region around 1800.
- **Consult published county histories.** 19th-century county histories for Washington County and neighboring counties often transcribe early deeds, court minutes, and list founding families by name — sometimes the only surviving copy of records later lost or damaged. Researching an ancestor in the Alabama area around 1800 means working with Mississippi Territory records, not Alabama state records, since Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction until 1819. # Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1780-1820)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **The jurisdiction in 1800:** Mississippi Territory (established 1798; the Alabama-area portion was called the Alabama Territory 1817-1819, then admitted as the state of Alabama in 1819)
- **Administrative center:** Territorial seat at Natchez (western section); Washington County courthouse served the Alabama area
- **Parent jurisdiction at the federal level:** United States federal government (territorial period); for the Mobile area specifically, Spain (1780-1813)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this period. The region was sparsely settled by European-Americans in 1800; the Creek and Cherokee nations occupied much of the interior. The Mobile Bay area had the largest European/Creole settlement.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, small-scale cotton planting beginning in the Tennessee Valley, fur trade, river commerce at Mobile
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (interior); French Creole, Anglo-American settlers, enslaved Africans (Mobile area and river valleys); Spanish colonial administrators at Mobile; Anglo-American migrants from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia arriving via the Tennessee River corridor
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area, dominant under French and Spanish rule); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders serving Anglo-American settlers in the interior
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory created 1798; expansion of territory 1804, 1812; Creek War 1813-1814 opened interior lands; Mobile seized from Spain 1813; Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood 1819

## Boundary changes

- **1702-1763:** Mobile area under French Louisiana administration
- **1763-1780:** British West Florida; boundary extended north to 32 degrees 28 minutes in 1764
- **1780-1813:** Spanish West Florida / Mobile District — Spain controlled Mobile and surrounding territory
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized by Congress from Georgia cession and disputed Spanish lands; covered only the southern strip initially
- **1804:** Territory expanded northward; present-day northern Alabama now included
- **1812:** Territory expanded to include Mobile Bay district (formally American after 1813)
- **1817:** Mississippi Territory split — western half became state of Mississippi; eastern half became Alabama Territory
- **1819:** Alabama admitted to statehood
- **Washington County** (organized 1800) was the first county in present-day Alabama; researchers must identify which county existed at the time of the event — for most of the 1800-1808 period, Washington County covered nearly all settled Alabama territory

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Mississippi Territory or Alabama Territory in 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Alabama-specific vital records page and does not state a statewide civil registration start date for Alabama from any page returned in this survey. County-level marriage registration appears in some Alabama collections beginning 1809 (FamilySearch collection 1598408, Alabama County Marriages, begins 1809).
- **What exists for 1800:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records created as a government system at this date.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (for post-1809 county marriages); Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, for state-era records
- **Gaps:** Complete gap for civil vital registration in the 1780-1809 window
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (Catholic sacramental registers in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist church minute books); land records naming family members; probate/estate records; census enumerations

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, continuous from French period); Baptist and Methodist (arriving with Anglo-American settlers ca. 1800-1810)
- **Record types:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); Protestant church minute books (membership, discipline, occasional vital data)
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic records (Mobile area): Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception archives, Mobile; Diocese of Mobile archives. FamilySearch collection 1986396 (Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950) covers some of this.
  - Spanish-era Catholic registers: Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress — per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
  - French-era Catholic records: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives — per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
  - Protestant church records: typically held by local churches, county historical societies, and partially microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Language:** Catholic registers in the colonial/territorial period are in French or Spanish; Latin for sacramental formulas

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1800 federal census nominally covered the Mississippi Territory, but coverage of the Alabama area was extremely limited (Washington County district only). The 1810 federal census is the first to enumerate Alabama Territory residents in reasonable numbers. FamilySearch collection 2016756 (Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890) begins in 1810; it is name-indexed with no images online.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory took unofficial censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery — per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). FamilySearch collection 1927171 (Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890) covers the territory starting 1792.
- **Access:** The Alabama compiled index (collection 2016756) is name-indexed but has no images online. The Mississippi compiled census collection (1927171) similarly has no images.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court minutes and petitions
- **Date range:** Washington County, Alabama, organized 1800; earliest deed and probate records date from 1803. FamilySearch collection 1537764 (Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985) begins 1809.
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch volume 004512890 contains 96 browse-only images of Washington County, Alabama deed and probate records, 1803-1820 (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). FamilySearch volume 004512889 contains 214 browse-only images of Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808-1819. Both must be browsed image by image — no name search is possible.
- **Mississippi Territory court records:** FamilySearch collection 1855293 (Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920) and volume 004498712 (143 browse-only images, Mississippi Territory land and court records, 1799-1817) cover the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Washington County Courthouse, Chatom, Alabama (originals); ADAH, Montgomery; FamilySearch (browse-only images listed above)

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal-land state — land was distributed by the U.S. federal government, not by the state or territory. The rectangular survey (township and range) system applies.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office (GLO) issued patents for land in Alabama. Original land patents are searchable at the BLM General Land Office website: https://glorecords.blm.gov. FamilySearch collection 1919694 (Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907) covers territorial-era patents and grants beginning 1798.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish land grants (Mobile area, pre-1813), British land grants (pre-1780), deed transfers, territorial court land records
- **Date range:** Federal land sales in Alabama began ca. 1803-1808 as the territory was surveyed. Spanish-era land grants predate this.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents); ADAH (territorial records); Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Spanish grants); county courthouses (deed transfers after organization)

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Frontier militia service (ca. 1798-1800); Creek War 1813-1814; War of 1812
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; War of 1812 service records and bounty land warrants; pension files
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C., and Southeast Region (Atlanta); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for War of 1812 records; ADAH for state militia records
- **Note:** Territorial militia muster rolls can establish that a person was present in a specific community around 1800, even when census coverage is thin.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries (Catholic, Baptist) and family burial grounds; formal municipal cemeteries did not exist in most of Alabama in 1800
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Alabama cemetery records, though pre-1820 coverage is thin
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely survive for this period; DAR and local genealogical society transcriptions are the main secondary source

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Alabama area in 1800. The first Alabama newspaper appeared ca. 1811.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices began appearing after 1811; not a source for 1800 events

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf of Mexico; Spanish-controlled until 1813); New Orleans (river traffic)
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial passenger and residency lists (Mobile District); federal passenger manifests at Mobile and New Orleans (post-1820)
- **Where held:** Spanish colonial lists: Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress copies. Federal manifests (post-1820): NARA; Ancestry.com
- **Content note:** For the 1800 period, the relevant lists are Spanish administrative censuses and residency registers, not federal arrival manifests. Naturalization petitions from the territorial period were filed in territorial/county courts, even inland.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; county property and poll tax lists once counties organized
- **Date range:** Washington County tax records begin ca. 1800-1801
- **Where held:** ADAH; county courthouses; partially covered by the compiled census substitutes collections (FamilySearch 2016756 and 1927171)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing or thin census coverage in 1800-1809 and can establish that a person was present in a specific county before the 1810 federal census

- **Colonial administrative records (Spanish):** Census returns (padrones), church confirmation and marriage registers, land grants, and militia lists from the Mobile District, 1780-1813. Repository: Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress — per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

output.text_response:
**Locality Guide: Arkansas before 1800 (Spanish Colonial Period)**

Locality guide written as `loc_001`.

---

Researching ancestors in what is now Arkansas before 1800 means working **outside U.S. records entirely**: the region was a tiny French and then Spanish colonial outpost centered on **Arkansas Post**, not any kind of American jurisdiction, and the records it produced are scattered between Little Rock, New Orleans, and Seville. Here is a summary of what survives and where:

---

## Catholic Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
These are the single most important personal record type for the period.
- **FamilySearch** has digitized **64 images** of the Spanish-period registers (1763–1800), but they are in Spanish, **0% name-indexed**, and must be browsed one image at a time (image group **008814402** at FamilySearch.org).
- The **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) holds additional colonial records and transcripts.

## Spanish Administrative Records
- **Padrones** (household censuses), land grants, and **military muster rolls** are held in the **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** in Seville, Spain — the full Spanish colonial administrative archive.
- These records name residents, soldiers, and landholders but are only accessible through the AGI directly or through microfilm copies held by some research libraries.

## Land Records
- If your ancestor held land under Spain, their claim was often confirmed (or disputed) after the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The **Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office (GLO) records** contain **Spanish land grant confirmation files** that frequently describe and document the original Spanish-era claims — a very practical access point.

## Indexed U.S. Genealogy Databases
The three FamilySearch indexed collections for Arkansas **all begin after 1800** — none cover the colonial era.

---

## Most Practical Next Steps

1. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** directly — they hold colonial-era transcripts and finding aids unavailable online.
2. **Browse the FamilySearch digitized colonial volume** (image group 008814402) — unindexed, requires page-by-page reading in Spanish.
3. **Search the BLM/GLO records** for post-1803 Spanish land grant confirmation files, which often document the original grantee's Spanish-period history.
4. For deeper research, consider engaging a researcher with access to the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region Under Spanish Colonial Administration (pre-1800, c. 1686-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Period of French control:** 1686–1763 (founded Arkansas Post 1686 as part of La Louisiane)
- **Period of Spanish control:** 1763–1800 (Treaty of Paris 1763; Spain secretly ceded back to France 1800)
- **Louisiana Purchase:** 1803 (region passed to the United States)
- **Arkansas Territory:** created 1819; Arkansas State: 1836
- **Principal administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste aux Arkansas / Puesto de Arkansas), located at the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi rivers
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana (French); later Governorate of Louisiana (Spanish), administered from New Orleans under the Captaincy General of Cuba
- **Population during period:** No tool result returned population figures for this period. European settlement was sparse and concentrated almost entirely at Arkansas Post. The broader region was predominantly Native American territory (Quapaw and others).
- **Economy:** Military garrison, fur trade, small agriculture
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers and officials, some Anglo traders, Quapaw and other Native Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only organized denomination under both French and Spanish colonial rule); no Protestant congregations existed in the region before 1800
- **Key historical events:** Establishment of Arkansas Post 1686; Treaty of Paris 1763 transferring Louisiana to Spain; Spanish colonial administration 1763-1800; Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800 (secret retrocession to France); Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763, the Arkansas district was part of French Louisiana, governed from New Orleans.
- From 1763 to 1800, the same territory fell under Spanish Louisiana, still administered from New Orleans.
- In 1800 Spain secretly ceded Louisiana back to France; in 1803 the United States acquired it through the Louisiana Purchase.
- Arkansas Territory was not created until 1819, and Arkansas was not a state until 1836.
- Records from before 1800 were therefore created under French or Spanish colonial authority, not under any U.S. or Arkansas governmental jurisdiction. Searching for "Arkansas" records in standard U.S. databases will find nothing from this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this region before 1800. The Catholic Church was the sole record-keeper for vital events (births/baptisms, marriages, burials).
- **What exists:** Catholic sacramental registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — at Arkansas Post, beginning in the early 1700s under French missionaries and continuing through the Spanish period (1763-1800).
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (original registers); transcribed copies at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock; FamilySearch has digitized one volume (image group 008814402, 64 images, covering 1763-1800). Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Gaps:** Records are fragmentary. Arkansas Post was a small, isolated garrison; not all events will have been formally registered.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 registers) and Spanish (post-1763 registers under Spanish administration). Researchers must read these languages.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively. French Jesuit and later Capuchin missionaries served the post.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including Native American converts), marriages, burials, and confirmations
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock holds the primary sacramental registers. The Arkansas History Commission holds transcripts. FamilySearch has digitized 1 volume (image group 008814402, 64 images, Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, record type: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)). Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Digitization level:** BROWSE-ONLY. The FamilySearch volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be examined image by image. The 64 images span the entire 1763-1800 Spanish period.
- **Language:** French and Spanish. Records in Latin for some sacramental formulas.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses (padrones):** Under Spanish administration, colonial governors periodically ordered household censuses called padrones, listing heads of household, family members, and sometimes enslaved people or servants. For the Arkansas district, surviving padrones are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Post-1800 substitutes:** The FamilySearch collection "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124, 178,345 records) begins in 1819 and does not cover the colonial period. It may be useful for tracing descendants of colonial-era families into the early American period.
- **Federal census:** The first federal census including Arkansas was 1820 (as a territory). No federal enumeration covers the pre-1800 period.
- **Access:** No colonial-era padrones for Arkansas are available in any indexed online database. These records require physical or microfilm access through the Arkansas History Commission or Archivo General de Indias.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under Spanish colonial law, notarial acts (notarías) recorded wills, inventories, contracts, and estate matters. Military post commandants also acted as civil judges.
- **Where held:** Surviving notarial and court records from the Arkansas Post are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Digitization level:** Physical only. No online database holds indexed probate or notarial records from this period for the Arkansas region.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concesiones de tierra) were issued under the Laws of the Indies, based on a system of grants to settlers at the discretion of the colonial governor. No rectangular survey system; grants described by metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Governor of Louisiana (New Orleans) issued land grants for the Arkansas district.
- **Types:** Land concessions, confirmations, plats
- **Critical secondary source:** After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the U.S. government required all holders of French and Spanish land grants to submit their claims for confirmation. The Board of Land Commissioners reviewed these claims. The resulting files — which include copies or descriptions of original Spanish grants — are held at the National Archives (NARA) and are partially available through the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM-GLO) at glorecords.blm.gov. This is often the most accessible path to a pre-1803 land grant.
- **Primary source:** The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds original land grant documentation for Spanish Louisiana. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Numerous frontier incidents and the American Revolutionary War period (Spain allied with the American colonies against Britain)
- **Record types:** Muster rolls (revistas de comisario), service records for Spanish garrison troops, officer records
- **Where held:** Spanish military records for Louisiana are in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Archivo General Militar de Segovia (Spain). The Arkansas History Commission holds microfilm of some Spanish colonial military records from Louisiana. NARA holds records from the post-1803 American period only.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only or microfilm. No online indexed database holds Spanish military records for the Arkansas district.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The only documented pre-1800 burial ground was at Arkansas Post, associated with the Catholic mission and fort.
- **Online coverage:** No pre-1800 Arkansas cemetery records appear in FindAGrave or BillionGraves with sufficient coverage to rely on.
- **Physical records:** Burials in this period are documented primarily through the Catholic sacramental burial registers (see Church records above).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspaper was published in the Arkansas region before 1800.
- **Relevant papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (New Orleans) and other Gulf Coast papers occasionally covered Arkansas Post events in the early American period, but not before 1800.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for the Louisiana Territory. Natchez (Spanish-controlled until 1798) was a secondary point.
- **Record types:** Spanish passport records (pasaportes) and entry permissions were occasionally issued for travel within the Louisiana territory. These are held in the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Note:** Most European settlers arrived through New Orleans. There are no pre-1800 passenger lists in the modern sense for the interior settlements.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and tribute records were maintained centrally in New Orleans and ultimately in Cuba/Spain.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Museum and Louisiana State Archives may hold some Louisiana-rooted colonial tax records.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (colonial censuses) can partially substitute for tax lists.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Spanish notaries recorded contracts, wills, sales, and other legal acts. Notarial records for Louisiana (which administered the Arkansas district) are held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Archivo General de Indias.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives:** Because Arkansas Post was administered from New Orleans, notarial acts involving Arkansas Post residents may appear in New Orleans records, particularly for estate and property matters.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized browse-only volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, image group 008814402, 64 images; 0% indexed, Spanish language | Free — browse only |
| FamilySearch (indexed, post-1800) | Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 (collection 2085124, 178,345 records) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Spanish and French land grant confirmations filed post-1803 — may document pre-1800 landowners | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Louisiana Purchase-era land claim files, post-1803 territorial records | Free finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume matching Arkansas and the pre-1800 period. This is the complete result set (no nextPageToken). FamilySearch's indexed collections for Arkansas (3 total from collections_search) all begin after 1800 and do not cover the colonial period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, military records), transcribed Catholic sacramental registers, microfilm of some Archivo General de Indias holdings | In-person; some finding aids online at archives.arkansas.gov |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish Catholic sacramental registers for Arkansas Post | Contact diocesan archives; in-person or written request |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Principal administrative records of Spanish Louisiana including Arkansas district: land grants, padrones, military records, notarial records, correspondence | In-person or contracted researcher; partial digitization through PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of Spanish colonial records for Louisiana | In-person; some holdings described in the LOC catalog |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives, New Orleans, LA | Notarial acts (contracts, wills, sales) from colonial Louisiana period, including some involving Arkansas Post residents | In-person; some indexes online at notarialarchives.org |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, LA | Spanish and French colonial records for Louisiana territory | In-person; some finding aids online |
| NARA (National Archives), Washington, DC | Land claim confirmation files post-1803; U.S. territorial records post-1803 | In-person or online at archives.gov |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish padrones (colonial household censuses) for the Arkansas district
- Spanish military muster rolls and service records for the Arkansas Post garrison
- Original land concessions granted by the Spanish Governor of Louisiana
- Notarial acts (wills, estate inventories, contracts) from the colonial period
- Spanish colonial court and administrative correspondence
- French-era Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763)

## Known record losses
No tool result for this survey specifically documented destruction or loss of colonial Arkansas records. The fragmented survival of records is noted by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) without attributing losses to specific events. Given the remote frontier nature of Arkansas Post, many records may never have been created or were routinely forwarded to New Orleans or Havana rather than kept locally — this is a documentation pattern, not a confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Think Louisiana, not Arkansas.** Before 1803, the Arkansas district was administered from New Orleans under Spanish Louisiana. Any researcher who searches only Arkansas-labeled databases will find nothing. The records chain runs: Arkansas Post → New Orleans → Havana → Seville. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Start with the Arkansas History Commission.** It holds the most accessible concentration of surviving colonial records and transcripts, and is the recommended first stop before attempting the Archivo General de Indias. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402.** This is the only digitized colonial-era volume for Arkansas and covers the entire Spanish period (1763-1800) in 64 images. It is browse-only, in Spanish, and requires working through every image. Access it free at FamilySearch.org.
- **Land grant confirmation files are the key to land ownership.** After 1803, the U.S. required all pre-existing French and Spanish land claimants to file for confirmation. These files — at NARA and BLM-GLO — document who held land under the Spanish regime and often include copies or summaries of original Spanish grants. This is typically the most accessible route to a pre-1800 Arkansas landowner. (BLM-GLO: glorecords.blm.gov)
- **The Archivo General de Indias is essential for serious research.** The PARES digital portal (pares.mcu.es) provides partial online access to some digitized documents from the Archivo General de Indias. Researchers who cannot travel to Seville may wish to engage a researcher based there.
- **Catholic records span both the French and Spanish periods.** The Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission both hold sacramental registers. Contact the Diocese before assuming all registers are transcribed; originals may contain detail the transcripts do not. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Arkansas-specific pages** (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips). Consult the Arkansas Genealogy article directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy for the most current guidance.
- **Cross into neighboring colonial territories.** The Arkansas district bordered Spanish Louisiana territory to the south (present-day Louisiana), Spanish West Florida to the east, and French-claimed Illinois Country to the north. Families near these borders may appear in New Orleans, Natchez, or St. Louis colonial records.

- **Period of Spanish control:** 1763–1800 (Treaty of Paris 1763; Spain secretly ceded back to France 1800)
- **Louisiana Purchase:** 1803 (region passed to the United States)
- **Arkansas Territory:** created 1819; Arkansas State: 1836
- **Principal administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste aux Arkansas / Puesto de Arkansas), located at the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi rivers
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana (French); later Governorate of Louisiana (Spanish), administered from New Orleans under the Captaincy General of Cuba
- **Population during period:** No tool result returned population figures for this period. European settlement was sparse and concentrated almost entirely at Arkansas Post. The broader region was predominantly Native American territory (Quapaw and others).
- **Economy:** Military garrison, fur trade, small agriculture
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers and officials, some Anglo traders, Quapaw and other Native Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only organized denomination under both French and Spanish colonial rule); no Protestant congregations existed in the region before 1800
- **Key historical events:** Establishment of Arkansas Post 1686; Treaty of Paris 1763 transferring Louisiana to Spain; Spanish colonial administration 1763-1800; Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800 (secret retrocession to France); Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763, the Arkansas district was part of French Louisiana, governed from New Orleans.
- From 1763 to 1800, the same territory fell under Spanish Louisiana, still administered from New Orleans.
- In 1800 Spain secretly ceded Louisiana back to France; in 1803 the United States acquired it through the Louisiana Purchase.
- Arkansas Territory was not created until 1819, and Arkansas was not a state until 1836.
- Records from before 1800 were therefore created under French or Spanish colonial authority, not under any U.S. or Arkansas governmental jurisdiction. Searching for "Arkansas" records in standard U.S. databases will find nothing from this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this region before 1800. The Catholic Church was the sole record-keeper for vital events (births/baptisms, marriages, burials).
- **What exists:** Catholic sacramental registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — at Arkansas Post, beginning in the early 1700s under French missionaries and continuing through the Spanish period (1763-1800).
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (original registers); transcribed copies at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock; FamilySearch has digitized one volume (image group 008814402, 64 images, covering 1763-1800). Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Gaps:** Records are fragmentary. Arkansas Post was a small, isolated garrison; not all events will have been formally registered.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 registers) and Spanish (post-1763 registers under Spanish administration). Researchers must read these languages.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively. French Jesuit and later Capuchin missionaries served the post.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including Native American converts), marriages, burials, and confirmations
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock holds the primary sacramental registers. The Arkansas History Commission holds transcripts. FamilySearch has digitized 1 volume (image group 008814402, 64 images, Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, record type: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)). Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Digitization level:** BROWSE-ONLY. The FamilySearch volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be examined image by image. The 64 images span the entire 1763-1800 Spanish period.
- **Language:** French and Spanish. Records in Latin for some sacramental formulas.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses (padrones):** Under Spanish administration, colonial governors periodically ordered household censuses called padrones, listing heads of household, family members, and sometimes enslaved people or servants. For the Arkansas district, surviving padrones are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Post-1800 substitutes:** The FamilySearch collection "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124, 178,345 records) begins in 1819 and does not cover the colonial period. It may be useful for tracing descendants of colonial-era families into the early American period.
- **Federal census:** The first federal census including Arkansas was 1820 (as a territory). No federal enumeration covers the pre-1800 period.
- **Access:** No colonial-era padrones for Arkansas are available in any indexed online database. These records require physical or microfilm access through the Arkansas History Commission or Archivo General de Indias.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under Spanish colonial law, notarial acts (notarías) recorded wills, inventories, contracts, and estate matters. Military post commandants also acted as civil judges.
- **Where held:** Surviving notarial and court records from the Arkansas Post are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Digitization level:** Physical only. No online database holds indexed probate or notarial records from this period for the Arkansas region.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concesiones de tierra) were issued under the Laws of the Indies, based on a system of grants to settlers at the discretion of the colonial governor. No rectangular survey system; grants described by metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Governor of Louisiana (New Orleans) issued land grants for the Arkansas district.
- **Types:** Land concessions, confirmations, plats
- **Critical secondary source:** After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the U.S. government required all holders of French and Spanish land grants to submit their claims for confirmation. The Board of Land Commissioners reviewed these claims. The resulting files — which include copies or descriptions of original Spanish grants — are held at the National Archives (NARA) and are partially available through the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM-GLO) at glorecords.blm.gov. This is often the most accessible path to a pre-1803 land grant.
- **Primary source:** The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds original land grant documentation for Spanish Louisiana. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Numerous frontier incidents and the American Revolutionary War period (Spain allied with the American colonies against Britain)
- **Record types:** Muster rolls (revistas de comisario), service records for Spanish garrison troops, officer records
- **Where held:** Spanish military records for Louisiana are in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Archivo General Militar de Segovia (Spain). The Arkansas History Commission holds microfilm of some Spanish colonial military records from Louisiana. NARA holds records from the post-1803 American period only.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only or microfilm. No online indexed database holds Spanish military records for the Arkansas district.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The only documented pre-1800 burial ground was at Arkansas Post, associated with the Catholic mission and fort.
- **Online coverage:** No pre-1800 Arkansas cemetery records appear in FindAGrave or BillionGraves with sufficient coverage to rely on.
- **Physical records:** Burials in this period are documented primarily through the Catholic sacramental burial registers (see Church records above).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspaper was published in the Arkansas region before 1800.
- **Relevant papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (New Orleans) and other Gulf Coast papers occasionally covered Arkansas Post events in the early American period, but not before 1800.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for the Louisiana Territory. Natchez (Spanish-controlled until 1798) was a secondary point.
- **Record types:** Spanish passport records (pasaportes) and entry permissions were occasionally issued for travel within the Louisiana territory. These are held in the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Note:** Most European settlers arrived through New Orleans. There are no pre-1800 passenger lists in the modern sense for the interior settlements.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and tribute records were maintained centrally in New Orleans and ultimately in Cuba/Spain.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Museum and Louisiana State Archives may hold some Louisiana-rooted colonial tax records.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (colonial censuses) can partially substitute for tax lists.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Spanish notaries recorded contracts, wills, sales, and other legal acts. Notarial records for Louisiana (which administered the Arkansas district) are held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Archivo General de Indias.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives:** Because Arkansas Post was administered from New Orleans, notarial acts involving Arkansas Post residents may appear in New Orleans records, particularly for estate and property matters.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized browse-only volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, image group 008814402, 64 images; 0% indexed, Spanish language | Free — browse only |
| FamilySearch (indexed, post-1800) | Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 (collection 2085124, 178,345 records) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Spanish and French land grant confirmations filed post-1803 — may document pre-1800 landowners | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Louisiana Purchase-era land claim files, post-1803 territorial records | Free finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume matching Arkansas and the pre-1800 period. This is the complete result set (no nextPageToken). FamilySearch's indexed collections for Arkansas (3 total from collections_search) all begin after 1800 and do not cover the colonial period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, military records), transcribed Catholic sacramental registers, microfilm of some Archivo General de Indias holdings | In-person; some finding aids online at archives.arkansas.gov |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish Catholic sacramental registers for Arkansas Post | Contact diocesan archives; in-person or written request |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Principal administrative records of Spanish Louisiana including Arkansas district: land grants, padrones, military records, notarial records, correspondence | In-person or contracted researcher; partial digitization through PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of Spanish colonial records for Louisiana | In-person; some holdings described in the LOC catalog |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives, New Orleans, LA | Notarial acts (contracts, wills, sales) from colonial Louisiana period, including some involving Arkansas Post residents | In-person; some indexes online at notarialarchives.org |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, LA | Spanish and French colonial records for Louisiana territory | In-person; some finding aids online |
| NARA (National Archives), Washington, DC | Land claim confirmation files post-1803; U.S. territorial records post-1803 | In-person or online at archives.gov |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish padrones (colonial household censuses) for the Arkansas district
- Spanish military muster rolls and service records for the Arkansas Post garrison
- Original land concessions granted by the Spanish Governor of Louisiana
- Notarial acts (wills, estate inventories, contracts) from the colonial period
- Spanish colonial court and administrative correspondence
- French-era Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763)

## Known record losses
No tool result for this survey specifically documented destruction or loss of colonial Arkansas records. The fragmented survival of records is noted by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) without attributing losses to specific events. Given the remote frontier nature of Arkansas Post, many records may never have been created or were routinely forwarded to New Orleans or Havana rather than kept locally — this is a documentation pattern, not a confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Think Louisiana, not Arkansas.** Before 1803, the Arkansas district was administered from New Orleans under Spanish Louisiana. Any researcher who searches only Arkansas-labeled databases will find nothing. The records chain runs: Arkansas Post → New Orleans → Havana → Seville. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Start with the Arkansas History Commission.** It holds the most accessible concentration of surviving colonial records and transcripts, and is the recommended first stop before attempting the Archivo General de Indias. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402.** This is the only digitized colonial-era volume for Arkansas and covers the entire Spanish period (1763-1800) in 64 images. It is browse-only, in Spanish, and requires working through every image. Access it free at FamilySearch.org.
- **Land grant confirmation files are the key to land ownership.** After 1803, the U.S. required all pre-existing French and Spanish land claimants to file for confirmation. These files — at NARA and BLM-GLO — document who held land under the Spanish regime and often include copies or summaries of original Spanish grants. This is typically the most accessible route to a pre-1800 Arkansas landowner. (BLM-GLO: glorecords.blm.gov)
- **The Archivo General de Indias is essential for serious research.** The PARES digital portal (pares.mcu.es) provides partial online access to some digitized documents from the Archivo General de Indias. Researchers who cannot travel to Seville may wish to engage a researcher based there.
- **Catholic records span both the French and Spanish periods.** The Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission both hold sacramental registers. Contact the Diocese before assuming all registers are transcribed; originals may contain detail the transcripts do not. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Arkansas-specific pages** (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips). Consult the Arkansas Genealogy article directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy for the most current guidance.
- **Cross into neighboring colonial territories.** The Arkansas district bordered Spanish Louisiana territory to the south (present-day Louisiana), Spanish West Florida to the east, and French-claimed Illinois Country to the north. Families near these borders may appear in New Orleans, Natchez, or St. Louis colonial records.

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality guide found for Ohio circa 1790:

---

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means working in a place that was not yet a state and had barely been organized as a territory. The **Northwest Ordinance of 1787** created the Northwest Territory, and by 1790 only two counties had been carved out of it:

- **Washington County** (from 1788, covering most of what is now Ohio)
- **Hamilton County** (from January 1790, covering the Cincinnati area)

Every record created in 1790 Ohio lives under one of those two county governments, and searching the wrong county is the single most common mistake for this era.

---

### Records Available Despite Early Gaps

**Vital Records:** There was no civil system for registering births or deaths in 1790. **Church baptism and burial registers** are the main substitute — FamilySearch holds a collection of Ohio church records beginning in 1787.

**Land Records (richest source for this period):** Ohio land was distributed under three separate systems with three separate repositories:

| Land District | Repository |
|---|---|
| Virginia Military District | Virginia State Library, Richmond |
| Connecticut Western Reserve | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| Federal Lands | BLM General Land Office website (free) |

**Census:** The **1790 federal census** enumerated the Northwest Territory and is a critical anchor document.

**Digitized Image Volumes:** Two digitized FamilySearch volumes exist for 1788–1803, but both are largely **unindexed** and must be browsed image by image. The **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus holds early county records not yet digitized.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Build a research plan targeting the specific county and land district your ancestor was in, using the 1790 census and land records as the starting point. Knowing whether your ancestor was in the Virginia Military District, the Western Reserve, or federal lands is essential — each has a different record trail and repository.

quirks: In 1790, Ohio was the Northwest Territory, not a state — records were created under territorial authority and under only two counties: Washington County (organized 1788, covering most of present-day Ohio) and Hamilton County (organized January 2, 1790, covering the southwestern corner). Determine which county covered the specific locality before searching any record set.

No civil vital registration existed in 1790 Ohio. Church records (FamilySearch collection 2246917, Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950) are the primary source for births, marriages, and deaths in this period.

Land records in Ohio are geographically split into three distinct systems with separate repositories: Virginia Military District records (between Scioto and Little Miami rivers) are at the Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve records (northeastern Ohio) are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland; federal land patents (remaining areas) are at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov). Which system held an ancestor's land depends on where in Ohio they settled.
DGS 005112233 (Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799, 51 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image.

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records, Land Records, Church Records, Probate Records, and Census all returned only generic fallback content during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for current record-level guidance.

Washington County (1788) records before Hamilton County's formation (1790) cover all of what is now southwestern Ohio — search Washington County for any event before January 2, 1790, even in areas that later became Hamilton County.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory era, ca. 1790)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of July 13, 1787. It included present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota (Wikipedia). Ohio was the first state carved from it, admitted March 1, 1803.
- **Administrative center (territorial era):** Marietta (Washington County seat from 1788); Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat from 1790).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (1787–1803); before 1787, no organized U.S. civil government existed over the region.

- Northwest Territory territorial court records (not surfaced in collections or volume_search)
- Washington County and Hamilton County probate records pre-1803 (not returned in volume_search)
- Virginia Military District warrants at the Virginia State Library (not confirmed digitized in tool results)
- Connecticut Western Reserve land records at the Western Reserve Historical Society (not confirmed in FamilySearch collections)
- Territorial legislative and administrative records

## Known record losses
No tool result returned during this survey stated that any specific Ohio or Northwest Territory record set was destroyed or lost. Sparse tool results for 1787–1803 reflect digitization gaps, not confirmed losses. Verify the survival of specific early county records with the Ohio History Connection or the relevant county courthouse before concluding a record is gone.

## Research tips
- **Determine the county first.** In 1790, only two counties existed in what is now Ohio: Washington County (formed 1788) and Hamilton County (formed January 2, 1790). Every record was created under one of them. For any event before January 2, 1790, search Washington County even if the location later became part of Hamilton County. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Land records are the primary genealogical source.** With no civil vital registration and sparse church records, land grants, warrants, patents, surveys, and deed books are the best evidence for 1790 Ohio ancestors. Know which of the three land systems (Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve, or federal) covered your ancestor's location before choosing a repository. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Virginia Military District warrants link service to settlement.** An ancestor with a VMD land claim almost certainly served in the Revolutionary War. The warrant file names the veteran and may name heirs; cross-reference with NARA pension files. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland, not Columbus.** Do not assume all early Ohio records are at the Ohio History Connection. The Western Reserve Historical Society holds land records specific to northeastern Ohio. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Use the 1790 federal census as your anchor.** It enumerated Washington and Hamilton counties of the Northwest Territory and places an ancestor in Ohio at that exact date. It is indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Church records substitute for missing vital records.** No civil birth or death registration existed in 1790 Ohio. Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker, and Catholic registers are the primary source for baptisms and burials. Search FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (id 2246917).
- **Browse-only volumes require image-by-image work.** DGS 005112233 (Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799, 51 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Plan time to browse every image.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Ohio-specific pages returned only generic content** during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for the most current record-level guidance on this jurisdiction.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

California in the 1850s was the destination of roughly 300,000 migrants drawn by the Gold Rush, and the records that survive reflect a population that was transient, ethnically diverse, and arriving by both sea and overland routes. The most important surviving sources are the 1852 California state census (88% name-indexed on FamilySearch), ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals held at the National Archives in San Bruno, county-level birth and marriage records beginning in 1850, the Great Registers (voter registration, beginning 1866), mining claim filings at county recorders' offices, and Gold Rush diaries and manuscripts at the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley. The biggest warnings are that the 1850 federal census was partially destroyed for California, that county boundaries shifted constantly through the 1850s and 1860s so a mining camp may have been in a different county than you expect, and that overland migrants left no arrival record comparable to a ship manifest and must be traced through census, mining claims, and newspapers instead.

The next step is to narrow to a specific county or mining district where your ancestor is believed to have been and run a county-level locality survey, since most records in California for this period were created and held at the county level.
