quirks: The 1850 federal census, the first taken in California, was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing; verify which counties survive before treating a negative result as conclusive.
Civil registration in the 1850s was at the county level only; no statewide vital registration requirement existed for this period.
Great Registers (voter registration) begin in 1866 and do not cover the first decade of the Gold Rush; they are the earliest comprehensive statewide name index for adult males.
Mining claim records are filed at county recorders' offices; the FamilySearch digitized volume covering San Francisco 1849-1855 is browse-only with no name index.
Ship passenger manifests cover sea arrivals at San Francisco only — held at NARA San Bruno; overland migrants left no equivalent arrival record.
California is a federal-land state — original land grants and patents are held by the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office, not the county courthouse.

14 digitized volumes match this place and period on FamilySearch; only 3 are detailed in this guide (first page of results). Additional volumes including probate, court, and other county records remain unsurveyed — request further pages for a complete picture.
Mission records (pre-statehood, largely in Latin and Spanish) primarily document Native Californian and Hispanic populations under Franciscan administration, not Gold Rush arrivals.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. It was previously under Mexican sovereignty (1821–1848) and before that Spanish colonial territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** State capital Sacramento (from 1854); San Francisco was the dominant port and commercial center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal land state)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 93,000 at the 1850 census; approximately 380,000 by 1860 (per Wikipedia). The population was initially transient and predominantly male.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855; agriculture, ranching, trade, and commerce expanded through the 1860s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Extraordinarily diverse — U.S.-born Anglo-Americans, Irish, German, French, Chilean, Mexican, Chinese, and smaller groups from across the world, plus California Native populations.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant pre-statehood via Spanish missions); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal) expanded rapidly after 1849; Chinese folk religion and Buddhist temples in mining camps.
- **Key historical events:** Discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill, Coloma (January 24, 1848); statehood (1850); end of the main gold rush c. 1855; Comstock Lode silver rush in adjacent Nevada (1859) drew population eastward; Civil War era saw California remain in the Union with significant volunteer military activity.

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union as a single state in 1850. Its internal county structure changed frequently: the original 27 counties of 1850 grew to 49 by 1870 as mining regions were subdivided.
- Records are filed at the **county** level for most civil purposes. When researching a specific mining camp or town, identify the county it belonged to at the event date — not the modern county, which may differ due to subdivision.
- Pre-statehood (before September 1850), California was under U.S. military governance (1848–1850) and Mexican civil law before that. Records from this brief transition period are sparse.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level birth and marriage records begin in 1850. FamilySearch's "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (collection 2017276) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (collection 1452832) confirm this. The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California vital records did not return California-specific content in this survey; a California-specific statewide registration requirement date is not confirmed by the tools used here. The general FamilySearch guidance (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s.
- **What exists:** County birth records (1850–), county marriage records (1850–), county death records (year range not confirmed by tool results for this survey).
- **Where held:** County clerks and county recorders. FamilySearch holds digitized collections: County Births (collection 2017276, 789,456 records) and County Marriages (collection 1452832, 567,890 records).
- **Gaps:** The 1850s were years of very high population mobility; many individuals died or left without generating local civil records. Recording compliance was inconsistent in the early years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); newspapers; probate records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant pre-1848 through mission network); Protestant denominations established rapidly after 1849.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Pre-statehood Mission records:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (98,765 records) covers Franciscan mission baptisms, marriages, and burials. These records are primarily in Latin and Spanish and document Native Californian and Hispanic populations — not Gold Rush arrivals.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Sacramento); FamilySearch microfilm. The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California church records did not return California-specific content in this survey.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Latin and Spanish. Post-1848 Catholic and Protestant records are predominantly in English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 (first taken in California — partially destroyed; some county returns are missing per the FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records); 1860; 1870. Mortality schedules accompany 1850, 1860, and 1870 censuses.
- **State census:** The California state census of 1852 is a critical Gold Rush-era source. FamilySearch has digitized a volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images) covering the state census 1850–1852, which is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **Indexed + images**.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census volume on FamilySearch is highly accessible. Federal census years (1850, 1860, 1870) are available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, naturalizations, name changes, civil and criminal suits.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850 for original counties).
- **Where held:** County courthouses and state archives. The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California probate records did not return California-specific content in this survey; consult the California State Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) and county superior court records directly.
- **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. California courts all accepted declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization. Search county court minute books as well as dedicated naturalization dockets.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (California is a public-land/federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government distributed public land. Original patents and homestead entries are held by the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO): https://www.glorecords.blm.gov/. County recorders hold deed books for subsequent transfers.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, deeds, mortgages, tax records, mining claims.
- **Mining claims specifically:** Filed at county recorders' offices. FamilySearch has digitized Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images) — **browse-only images** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California land and property records did not return California-specific content in this survey.**

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) preceded the Gold Rush; many veterans settled in California. The Civil War (1861–1865) saw California raise volunteer regiments; there was also conflict with Native populations throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); bounty land warrant records for Mexican-American War veterans; Civil War draft registrations (1863); California volunteer unit muster rolls at the California State Military Museum and California State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA Washington D.C. and San Bruno, CA; California State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Rush-era cemeteries are scattered across Sierra Nevada foothills mining counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne). Many were informal camp burials.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has transcriptions for many California cemeteries, including Gold Rush counties.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for early cemeteries are often held by local historical societies; many early camp burials have no surviving records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco had multiple newspapers by 1849 (Alta California, Daily Herald). Mining county papers proliferated through the 1850s.
- **Where held:** California State Library (Sacramento); Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) carries historical California newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mining partnership notices, legal notices, ship arrival announcements. For men who left no vital records, a newspaper death notice may be the only documentation of their presence and death in California.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was by far the primary port of entry for sea arrivals. Sacramento served as an inland arrival point for riverboat connections.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (ship manifests) held at NARA San Bruno for San Francisco arrivals (per FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849–1858 are digitized on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images) — **browse-only images** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Overland migrants:** Those who came via the Overland Trail, Santa Fe Trail, or Panama route left no formal arrival record comparable to ship manifests. Document their presence through census, mining claims, and church records instead.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Naturalization:** Declarations of intention and petitions were filed in California courts (any court of record, pre-1906). These often state the country of origin and can predate other identifying records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax; the state also levied a Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, renewed 1852) specifically targeting non-citizen miners — primarily Chinese and Latin American.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850).
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and state archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can place a person in a county in years between censuses and are especially valuable for the 1853–1859 intercensal gap.
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records** are a unique source for tracking Chinese and other immigrant miners.

### Other record types
- **Mining partnership and claim records:** County recorders' offices hold mining claim filings. FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume of San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (006601002).
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** FamilySearch collection 1923340 "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (1,345,678 records) provides a near-comprehensive name index of adult male citizens from 1866 onward. Does not cover the 1848–1865 period. Records typically include name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description — valuable for linking a Gold Rush arrival to a later settled identity.
- **City directories:** San Francisco city directories began in the late 1840s and continued through the period; Sacramento and other cities followed. Held at the California State Library and Bancroft Library.
- **Overland trail diaries and journals:** The Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley holds extensive manuscript collections of Gold Rush diaries, letters, and journals that may document your ancestor's journey and early California years (per FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/) | County Births 1850–1919 (collection 2017276, 789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (collection 1452832, 567,890 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (collection 1923340, 1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (collection 1804372, 98,765 records); California State Census 1850–1852 (imageGroup 006601001, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers San Francisco 1849–1855 (imageGroup 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849–1858 (imageGroup 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census 1850, 1860, 1870; additional California collections | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records including ship manifests, naturalization, military | Free/fee varies |
| BLM GLO (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov/) | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848–1870 on FamilySearch. The 3 volumes detailed above represent the first page of results only. A `nextPageToken` was returned, meaning 11 additional volumes were not examined. The researcher should request further pages for a complete picture of digitized holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County court records, state government records, naturalization records | In-person / online finding aids |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, journals, maps | In-person; some digitized |
| California State Library, Sacramento | State publications, newspapers, city directories, local histories | In-person / some digital |
| NARA San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco; federal court records; military records for the Pacific region | In-person / records request |
| County courthouses (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne, etc.) | Deeds, probate files, mining claims, court minutes | In-person / correspondence |
| Archdiocese of San Francisco / Diocese of Sacramento archives | Catholic sacramental registers | Contact archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- Most **county court minute books** for 1850s California: physical at county courthouses and California State Archives.
- Most **county deed books and grantor-grantee indexes** for the 1850s: physical at county recorders' offices (some partially digitized).
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records**: physical at county level; digitization status not confirmed by tool results.
- **City directory originals** beyond major cities: physical at California State Library and Bancroft Library.
- **Overland trail diaries and Gold Rush manuscripts**: primarily physical or digitized only at holding institution (Bancroft Library).
- **Probate estate files** for most counties: physical at county superior courts or California State Archives; digitization coverage is not confirmed for the 1850s by this survey.

## Known record losses
- The **1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing (per FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census is the primary substitute for missing 1850 returns.
- Many early mining camp and informal community records were never formally created or have not survived. No tool result in this survey specified destruction of additional record sets.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census**, which is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroup 006601001) and partially fills the gap caused by partial destruction of the 1850 federal census. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

California in the 1850s was the destination of roughly 300,000 migrants drawn by the Gold Rush, and the records that survive reflect a population that was transient, ethnically diverse, and arriving by both sea and overland routes. The most important surviving sources are the 1852 California state census (88% name-indexed on FamilySearch), ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals held at the National Archives in San Bruno, county-level birth and marriage records beginning in 1850, the Great Registers (voter registration, beginning 1866), mining claim filings at county recorders' offices, and Gold Rush diaries and manuscripts at the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley. The biggest warnings are that the 1850 federal census was partially destroyed for California, that county boundaries shifted constantly through the 1850s and 1860s so a mining camp may have been in a different county than you expect, and that overland migrants left no arrival record comparable to a ship manifest and must be traced through census, mining claims, and newspapers instead.

The next step is to narrow to a specific county or mining district where your ancestor is believed to have been and run a county-level locality survey, since most records in California for this period were created and held at the county level.

quirks: The 1850 federal census, the first taken in California, was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing; verify which counties survive before treating a negative result as conclusive.
Civil registration in the 1850s was at the county level only; no statewide vital registration requirement existed for this period.
Great Registers (voter registration) begin in 1866 and do not cover the first decade of the Gold Rush; they are the earliest comprehensive statewide name index for adult males.
Mining claim records are filed at county recorders' offices; the FamilySearch digitized volume covering San Francisco 1849-1855 is browse-only with no name index.
Ship passenger manifests cover sea arrivals at San Francisco only — held at NARA San Bruno; overland migrants left no equivalent arrival record.
California is a federal-land state — original land grants and patents are held by the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office, not the county courthouse.

Mission records (pre-statehood, largely in Latin and Spanish) primarily document Native Californian and Hispanic populations under Franciscan administration, not Gold Rush arrivals.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. It was previously under Mexican sovereignty (1821–1848) and before that Spanish colonial territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** State capital Sacramento (from 1854); San Francisco was the dominant port and commercial center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal land state)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 93,000 at the 1850 census; approximately 380,000 by 1860 (per Wikipedia). The population was initially transient and predominantly male.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855; agriculture, ranching, trade, and commerce expanded through the 1860s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Extraordinarily diverse — U.S.-born Anglo-Americans, Irish, German, French, Chilean, Mexican, Chinese, and smaller groups from across the world, plus California Native populations.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant pre-statehood via Spanish missions); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal) expanded rapidly after 1849; Chinese folk religion and Buddhist temples in mining camps.
- **Key historical events:** Discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill, Coloma (January 24, 1848); statehood (1850); end of the main gold rush c. 1855; Comstock Lode silver rush in adjacent Nevada (1859) drew population eastward; Civil War era saw California remain in the Union with significant volunteer military activity.

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union as a single state in 1850. Its internal county structure changed frequently: the original 27 counties of 1850 grew to 49 by 1870 as mining regions were subdivided.
- Records are filed at the **county** level for most civil purposes. When researching a specific mining camp or town, identify the county it belonged to at the event date — not the modern county, which may differ due to subdivision.
- Pre-statehood (before September 1850), California was under U.S. military governance (1848–1850) and Mexican civil law before that. Records from this brief transition period are sparse.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level birth and marriage records begin in 1850. FamilySearch's "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (collection 2017276) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (collection 1452832) confirm this. The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California vital records did not return California-specific content in this survey; a California-specific statewide registration requirement date is not confirmed by the tools used here. The general FamilySearch guidance (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s.
- **What exists:** County birth records (1850–), county marriage records (1850–), county death records (year range not confirmed by tool results for this survey).
- **Where held:** County clerks and county recorders. FamilySearch holds digitized collections: County Births (collection 2017276, 789,456 records) and County Marriages (collection 1452832, 567,890 records).
- **Gaps:** The 1850s were years of very high population mobility; many individuals died or left without generating local civil records. Recording compliance was inconsistent in the early years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); newspapers; probate records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant pre-1848 through mission network); Protestant denominations established rapidly after 1849.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Pre-statehood Mission records:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (98,765 records) covers Franciscan mission baptisms, marriages, and burials. These records are primarily in Latin and Spanish and document Native Californian and Hispanic populations — not Gold Rush arrivals.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Sacramento); FamilySearch microfilm. The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California church records did not return California-specific content in this survey.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Latin and Spanish. Post-1848 Catholic and Protestant records are predominantly in English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 (first taken in California — partially destroyed; some county returns are missing per the FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records); 1860; 1870. Mortality schedules accompany 1850, 1860, and 1870 censuses.
- **State census:** The California state census of 1852 is a critical Gold Rush-era source. FamilySearch has digitized a volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images) covering the state census 1850–1852, which is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **Indexed + images**.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census volume on FamilySearch is highly accessible. Federal census years (1850, 1860, 1870) are available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, naturalizations, name changes, civil and criminal suits.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850 for original counties).
- **Where held:** County courthouses and state archives. The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California probate records did not return California-specific content in this survey; consult the California State Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) and county superior court records directly.
- **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. California courts all accepted declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization. Search county court minute books as well as dedicated naturalization dockets.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (California is a public-land/federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government distributed public land. Original patents and homestead entries are held by the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO): https://www.glorecords.blm.gov/. County recorders hold deed books for subsequent transfers.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, deeds, mortgages, tax records, mining claims.
- **Mining claims specifically:** Filed at county recorders' offices. FamilySearch has digitized Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images) — **browse-only images** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page specific to California land and property records did not return California-specific content in this survey.**

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) preceded the Gold Rush; many veterans settled in California. The Civil War (1861–1865) saw California raise volunteer regiments; there was also conflict with Native populations throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); bounty land warrant records for Mexican-American War veterans; Civil War draft registrations (1863); California volunteer unit muster rolls at the California State Military Museum and California State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA Washington D.C. and San Bruno, CA; California State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Rush-era cemeteries are scattered across Sierra Nevada foothills mining counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne). Many were informal camp burials.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has transcriptions for many California cemeteries, including Gold Rush counties.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for early cemeteries are often held by local historical societies; many early camp burials have no surviving records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco had multiple newspapers by 1849 (Alta California, Daily Herald). Mining county papers proliferated through the 1850s.
- **Where held:** California State Library (Sacramento); Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) carries historical California newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mining partnership notices, legal notices, ship arrival announcements. For men who left no vital records, a newspaper death notice may be the only documentation of their presence and death in California.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was by far the primary port of entry for sea arrivals. Sacramento served as an inland arrival point for riverboat connections.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (ship manifests) held at NARA San Bruno for San Francisco arrivals (per FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849–1858 are digitized on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images) — **browse-only images** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Overland migrants:** Those who came via the Overland Trail, Santa Fe Trail, or Panama route left no formal arrival record comparable to ship manifests. Document their presence through census, mining claims, and church records instead.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Naturalization:** Declarations of intention and petitions were filed in California courts (any court of record, pre-1906). These often state the country of origin and can predate other identifying records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax; the state also levied a Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, renewed 1852) specifically targeting non-citizen miners — primarily Chinese and Latin American.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850).
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and state archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can place a person in a county in years between censuses and are especially valuable for the 1853–1859 intercensal gap.
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records** are a unique source for tracking Chinese and other immigrant miners.

### Other record types
- **Mining partnership and claim records:** County recorders' offices hold mining claim filings. FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume of San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (006601002).
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** FamilySearch collection 1923340 "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (1,345,678 records) provides a near-comprehensive name index of adult male citizens from 1866 onward. Does not cover the 1848–1865 period. Records typically include name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description — valuable for linking a Gold Rush arrival to a later settled identity.
- **City directories:** San Francisco city directories began in the late 1840s and continued through the period; Sacramento and other cities followed. Held at the California State Library and Bancroft Library.
- **Overland trail diaries and journals:** The Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley holds extensive manuscript collections of Gold Rush diaries, letters, and journals that may document your ancestor's journey and early California years (per FamilySearch Wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/) | County Births 1850–1919 (collection 2017276, 789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (collection 1452832, 567,890 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (collection 1923340, 1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (collection 1804372, 98,765 records); California State Census 1850–1852 (imageGroup 006601001, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers San Francisco 1849–1855 (imageGroup 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849–1858 (imageGroup 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census 1850, 1860, 1870; additional California collections | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records including ship manifests, naturalization, military | Free/fee varies |
| BLM GLO (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov/) | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848–1870 on FamilySearch. The 3 volumes detailed above represent the first page of results only. A `nextPageToken` was returned, meaning 11 additional volumes were not examined. The researcher should request further pages for a complete picture of digitized holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County court records, state government records, naturalization records | In-person / online finding aids |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, journals, maps | In-person; some digitized |
| California State Library, Sacramento | State publications, newspapers, city directories, local histories | In-person / some digital |
| NARA San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco; federal court records; military records for the Pacific region | In-person / records request |
| County courthouses (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne, etc.) | Deeds, probate files, mining claims, court minutes | In-person / correspondence |
| Archdiocese of San Francisco / Diocese of Sacramento archives | Catholic sacramental registers | Contact archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- Most **county court minute books** for 1850s California: physical at county courthouses and California State Archives.
- Most **county deed books and grantor-grantee indexes** for the 1850s: physical at county recorders' offices (some partially digitized).
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records**: physical at county level; digitization status not confirmed by tool results.
- **City directory originals** beyond major cities: physical at California State Library and Bancroft Library.
- **Overland trail diaries and Gold Rush manuscripts**: primarily physical or digitized only at holding institution (Bancroft Library).
- **Probate estate files** for most counties: physical at county superior courts or California State Archives; digitization coverage is not confirmed for the 1850s by this survey.

## Known record losses

- **The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** holds the most extensive Gold Rush manuscript collection in existence, including diaries, letters, and reminiscences that may document specific individuals not found in official records. ---

New York City in the 1700s was part of the **Province of New York** under British colonial rule (the Dutch had founded it as New Amsterdam in 1626 and the English took it in 1664), governed at the county level through **New York County** — essentially Manhattan island.

**Key context: no civil registration existed** during the entire 1700s, so church registers are the only primary source for vital events (births, marriages, deaths).

---

### Most Important Record Types & Repositories

**Church Registers (the backbone of colonial NYC research)**
- **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest continuous records, beginning 1639 through the colonial period (written in Dutch; patronymic naming conventions complicate indexing through the mid-1700s)
- **Trinity Church (Anglican)** — founded 1697, continuous registers
- **Presbyterian registers**
- FamilySearch holds a **New York Church Records (1640–1940)** collection covering this period; Dutch Reformed volumes for 1700–1776 exist but must be browsed image-by-image (no name index)

**Probate Records**
- Colonial probate was handled by the **Prerogative Court of New York** (state level, not local county court)
- The **New-York Historical Society's *Abstracts of Wills*** series is the essential published index before searching original volumes
- FamilySearch: **New York Probate Records (1629–1971)**

**Land Records**
- FamilySearch: **New York Land Records (1630–1975)**

**Tax & Assessment Lists**
- Ward-level tax assessment rolls serve as a substitute census before 1790; however, FamilySearch's Tax Assessment Rolls collection begins only in 1799
- Earlier ward lists exist in manuscript at physical repositories

**Census / Population**
- The **first federal census was 1790**, so for earlier decades you rely on church registers and tax lists to place people in time and location

---

### Key Physical Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | Colonial manuscripts, Prerogative Court probate records |
| **New-York Historical Society** (Manhattan) | Probate abstracts, manuscripts, church records |
| **New York Genealogical and Biographical Society** (Manhattan) | Published abstracts, vital record compilations |

---

### Research Strategy for the 1700s

1. **Start with church registers** — identify the family's denomination, then search Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity), and Presbyterian registers in sequence
2. **Search probate records** — the Prerogative Court wills and administrations establish family relationships and name heirs
3. **Use land records** — deeds name grantors/grantees and sometimes family members
4. **Watch for Dutch patronymics** — through the mid-1700s, a son took his father's given name as a surname (e.g., Jan Pietersen = Jan, son of Pieter), which creates indexing mismatches

For families who remain elusive through these sources, a research plan sequencing church registers by denomination, followed by probate and land records, is the recommended path forward.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established as a Dutch colonial settlement in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York.
- **County-level jurisdiction during 1700s:** New York County (Manhattan island). The broader provincial government was the Province of New York.
- **Administrative center:** City of New York (lower Manhattan).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colony, 1664–1783); became New York State after 1783.
- **Population during period:** No reliable population figure was returned by the population tool for this place and period. Wikipedia notes NYC was a major commercial port and administrative center throughout the 1700s with substantial growth through the century.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, merchant commerce, artisan manufacturing, a major transatlantic port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch (the founding population, prominent through the 1700s), English (dominant administratively after 1664), French Huguenot, German, and Jewish communities also present. A significant enslaved African population was present throughout the colonial period.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous institutional presence), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, established 1697), Presbyterian (First Presbyterian Church), Lutheran, French Huguenot, Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation, established 1654), and Quaker congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Leisler's Rebellion (1689–1691); Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); King George's War (1744–1748); French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783, British occupation of NYC 1776–1783); NYC serves as first U.S. capital (1785–1790).

## Boundary changes
- Throughout the 1700s, New York City was coterminous with New York County (present-day Manhattan). The five modern boroughs did not exist; the surrounding counties (Kings, Queens, Richmond, Westchester) were separate jurisdictions.
- The transition from Provincial to State government in 1783 did not change the geographic jurisdiction but shifted custody of ongoing record series from colonial to state authorities.
- No internal boundary change split the city during this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** New York State did not have civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records, Church Records, and related topics all returned only generic content rather than New York-specific registration dates — no specific statewide start date is confirmed by tool results for this survey. The FamilySearch collection "New York, County Marriages" (id: 1920153) begins in 1847, confirming that county-level civil marriage registration did not exist in the 1700s.
- **What exists in this period:** None. There was no civil registration system.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the only primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials during the 1700s. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records from 1639, the oldest continuous series in NYC); Anglican/Trinity Church (established 1697); First Presbyterian Church; Lutheran; French Huguenot; Jewish congregation Shearith Israel; Quaker. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (christenings), marriages, burials, and confirmations. Dutch Reformed registers are the most extensive for the early 1700s.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id: 1469062) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062 — this state-level collection covers the target period.
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers for New York City, covering 1700–1776 (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images). This volume is **browse-only** — it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed image by image. The language is Dutch; the researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script to use it.
- **Where held:** Original registers are held by individual denominational archives. The Dutch Reformed registers are held by the Reformed Church in America archives (New Brunswick, NJ). Anglican/Trinity Church records are held by Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan). The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold transcripts and published abstracts of many colonial church records. (Source: wiki_search result.)
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch through at least the mid-1700s. Anglican registers are in English. Latin may appear in some Lutheran or formal ecclesiastical entries.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790. No national enumeration exists for 1700–1789.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No colonial enumeration specific to NYC was identified in tool results. Colonial militia rolls listing men of military age were maintained by the Province of New York and are noted in wiki_search results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records) as surviving for some years.
- **Substitute sources:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards (see Tax Records below). Church registers can partially substitute for population enumeration.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is available indexed online through FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Colonial-era probate:** Wills and administrations in colonial New York were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York**, not at the local county court level. This is a critical quirk — searching a county court series will not find 18th-century wills.
- **Published index:** The New-York Historical Society published "Abstracts of Wills" covering the colonial and early statewide period. This is the recommended starting point for probate searches before browsing original court records.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780 — date range spans the target period.
- **Other court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City handled civil and some criminal matters. Records of the Mayor's Court are noted as a key colonial source in wiki_search results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). The New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives also contain court-related materials.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany) holds the colonial Prerogative Court records and colonial manuscripts. FamilySearch has microfilmed portions.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not rectangular survey — New York is an original-colony state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Province of New York (and before it, New Netherland) granted land patents through the colonial governor. The specific office holding those grants is the New York State Archives and the New York State Office of General Services; the FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Land and Property returned only generic content for this survey.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654 — covers the entire colonial and target period.
- **Types:** Land patents, grants, deeds, and conveyances. Wiki_search results specifically name land conveyances as a key colonial record type (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk (Manhattan) for deed records; New York State Archives for colonial patents and grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Provincial militia rolls (men of military age; noted by wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records as surviving for some years); Revolutionary War service records and pension files for post-1775 service.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) holds Revolutionary War service and pension records. The New York State Archives holds colonial militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized NARA military records online.
- **Access:** Revolutionary War pension files are indexed and available through NARA and Fold3. Colonial militia rolls are not fully indexed; status online is not confirmed by tool results.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (lower Manhattan) is one of the oldest and most documented. Dutch Reformed congregation had associated burial grounds. Jewish congregation Shearith Israel had its own cemetery (the Chatham Square Cemetery, dating to the 1680s, is among the oldest Jewish cemeteries in North America).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes headstone inscriptions for many NYC colonial cemeteries. Coverage is uneven for 1700s stones.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers vary by congregation; many were kept only by the church. Trinity Church has published transcripts of its early burial register.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (established 1725, the first newspaper in New York) published legal notices, shipping news, and some vital notices. Additional papers appeared later in the century.
- **Content value:** Obituaries were uncommon in 18th-century papers; legal notices, estate advertisements, and runaway servant/slave notices are more typical.
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper digitization varies. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some holdings. The New-York Historical Society and NYPL hold original and microfilmed runs.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of New York was the primary port of entry for colonial NYC. Ships arrived from England, the Netherlands, Germany, France, and West Africa (the latter via the slave trade).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for the 1700s are incomplete and fragmentary; systematic manifests did not begin until the 1820 Steerage Act. Earlier arrivals may appear in published ship passenger abstracts compiled by genealogical societies.
- **Naturalization:** Before 1790, naturalization in colonial New York was handled at the colony level; records are in the colonial manuscripts at the New York State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; published abstracts held by NYGS and NY Historical Society.
- **Content note:** Systematic passenger manifests listing all persons aboard (including children) did not apply to the colonial 1700s. Published abstracts are the primary research tool.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Ward-level tax assessment lists for real and personal property. Wiki_search results note that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial NYC (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432 — this collection only reaches the very end of the target period (1799–1804) and covers only those years.
- **Substitute value:** For years before 1790 (before the federal census), surviving ward tax lists are among the best substitutes for population enumeration, placing individuals at a specific ward in a specific year.
- **Where held:** New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives hold pre-1799 assessment materials; their digitization status is not confirmed by tool results for this survey.

### Other record types
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York State Archives holds the colonial government's administrative records — council minutes, governor's correspondence, colonial laws, and related materials — which name merchants, officeholders, and others who appear nowhere else. Wiki_search identifies these as a key source (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&BS):** Holds and has published extensive transcripts, abstracts, and indexes of colonial NYC records. Their journal and database are major research resources.
- **New-York Historical Society:** Holds manuscript collections, published "Abstracts of Wills," and other colonial-era finding aids.
- **City directories:** New York City directories began in the 1780s. These are useful for locating individuals after that date.
- **Records of enslaved persons:** Bills of sale, estate inventories listing enslaved people as property, runaway advertisements in newspapers, and manumission records all name enslaved individuals. These are the primary record types for researching African American ancestors in colonial NYC. The NYC Municipal Archives and NYHS hold relevant collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (id 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (id 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (id 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id 1678432); 1 digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776 (browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | Federal census 1790 and later; some colonial records via digitization partnerships | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Revolutionary War military records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions including Trinity Church and colonial graveyards | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Federal records, Revolutionary War pension and service files | Free (some records) |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for New York City, 1700–1800 (totalResults: 1; this is the complete result set). Collections_search returned 5 indexed collections at the New York state scope; 4 of those overlap the target period. The external links search returned 6 results that appear to be generic national-level resources rather than NYC-specific curated links.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; Prerogative Court probate records; colonial militia rolls; colonial land patents | In-person; some online finding aids |
| New York City Municipal Archives (Manhattan) | City government records including some tax and administrative records | In-person; some online |
| New-York Historical Society (Manhattan) | Manuscripts; Abstracts of Wills; colonial-era finding aids | In-person; some materials digitized |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (Manhattan) | Transcripts, indexes, and published abstracts of colonial NYC records; the NYG&B Record journal | In-person and online membership database |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (New Brunswick, NJ) | Original Dutch Reformed church registers | In-person; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan) | Anglican registers from 1697; burial records | In-person by appointment |
| New York Public Library (Manhattan) | Local history and genealogy division; city directories from 1780s; newspapers | In-person; some digital |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1799 ward tax assessment lists: existence confirmed by wiki_search; digitization status not confirmed.
- Colonial militia rolls (pre-1775): existence confirmed by wiki_search; not confirmed as indexed or fully digitized.
- Mayor's Court records (colonial): existence confirmed by wiki_search; online status not confirmed.
- Original Dutch Reformed registers beyond imageGroupNumber 007733180: the single digitized volume covers 1700–1776 at 0% indexing; additional volumes or post-1776 registers are not confirmed as digitized in this survey.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) registers: physical archives confirmed; online digitization status beyond what FamilySearch's Church Records collection may include is not confirmed by tool results.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts: held at New York State Archives; digitization status not confirmed.
- Records relating to enslaved persons (bills of sale, manumissions, inventories): held at NYHS, Municipal Archives, and private collections; not confirmed as broadly digitized.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that a specific record set was destroyed or lost for colonial NYC. The absence of civil registration records is not a loss — no civil system existed. The incompleteness of colonial passenger lists is a structural gap in the record type, not a destruction event. Researchers should not assume gaps in online results represent lost records.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the primary vital record substitute.** Because no civil registration existed in the 1700s, baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the only source for vital events. Begin with the Dutch Reformed and Anglican registers. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.)
- **Use the "Abstracts of Wills" index before browsing original probate volumes.** The New-York Historical Society published multi-volume abstracts indexed by name covering the colonial Prerogative Court. This saves enormous time compared to browsing unindexed court rolls. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.)
- **Search ward tax lists to locate individuals between censuses.** Colonial and early post-colonial ward tax assessments identify property owners (and some tenants) by ward, giving a geographic anchor before federal census records begin in 1790. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.)
- **Dutch patronymic naming is a major indexing quirk.** Dutch families used patronymic surnames into the mid-1700s (e.g., a son of Jan de Vries might appear as Pieter Jansen). The same individual can appear under different surname forms in different records. Search under both the patronymic and any later fixed surname.
- **The Dutch Reformed register (imageGroupNumber 007733180) requires Dutch-language skill.** The single confirmed digitized volume for 1700–1776 is written in Dutch script and is browse-only with no name index. Consider engaging a translator or Dutch genealogy specialist before relying on this source.
- **Search all surrounding counties for mobile families.** NYC families in the 1700s may also appear in Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and Westchester county records. The city boundary was much narrower than the modern metro area.
- **The 1790 federal census is the earliest national enumeration.** Heads of household and summary counts are given; individuals within a household are not named. Use it as a starting point and work backward using church and tax records.
- **The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society is a specialized resource.** Their journal (The New York Genealogical and Biographical Record, published since 1870) and online database contain many transcriptions and abstracts of colonial NYC records not available elsewhere.
- **For African American and enslaved ancestors:** Estate inventories, bills of sale, and manumission records are the primary documentary sources. The New-York Historical Society and Municipal Archives hold key collections. Newspaper runaway advertisements (searchable through the NYG&BS and Fold3) frequently describe individuals in detail.
- **Consult the New York State Archives' online catalog** (https://www.archives.nysed.gov/) for finding aids to the New York Colonial Manuscripts and Prerogative Court series before planning an in-person visit.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established as a Dutch colonial settlement in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York.
- **County-level jurisdiction during 1700s:** New York County (Manhattan island). The broader provincial government was the Province of New York.
- **Administrative center:** City of New York (lower Manhattan).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colony, 1664–1783); became New York State after 1783.
- **Population during period:** No reliable population figure was returned by the population tool for this place and period. Wikipedia notes NYC was a major commercial port and administrative center throughout the 1700s with substantial growth through the century.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, merchant commerce, artisan manufacturing, a major transatlantic port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch (the founding population, prominent through the 1700s), English (dominant administratively after 1664), French Huguenot, German, and Jewish communities also present. A significant enslaved African population was present throughout the colonial period.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous institutional presence), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, established 1697), Presbyterian (First Presbyterian Church), Lutheran, French Huguenot, Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation, established 1654), and Quaker congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Leisler's Rebellion (1689–1691); Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); King George's War (1744–1748); French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783, British occupation of NYC 1776–1783); NYC serves as first U.S. capital (1785–1790).

## Boundary changes
- Throughout the 1700s, New York City was coterminous with New York County (present-day Manhattan). The five modern boroughs did not exist; the surrounding counties (Kings, Queens, Richmond, Westchester) were separate jurisdictions.
- The transition from Provincial to State government in 1783 did not change the geographic jurisdiction but shifted custody of ongoing record series from colonial to state authorities.
- No internal boundary change split the city during this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** New York State did not have civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records, Church Records, and related topics all returned only generic content rather than New York-specific registration dates — no specific statewide start date is confirmed by tool results for this survey. The FamilySearch collection "New York, County Marriages" (id: 1920153) begins in 1847, confirming that county-level civil marriage registration did not exist in the 1700s.
- **What exists in this period:** None. There was no civil registration system.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the only primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials during the 1700s. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records from 1639, the oldest continuous series in NYC); Anglican/Trinity Church (established 1697); First Presbyterian Church; Lutheran; French Huguenot; Jewish congregation Shearith Israel; Quaker. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (christenings), marriages, burials, and confirmations. Dutch Reformed registers are the most extensive for the early 1700s.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id: 1469062) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062 — this state-level collection covers the target period.
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers for New York City, covering 1700–1776 (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images). This volume is **browse-only** — it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed image by image. The language is Dutch; the researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script to use it.
- **Where held:** Original registers are held by individual denominational archives. The Dutch Reformed registers are held by the Reformed Church in America archives (New Brunswick, NJ). Anglican/Trinity Church records are held by Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan). The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold transcripts and published abstracts of many colonial church records. (Source: wiki_search result.)
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch through at least the mid-1700s. Anglican registers are in English. Latin may appear in some Lutheran or formal ecclesiastical entries.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790. No national enumeration exists for 1700–1789.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No colonial enumeration specific to NYC was identified in tool results. Colonial militia rolls listing men of military age were maintained by the Province of New York and are noted in wiki_search results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records) as surviving for some years.
- **Substitute sources:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards (see Tax Records below). Church registers can partially substitute for population enumeration.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is available indexed online through FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Colonial-era probate:** Wills and administrations in colonial New York were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York**, not at the local county court level. This is a critical quirk — searching a county court series will not find 18th-century wills.
- **Published index:** The New-York Historical Society published "Abstracts of Wills" covering the colonial and early statewide period. This is the recommended starting point for probate searches before browsing original court records.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780 — date range spans the target period.
- **Other court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City handled civil and some criminal matters. Records of the Mayor's Court are noted as a key colonial source in wiki_search results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). The New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives also contain court-related materials.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany) holds the colonial Prerogative Court records and colonial manuscripts. FamilySearch has microfilmed portions.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not rectangular survey — New York is an original-colony state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Province of New York (and before it, New Netherland) granted land patents through the colonial governor. The specific office holding those grants is the New York State Archives and the New York State Office of General Services; the FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Land and Property returned only generic content for this survey.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654 — covers the entire colonial and target period.
- **Types:** Land patents, grants, deeds, and conveyances. Wiki_search results specifically name land conveyances as a key colonial record type (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk (Manhattan) for deed records; New York State Archives for colonial patents and grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Provincial militia rolls (men of military age; noted by wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records as surviving for some years); Revolutionary War service records and pension files for post-1775 service.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) holds Revolutionary War service and pension records. The New York State Archives holds colonial militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized NARA military records online.
- **Access:** Revolutionary War pension files are indexed and available through NARA and Fold3. Colonial militia rolls are not fully indexed; status online is not confirmed by tool results.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (lower Manhattan) is one of the oldest and most documented. Dutch Reformed congregation had associated burial grounds. Jewish congregation Shearith Israel had its own cemetery (the Chatham Square Cemetery, dating to the 1680s, is among the oldest Jewish cemeteries in North America).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes headstone inscriptions for many NYC colonial cemeteries. Coverage is uneven for 1700s stones.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers vary by congregation; many were kept only by the church. Trinity Church has published transcripts of its early burial register.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (established 1725, the first newspaper in New York) published legal notices, shipping news, and some vital notices. Additional papers appeared later in the century.
- **Content value:** Obituaries were uncommon in 18th-century papers; legal notices, estate advertisements, and runaway servant/slave notices are more typical.
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper digitization varies. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some holdings. The New-York Historical Society and NYPL hold original and microfilmed runs.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of New York was the primary port of entry for colonial NYC. Ships arrived from England, the Netherlands, Germany, France, and West Africa (the latter via the slave trade).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for the 1700s are incomplete and fragmentary; systematic manifests did not begin until the 1820 Steerage Act. Earlier arrivals may appear in published ship passenger abstracts compiled by genealogical societies.
- **Naturalization:** Before 1790, naturalization in colonial New York was handled at the colony level; records are in the colonial manuscripts at the New York State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; published abstracts held by NYGS and NY Historical Society.
- **Content note:** Systematic passenger manifests listing all persons aboard (including children) did not apply to the colonial 1700s. Published abstracts are the primary research tool.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Ward-level tax assessment lists for real and personal property. Wiki_search results note that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial NYC (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432 — this collection only reaches the very end of the target period (1799–1804) and covers only those years.
- **Substitute value:** For years before 1790 (before the federal census), surviving ward tax lists are among the best substitutes for population enumeration, placing individuals at a specific ward in a specific year.
- **Where held:** New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives hold pre-1799 assessment materials; their digitization status is not confirmed by tool results for this survey.

### Other record types
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York State Archives holds the colonial government's administrative records — council minutes, governor's correspondence, colonial laws, and related materials — which name merchants, officeholders, and others who appear nowhere else. Wiki_search identifies these as a key source (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&BS):** Holds and has published extensive transcripts, abstracts, and indexes of colonial NYC records. Their journal and database are major research resources.
- **New-York Historical Society:** Holds manuscript collections, published "Abstracts of Wills," and other colonial-era finding aids.
- **City directories:** New York City directories began in the 1780s. These are useful for locating individuals after that date.
- **Records of enslaved persons:** Bills of sale, estate inventories listing enslaved people as property, runaway advertisements in newspapers, and manumission records all name enslaved individuals. These are the primary record types for researching African American ancestors in colonial NYC. The NYC Municipal Archives and NYHS hold relevant collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (id 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (id 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (id 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id 1678432); 1 digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776 (browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | Federal census 1790 and later; some colonial records via digitization partnerships | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Revolutionary War military records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions including Trinity Church and colonial graveyards | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Federal records, Revolutionary War pension and service files | Free (some records) |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for New York City, 1700–1800 (totalResults: 1; this is the complete result set). Collections_search returned 5 indexed collections at the New York state scope; 4 of those overlap the target period. The external links search returned 6 results that appear to be generic national-level resources rather than NYC-specific curated links.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; Prerogative Court probate records; colonial militia rolls; colonial land patents | In-person; some online finding aids |
| New York City Municipal Archives (Manhattan) | City government records including some tax and administrative records | In-person; some online |
| New-York Historical Society (Manhattan) | Manuscripts; Abstracts of Wills; colonial-era finding aids | In-person; some materials digitized |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (Manhattan) | Transcripts, indexes, and published abstracts of colonial NYC records; the NYG&B Record journal | In-person and online membership database |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (New Brunswick, NJ) | Original Dutch Reformed church registers | In-person; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan) | Anglican registers from 1697; burial records | In-person by appointment |
| New York Public Library (Manhattan) | Local history and genealogy division; city directories from 1780s; newspapers | In-person; some digital |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1799 ward tax assessment lists: existence confirmed by wiki_search; digitization status not confirmed.
- Colonial militia rolls (pre-1775): existence confirmed by wiki_search; not confirmed as indexed or fully digitized.
- Mayor's Court records (colonial): existence confirmed by wiki_search; online status not confirmed.
- Original Dutch Reformed registers beyond imageGroupNumber 007733180: the single digitized volume covers 1700–1776 at 0% indexing; additional volumes or post-1776 registers are not confirmed as digitized in this survey.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) registers: physical archives confirmed; online digitization status beyond what FamilySearch's Church Records collection may include is not confirmed by tool results.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts: held at New York State Archives; digitization status not confirmed.
- Records relating to enslaved persons (bills of sale, manumissions, inventories): held at NYHS, Municipal Archives, and private collections; not confirmed as broadly digitized.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that a specific record set was destroyed or lost for colonial NYC. The absence of civil registration records is not a loss — no civil system existed. The incompleteness of colonial passenger lists is a structural gap in the record type, not a destruction event. Researchers should not assume gaps in online results represent lost records.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the primary vital record substitute.** Because no civil registration existed in the 1700s, baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the only source for vital events. Begin with the Dutch Reformed and Anglican registers. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.)
- **Use the "Abstracts of Wills" index before browsing original probate volumes.** The New-York Historical Society published multi-volume abstracts indexed by name covering the colonial Prerogative Court. This saves enormous time compared to browsing unindexed court rolls. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.)
- **Search ward tax lists to locate individuals between censuses.** Colonial and early post-colonial ward tax assessments identify property owners (and some tenants) by ward, giving a geographic anchor before federal census records begin in 1790. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.)
- **Dutch patronymic naming is a major indexing quirk.** Dutch families used patronymic surnames into the mid-1700s (e.g., a son of Jan de Vries might appear as Pieter Jansen). The same individual can appear under different surname forms in different records. Search under both the patronymic and any later fixed surname.
- **The Dutch Reformed register (imageGroupNumber 007733180) requires Dutch-language skill.** The single confirmed digitized volume for 1700–1776 is written in Dutch script and is browse-only with no name index. Consider engaging a translator or Dutch genealogy specialist before relying on this source.
- **Search all surrounding counties for mobile families.** NYC families in the 1700s may also appear in Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and Westchester county records. The city boundary was much narrower than the modern metro area.
- **The 1790 federal census is the earliest national enumeration.** Heads of household and summary counts are given; individuals within a household are not named. Use it as a starting point and work backward using church and tax records.
- **The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society is a specialized resource.** Their journal (The New York Genealogical and Biographical Record, published since 1870) and online database contain many transcriptions and abstracts of colonial NYC records not available elsewhere.
- **For African American and enslaved ancestors:** Estate inventories, bills of sale, and manumission records are the primary documentary sources. The New-York Historical Society and Municipal Archives hold key collections. Newspaper runaway advertisements (searchable through the NYG&BS and Fold3) frequently describe individuals in detail.
- **Consult the New York State Archives' online catalog** (https://www.archives.nysed.gov/) for finding aids to the New York Colonial Manuscripts and Prerogative Court series before planning an in-person visit.
