Here is what the locality guide found for Virginia during the Revolutionary War (1775–1783):

---

## Virginia Revolutionary War Records — Locality Guide

Virginia is one of the best-documented jurisdictions for this era, but with an important caveat: the **1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The standard substitute is the **1782–1785 Virginia personal property tax lists**, which serve as the effective statewide population enumeration for this period.

---

### Primary Repositories

**1. National Archives (NARA)**
- Continental Army service records
- Revolutionary War pension files and bounty-land warrant applications

**2. Library of Virginia (Richmond)**
- Virginia militia records and state navy records
- Land patents and grants
- Church registers
- County court books (deed books, order books, will books)

---

### Key Record Types

| Record Type | What It Shows | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| Military service records (Continental Army) | Enlistment, rank, unit, discharge | NARA |
| Virginia militia records | Local defense service, muster rolls | Library of Virginia |
| Revolutionary War pension files | Veteran identity, widow's testimony, family data | NARA / FamilySearch |

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies. It declared itself a Commonwealth in 1776 under its own constitution and was admitted to the United States as a state in 1788. During the Revolutionary War period (1775–1783) it transitioned from a royal colony to an independent commonwealth.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital until 1780); Richmond (capital from 1780).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain (to 1776); independent Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter.
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this period. Wikipedia describes Virginia as the most populous colony. The earliest surviving statewide enumeration is the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists, because the 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, subsistence farming, iron manufacturing, maritime trade; wartime activity shifted many counties toward militia support, provisioning, and supply.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English and Scots-Irish settlers; enslaved African Americans made up a large portion of the population; German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley; Welsh and Irish immigrants in some coastal counties.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Church of England, reorganized as Protestant Episcopal after the Revolution) was the established church before 1776; Baptist, Presbyterian, and Methodist congregations grew rapidly during and after the Revolution; German Lutheran and Reformed congregations in the Valley.
- **Key historical events:** Virginia's Declaration of Rights and Constitution (1776); Lord Dunmore's proclamation offering freedom to enslaved persons joining British forces (1775); Siege of Yorktown and British surrender (1781); Virginia's cession of trans-Appalachian lands; Kentucky County created (1776).

## Boundary changes
- Present-day Kentucky was part of Virginia as Kentucky County (created 1776, later subdivided) until 1792 when Kentucky became a separate state. Ancestors in what is now Kentucky generated Virginia records during 1775–1783.
- Present-day West Virginia was part of Virginia until the Civil War era (1863).
- Numerous new Virginia counties were created from existing ones throughout the 1770s–1780s. A family's county of residence can differ from modern expectations. Always verify which county had jurisdiction at the exact date of the event.
- Records created before a county's formation are held by the parent county.

## Available record types

Note: Virginia kept records at the county level during this period. No statewide civil registration system existed for births, marriages, or deaths in 1775–1783.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed at the statewide level during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records and Virginia Military Records both returned only generic content and did not state a Virginia-specific civil registration start date.
- **What exists:** County marriage bonds and licenses, banns, and consent affidavits are the closest formal marriage records. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900' (id: 1734285) covers these. Baptism and burial records are in church registers: FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929' (id: 1598230).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); county courthouses; individual church archives; FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** No statewide vital registration during the target period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers; Baptist and Presbyterian congregational records; vestry minutes listing orphans and poor relief recipients.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church, parish registers most complete for this era); Baptist; Presbyterian; Methodist; German Lutheran and Reformed (Shenandoah Valley).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; vestry minutes (including poor-relief lists naming indigent parishioners and orphans bound as apprentices).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929' (id: 1598230); Library of Virginia; individual denominational archives.
- **Language:** English for most records; German for some Shenandoah Valley Lutheran and Reformed registers.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1790 federal census schedules for Virginia were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The earliest surviving Virginia federal census is 1800. No federal census was conducted during 1775–1783.
- **State/provincial census:** Virginia conducted personal property tax enumerations beginning in 1782 that function as a census substitute. FamilySearch volume 005301449 (87 images, full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed) covers Virginia state enumerations/tax lists 1782–1799.
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial-era tithable lists from the decades before the Revolution provide earlier population snapshots.
- **Access:** Volume 005301449 is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — it can be searched by keyword but must be examined image by image for name variants. It must not be treated as a fully searchable database.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; county court order books (which also record militia appointments, road assignments, poor relief, and loyalty oaths).
- **Date range:** From county formation; many Virginia counties trace records to the 1630s–1700s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920' (id: 2134567); Library of Virginia; individual county courthouses. FamilySearch volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — **indexed + images**) illustrates the war-period county court record type.
- **Testate or intestate:** Wills are in will books; when no will exists, an administration bond was filed instead. Both are in the county court records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds. Virginia is a state-land (colony-land) state — land patents were issued by the Crown before 1776 and by the Commonwealth thereafter.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia issued colonial land patents through the Crown and, after 1776, through the Commonwealth Land Office. The Library of Virginia holds the Virginia Land Office patent books. The FamilySearch Wiki pages returned for land and property were generic and did not supply Virginia-specific grant-office details.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages; Revolutionary War bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio (post-war). FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900' (id: 1734285) covers deed and will records. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800, 341 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) is **browse-only**.
- **Date range:** Colonial patents from the 1600s; war-era warrants from 1779.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county recorder of deeds; Virginia State Library for bounty-warrant records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:**
  - **Service records and muster rolls:** Continental Line service records at NARA (Record Group 93); Virginia militia muster rolls at the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783' (id: 1945678) covers this period specifically. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant files:** NARA (Record Group 15). These are among the richest genealogical sources — applications required affidavits from the veteran, widow, or family members, often recording age, birthplace, marriage date, and children's names. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized these files. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
  - **Revolutionary War bounty land warrants:** Virginia issued warrants for land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (341 images, browse-only, 1779–1800). Warrant and survey records also at the Virginia State Library. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands
  - **Virginia State Navy records:** Virginia maintained its own navy; service records are at the Library of Virginia. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
- **Where held:** NARA (RG 93, RG 15); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch (collection 1945678, volume 005301447).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Anglican/Episcopal parish churchyards are among the oldest surviving burial grounds; Presbyterian and Baptist churchyards from the 1770s–1780s.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated FamilySearch resource for Virginia.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are uncommon for this early a period; headstone inscriptions are the primary source. Some church records include burial registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg, published from 1736 with interruptions; multiple competing editions during the Revolution). Richmond-area papers began in the 1780s.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated FamilySearch resource.
- **Content value:** Military appointments, death notices, estate administration notices, loyalty oath publications, deserter advertisements, and legal notices. The Virginia Gazette is particularly valuable for the war years.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Hampton Roads (primary Virginia ports); Alexandria and Fredericksburg (northern counties).
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger lists (pre-Revolution); post-war Loyalist emigration records; naturalization records for foreign-born Continental soldiers. Declarations of intention and naturalization records were filed in county courts of record before 1906.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Library of Virginia for some colonial-era materials.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists from 1775–1783 are sparse and not systematically preserved. Loyalist claims filed with the British government post-war name families who departed Virginia. Examine full passenger manifests for all family members when an immigrant soldier is located — family members including infants appear on the same manifest.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (annual from 1782); colonial tithable lists (pre-war); land tax records.
- **Date range:** Colonial tithables predate the war; personal property tax lists begin 1782.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850' (id: 1456723); Library of Virginia. Volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed, 1782–1799) is part of this series.
- **Substitute value:** The 1782 and later personal property tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. They list free white male heads of household and in many counties enumerate enslaved persons by first name — a critical source for reconstructing war-era households.

### Other record types
- **Loyalty oaths and test oaths:** Virginia required oaths of loyalty beginning in 1777; non-signers (potential Loyalists) appear in county court order books, providing evidence of community presence.
- **Pension narratives and depositions:** Pension application files (NARA RG 15) often contain detailed first-person family histories given by the veteran or widow decades after the war, sometimes naming wives, children, and places of birth.
- **Vestry minutes and poor relief records:** Anglican vestry records name the poor receiving parish relief, orphaned children bound as apprentices, and church wardens — persons who may appear in no other record type.
- **Published county and town histories:** Nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century county histories frequently reprint militia lists, courthouse records, and family traditions not preserved elsewhere, and sometimes represent the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (id: 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (id: 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (id: 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (id: 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (id: 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War pension files, service records, muster rolls | Subscription |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. census and other compiled collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery and burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Virginia newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Continental Army records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free to search; fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search (Military record-type filter) returned 3 digitized volumes total; no nextPageToken was present, so this is the complete set matching that filter for the place and period. Additional volumes for other record types (church, court, land) were not queried in this run and may exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; Virginia State Navy records; land patents; county court records; church records; tax lists; Virginia Gazette | In-person; many collections also on FamilySearch microfilm |
| NARA, Washington D.C. / College Park | Continental Army service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person; online request at archives.gov; Fold3 digitized version |
| County courthouses | Original deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person or mail; many records also at Library of Virginia |
| Virginia Museum of History & Culture, Richmond | Manuscript collections, family papers, published county histories | In-person; some online |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette archive; colonial manuscript materials | In-person; some online |
| Individual church archives | Vestry minutes, parish registers | Contact each denomination's archive |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia muster rolls at the Library of Virginia are not uniformly digitized or name-indexed; many require in-person access or microfilm.
- Pre-1782 colonial tithable lists vary in digitization status by county and are not systematically available online.
- Vestry minutes and Anglican poor-relief records are not broadly digitized.
- Loyalty oath and test-oath records in county court books vary by county in digitization status.
- FamilySearch volume 005301447 (341 images, Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779–1800) is browse-only — no name index, no full-text search.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census schedules for Virginia were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Source: FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands. The 1782–1785 personal property tax lists are the substitute.
- Virginia is sometimes called a 'burned county state' — numerous courthouse fires over the centuries have destroyed county-level records. The tool results for this survey did not specify which counties lost records in which fires; consult the Library of Virginia's Virginia County Records survey for a detailed list before concluding that a record does not exist. A courthouse fire is a coverage gap, not proof that a record was never created.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files for any veteran.** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant applications (NARA RG 15, Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/) are among the richest genealogical sources in American records. Affidavits and widow's depositions often contain ages, birthplaces, marriage dates, and children's names not found elsewhere.
- **Use the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists as the census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia census was destroyed, these lists — FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850' (id: 1456723) — are the earliest surviving statewide enumeration and the closest proxy to a war-era household census. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands
- **Distinguish Continental Line from Virginia Militia service.** Continental service records are at NARA (RG 93); Virginia militia records are at the Library of Virginia. Pension eligibility and surviving documentation differ between the two. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
- **Search the Virginia Military District of Ohio.** Virginia administered bounty land warrants for its veterans in present-day Ohio, not in Virginia. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (browse-only) and the Virginia State Library both hold these records. A warrant links a named veteran to a post-war land claim. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands
- **Check county court order books for wartime civilian activity.** Militia appointments, supply requisitions, road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and loyalty oaths were all transacted in county court minutes. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920' (id: 2134567) and volume 005301448 (Augusta County, 61% indexed) provide access to these records.
- **Account for Kentucky and West Virginia ancestors.** During 1775–1783, present-day Kentucky was Virginia's westernmost territory (Kentucky County). Ancestors settled there generated Virginia records during this period; search both the Library of Virginia and Kentucky repositories.
- **Check vestry minutes for non-military family members.** Anglican vestry records name the poor receiving parish relief and orphaned children bound as apprentices — persons who may appear in no other source of this period. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929' (id: 1598230) may include vestry material.
- **Consult the Library of Virginia's county-records survey before treating a null result as a loss.** Virginia courthouse fires have created gaps, but published transcriptions and microfilm copies of many 'burned' records survive at the Library of Virginia.

- **Relevant conflicts:** The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:**
  - **Service records and muster rolls:** Continental Line service records at NARA (Record Group 93); Virginia militia muster rolls at the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783' (id: 1945678) covers this period specifically. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant files:** NARA (Record Group 15). These are among the richest genealogical sources — applications required affidavits from the veteran, widow, or family members, often recording age, birthplace, marriage date, and children's names. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized these files. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
  - **Revolutionary War bounty land warrants:** Virginia issued warrants for land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (341 images, browse-only, 1779–1800). Warrant and survey records also at the Virginia State Library. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands
  - **Virginia State Navy records:** Virginia maintained its own navy; service records are at the Library of Virginia. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
- **Where held:** NARA (RG 93, RG 15); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch (collection 1945678, volume 005301447).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Anglican/Episcopal parish churchyards are among the oldest surviving burial grounds; Presbyterian and Baptist churchyards from the 1770s–1780s.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated FamilySearch resource for Virginia.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are uncommon for this early a period; headstone inscriptions are the primary source. Some church records include burial registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg, published from 1736 with interruptions; multiple competing editions during the Revolution). Richmond-area papers began in the 1780s.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated FamilySearch resource.
- **Content value:** Military appointments, death notices, estate administration notices, loyalty oath publications, deserter advertisements, and legal notices. The Virginia Gazette is particularly valuable for the war years.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Hampton Roads (primary Virginia ports); Alexandria and Fredericksburg (northern counties).
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger lists (pre-Revolution); post-war Loyalist emigration records; naturalization records for foreign-born Continental soldiers. Declarations of intention and naturalization records were filed in county courts of record before 1906.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Library of Virginia for some colonial-era materials.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists from 1775–1783 are sparse and not systematically preserved. Loyalist claims filed with the British government post-war name families who departed Virginia. Examine full passenger manifests for all family members when an immigrant soldier is located — family members including infants appear on the same manifest.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (annual from 1782); colonial tithable lists (pre-war); land tax records.
- **Date range:** Colonial tithables predate the war; personal property tax lists begin 1782.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850' (id: 1456723); Library of Virginia. Volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed, 1782–1799) is part of this series.
- **Substitute value:** The 1782 and later personal property tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. They list free white male heads of household and in many counties enumerate enslaved persons by first name — a critical source for reconstructing war-era households.

### Other record types
- **Loyalty oaths and test oaths:** Virginia required oaths of loyalty beginning in 1777; non-signers (potential Loyalists) appear in county court order books, providing evidence of community presence.
- **Pension narratives and depositions:** Pension application files (NARA RG 15) often contain detailed first-person family histories given by the veteran or widow decades after the war, sometimes naming wives, children, and places of birth.
- **Vestry minutes and poor relief records:** Anglican vestry records name the poor receiving parish relief, orphaned children bound as apprentices, and church wardens — persons who may appear in no other record type.
- **Published county and town histories:** Nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century county histories frequently reprint militia lists, courthouse records, and family traditions not preserved elsewhere, and sometimes represent the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (id: 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (id: 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (id: 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (id: 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (id: 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War pension files, service records, muster rolls | Subscription |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. census and other compiled collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery and burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Virginia newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Continental Army records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free to search; fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search (Military record-type filter) returned 3 digitized volumes total; no nextPageToken was present, so this is the complete set matching that filter for the place and period. Additional volumes for other record types (church, court, land) were not queried in this run and may exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; Virginia State Navy records; land patents; county court records; church records; tax lists; Virginia Gazette | In-person; many collections also on FamilySearch microfilm |
| NARA, Washington D.C. / College Park | Continental Army service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person; online request at archives.gov; Fold3 digitized version |
| County courthouses | Original deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person or mail; many records also at Library of Virginia |
| Virginia Museum of History & Culture, Richmond | Manuscript collections, family papers, published county histories | In-person; some online |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette archive; colonial manuscript materials | In-person; some online |
| Individual church archives | Vestry minutes, parish registers | Contact each denomination's archive |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia muster rolls at the Library of Virginia are not uniformly digitized or name-indexed; many require in-person access or microfilm.
- Pre-1782 colonial tithable lists vary in digitization status by county and are not systematically available online.
- Vestry minutes and Anglican poor-relief records are not broadly digitized.
- Loyalty oath and test-oath records in county court books vary by county in digitization status.
- FamilySearch volume 005301447 (341 images, Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779–1800) is browse-only — no name index, no full-text search.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census schedules for Virginia were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Source: FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands. The 1782–1785 personal property tax lists are the substitute.
- Virginia is sometimes called a 'burned county state' — numerous courthouse fires over the centuries have destroyed county-level records. The tool results for this survey did not specify which counties lost records in which fires; consult the Library of Virginia's Virginia County Records survey for a detailed list before concluding that a record does not exist. A courthouse fire is a coverage gap, not proof that a record was never created.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files for any veteran.** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant applications (NARA RG 15, Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/) are among the richest genealogical sources in American records. Affidavits and widow's depositions often contain ages, birthplaces, marriage dates, and children's names not found elsewhere.
- **Use the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists as the census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia census was destroyed, these lists — FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850' (id: 1456723) — are the earliest surviving statewide enumeration and the closest proxy to a war-era household census. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands
- **Distinguish Continental Line from Virginia Militia service.** Continental service records are at NARA (RG 93); Virginia militia records are at the Library of Virginia. Pension eligibility and surviving documentation differ between the two. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War
- **Search the Virginia Military District of Ohio.** Virginia administered bounty land warrants for its veterans in present-day Ohio, not in Virginia. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (browse-only) and the Virginia State Library both hold these records. A warrant links a named veteran to a post-war land claim. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands
- **Check county court order books for wartime civilian activity.** Militia appointments, supply requisitions, road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and loyalty oaths were all transacted in county court minutes. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920' (id: 2134567) and volume 005301448 (Augusta County, 61% indexed) provide access to these records.
- **Account for Kentucky and West Virginia ancestors.** During 1775–1783, present-day Kentucky was Virginia's westernmost territory (Kentucky County). Ancestors settled there generated Virginia records during this period; search both the Library of Virginia and Kentucky repositories.
- **Check vestry minutes for non-military family members.** Anglican vestry records name the poor receiving parish relief and orphaned children bound as apprentices — persons who may appear in no other source of this period. FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929' (id: 1598230) may include vestry material.
- **Consult the Library of Virginia's county-records survey before treating a null result as a loss.** Virginia courthouse fires have created gaps, but published transcriptions and microfilm copies of many 'burned' records survive at the Library of Virginia.

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality guide found for New Orleans research in the early 1800s:

---

**Locality Guide: New Orleans, Early 1800s**

New Orleans in the early 1800s is a particularly layered research environment because the city passed through French, Spanish, and American governance in quick succession, and two catastrophic fires (1788 and 1794) had already destroyed large portions of the colonial-era civic records before the 1800s even began.

### What Survived — and Where

Despite those losses, substantial sources survive:

- **St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers** — Records baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps). These are the **main substitute for civil vital records** wiped out by the fires. This is typically the first stop for any early New Orleans family.

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — Holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734, covering sales, contracts, wills, and other legal transactions that would be courthouse records elsewhere. This is an enormously rich repository precisely because Louisiana's civil-law tradition routed so much legal activity through notaries.

- **Cabildo Records** — Records of the Spanish colonial governing body also survived and can document civic and legal matters from the Spanish period.

### FamilySearch Online Collections

FamilySearch holds four online Louisiana collections covering the period:
- Church records from **1718**
- Probate records from **1756**
- A death index from **1819**
- One browse-only digitized volume of notarial acts covering **1803–1820** (167 images, no name index — must be read image by image)

### Critical Warning: Louisiana Terminology

Louisiana's civil-law tradition uses **different terminology** than common-law states. Catalog searches must use these terms or records will not be found:
- **"Successions"** instead of *probate*
- **"Tutorships"** instead of *guardianships*
- **"Interdictions"** instead of *incompetency proceedings*

### Managing the Digitization Gap

The most important caution: the bulk of un-digitized holdings at the Notarial Archives alone means a **negative online result almost certainly reflects a digitization gap, not the absence of a record.** Plan for in-person or correspondence research at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for anything not found online.

---

The next step is to build a research plan targeting the specific ancestor or family you are trying to trace, routing searches in priority order based on what you already know. Would you like to proceed with that?

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Founded:** 1718 by the French; passed to Spain 1763, briefly returned to France 1800, acquired by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans is itself the administrative seat of Orleans Parish
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana (1812–present)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this query
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port; cotton and sugar trading; slave trade; shipping and commerce; early manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American (post-1803), free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African Americans, German and Irish immigrants arriving in the 1830s–1850s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral, founded 1718); Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian) grew after US acquisition; Jewish congregations established by early 19th century
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics; Mississippi River floods; two catastrophic fires 1788 and 1794 that destroyed colonial-era records (the fires predate the target period but created record gaps that affect early 1800s research)

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans was founded as a French colonial city and was the seat of the Province of Louisiana. Spanish rule began 1763; the Cabildo replaced French governance.
- After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), it was capital of Orleans Territory (1804–1812).
- Louisiana was admitted as the 18th state in 1812. Orleans Parish is coterminous with the city of New Orleans in this period.
- The parish boundaries were stable during the early 1800s. No boundary splits affect record custody within the target period.
- **Important:** The transition from French to Spanish to American governance means records from different eras are in different languages and were kept by different authorities. The series do not form one continuous run.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date and level:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content (not Louisiana-specific); the exact mandatory registration start date and the governmental level at which it applied cannot be confirmed from the tools used in this survey. The "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (FamilySearch collection 1543892) begins in 1819, suggesting some death registration existed at least for New Orleans from that year, but the level is unconfirmed. The "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection 1798054) suggests parish-level marriage registration by 1837.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds a statewide death index (1819–1964, no images, index only) and a parish marriages collection (1837–1957). For births in the early 1800s, no indexed civil birth collection was returned by the tools.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Civil District Court records; FamilySearch online collections
- **Gaps:** The early 1800s are largely a pre-civil-registration period for New Orleans. The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many colonial records; yellow fever epidemics and floods created further gaps in subsequent decades.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) are the primary substitute — see Church Records below. Notarial records document marriages, acts of recognition, and other vital events.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary; St. Louis Cathedral from 1731); Protestant churches grew post-1803
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (sacramental registers); confirmations
- **What survives:** The wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters states that despite the 1788 and 1794 fires, the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 with gaps and are a primary genealogical source for this period.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) covers this period and is available online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives; FamilySearch microfilm and digital images
- **Language:** Records may be in Latin, French, Spanish, or English depending on the year and officiating priest

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal censuses were taken in 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860 and cover New Orleans. The 1800 census predates Louisiana's statehood (1812) but Orleans Territory was enumerated. Note: the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed; it does not affect the 1800–1860 window.
- **State/territorial census:** Orleans Territory and Louisiana conducted some territorial and state enumerations. The FamilySearch Wiki for Louisiana Census returned only generic content; specific enumeration dates beyond the federal schedule could not be confirmed from tool results.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and widely available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses the term "successions" for what common-law states call probate (wills and administrations). "Tutorships" are guardianship records. "Interdictions" are incompetency proceedings. These terms must be used when searching catalogs.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) covers the target period and is available at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives; FamilySearch digitized images
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** A person who left a will (testate) generates a succession with a testament; one who died intestate generates an administration succession. Both series should be checked.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot (arpent) system in older settled areas, overlaid with the US Public Land Survey System after 1803. Both systems may appear in the same period.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French and Spanish crown grants predate US acquisition. After 1803, federal land grants and patents apply. The FamilySearch Wiki for Louisiana Land and Property returned only generic content; the specific granting authority and holding office for French and Spanish era grants could not be confirmed from tool results.
- **Types:** Notarial acts (sales, mortgages, donations); deeds; federal patents; Spanish and French land grants
- **Key repository:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). This is a central repository for land and property transactions when other records are missing.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives; Orleans Parish Conveyance Office; Bureau of Land Management GLO website for federal-era patents

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, 1815); Mexican-American War 1846–1848
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, muster rolls
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) at https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ for digitized military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), No. 2 (est. 1823), and No. 3 (est. 1854) are the primary Catholic above-ground cemeteries; Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1833) served the Garden District
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/ indexes many New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans and the individual cemetery offices; completeness varies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (from 1804), New Orleans Bee/L'Abeille (from 1827, bilingual French-English), Daily Picayune (from 1837) and others published during this period
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com at https://www.newspapers.com/ has digitized holdings; the Louisiana State Library and Tulane University hold microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices (successions, sheriff's sales), ship arrivals, and marriage announcements appear in New Orleans papers earlier and more consistently than in many other US cities of the period

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest US ports of entry in the 19th century
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; declarations of intention; naturalization petitions (could be filed in any court of record before 1906, including Orleans Parish courts); border crossings
- **Where held:** NARA at https://www.archives.gov/; FamilySearch; Ancestry at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ (note: link returned is census-specific; passenger list collections are separate)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants. The full manifest should be examined when researching a family. New Orleans manifests are particularly rich for 1820–1860 as immigration surged.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax; personal property tax; poll tax
- **Date range:** Orleans Parish tax records exist from the early 1800s
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years or help locate an ancestor between censuses

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **What they are:** In Louisiana's civil law system, notaries public (notaires) recorded virtually all significant legal transactions: sales of property and enslaved persons, mortgages, marriage contracts, wills, successions, business agreements, manumissions of enslaved people, and acts of recognition of children
- **Why they matter for disaster research:** Notarial records at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center survived the 1788 and 1794 fires and hold over 30 million pages from 1734 (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). They are often the only surviving record of a legal transaction from the early 1800s.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** imageGroupNumber 004990115 covers Notarial Acts 1803–1820, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only. The volume is explicitly described as "surviving microfilm copies," indicating partial survival.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical and some online access); FamilySearch microfilm

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892); Notarial Acts 1803–1820 browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115) | Free |
| NARA | Military records, passenger lists, naturalization records | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume for this place and period (the complete result set). The external_links_search returned 6 results, but all are generic national-level links (Census, Vital Records, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — none are New Orleans-specific curated third-party collections, suggesting FamilySearch's curated external link set for this specific place and time window is sparse.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person research; some remote access |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records; vital records; succession records | In-person / mail requests |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers; cemetery records | Appointment |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) records; court filings | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Local history; newspapers; maps | In-person |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Maps, photographs, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person and some online |

## Records NOT online
- **Most notarial records:** Only 1 digitized FamilySearch volume (167 images, browse-only, 1803–1820) was found. The bulk of the 30+ million pages at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center are not in any indexed online database.
- **Civil birth records for the early 1800s:** No indexed online birth collection for Orleans Parish covering this period was returned by the tools.
- **Many church records beyond the FamilySearch collection:** Individual congregation records for Protestant denominations, and gaps within the Catholic series, are not fully digitized.
- **Tax records:** Not returned by any tool as an online collection for this place and period.
- **Orleans Parish court records (civil and criminal):** Not returned as an online indexed collection; physical repository access required.
- **Sexton and burial registers:** Beyond what Find A Grave volunteers have transcribed, these are physical-only.

## Known record losses
- The Wikipedia summary returned for New Orleans (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) states that the catastrophic fires of 1788 and 1794 "destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records." Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods "further damaged archival holdings."
- The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) states that the 1788 and 1794 fires "destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records." However, it also states that significant genealogical sources survive: the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (from 1731, with gaps), notarial records, and Cabildo records.
- The FamilySearch digitized notarial volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115) is explicitly described as "surviving microfilm copies," indicating only partial survival of the notarial series from 1803–1820.
- No tool result in this survey stated that specific record sets from the early 1800s (post-1800) were destroyed or lost; the confirmed losses cited above apply primarily to the colonial-era (pre-1800) records. The fires predate the 1800–1860 target window, but they mean researchers arriving at the early 1800s are already working with a partially depleted archive.
- **Substitute sources for confirmed gaps:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; New Orleans Notarial Archives; Cabildo records; newspapers; federal census records; tax lists.

## Research tips
- **Search notarial records systematically.** Because Louisiana's civil law system routed most legal business through notaries, these records fill the gap left by fire losses more completely than courthouse records do in other states. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) is the starting point.
- **Use Louisiana-specific terminology in catalog searches.** Search for "successions" not "probate," "tutorships" not "guardianships," and "interdictions" not "incompetency" to find the correct record series.
- **Expect multilingual records.** French, Spanish, and English all appear in New Orleans records of this period, sometimes in the same notarial volume. A researcher must be able to read all three, or work with translations.
- **Check the Cabildo records for 1763–1803 context.** Ancestors living in New Orleans at the start of the early 1800s were governed under Spanish law during their formative years; their legal and property history may be in Spanish-era Cabildo records.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, Census, and Naming Customs all returned only generic content** (not Louisiana-specific) during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly at familysearch.org for the most current Louisiana-specific guidance, particularly for civil registration start dates and levels.
- **Do not treat an empty online search as proof a record does not exist.** Given the magnitude of un-digitized holdings at the Notarial Archives alone (30+ million pages), a negative online result for an early 1800s New Orleans ancestor is most likely a digitization gap, not an absence of records.

| NARA | Military records, passenger lists, naturalization records | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume for this place and period (the complete result set). The external_links_search returned 6 results, but all are generic national-level links (Census, Vital Records, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — none are New Orleans-specific curated third-party collections, suggesting FamilySearch's curated external link set for this specific place and time window is sparse.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person research; some remote access |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records; vital records; succession records | In-person / mail requests |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers; cemetery records | Appointment |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) records; court filings | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Local history; newspapers; maps | In-person |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Maps, photographs, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person and some online |

## Records NOT online
- **Most notarial records:** Only 1 digitized FamilySearch volume (167 images, browse-only, 1803–1820) was found. The bulk of the 30+ million pages at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center are not in any indexed online database.
- **Civil birth records for the early 1800s:** No indexed online birth collection for Orleans Parish covering this period was returned by the tools.
- **Many church records beyond the FamilySearch collection:** Individual congregation records for Protestant denominations, and gaps within the Catholic series, are not fully digitized.
- **Tax records:** Not returned by any tool as an online collection for this place and period.
- **Orleans Parish court records (civil and criminal):** Not returned as an online indexed collection; physical repository access required.
- **Sexton and burial registers:** Beyond what Find A Grave volunteers have transcribed, these are physical-only.

## Known record losses
- The Wikipedia summary returned for New Orleans (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) states that the catastrophic fires of 1788 and 1794 "destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records." Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods "further damaged archival holdings."
- The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) states that the 1788 and 1794 fires "destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records." However, it also states that significant genealogical sources survive: the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (from 1731, with gaps), notarial records, and Cabildo records.
- The FamilySearch digitized notarial volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115) is explicitly described as "surviving microfilm copies," indicating only partial survival of the notarial series from 1803–1820.
- No tool result in this survey stated that specific record sets from the early 1800s (post-1800) were destroyed or lost; the confirmed losses cited above apply primarily to the colonial-era (pre-1800) records. The fires predate the 1800–1860 target window, but they mean researchers arriving at the early 1800s are already working with a partially depleted archive.
- **Substitute sources for confirmed gaps:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; New Orleans Notarial Archives; Cabildo records; newspapers; federal census records; tax lists.

## Research tips
- **Search notarial records systematically.** Because Louisiana's civil law system routed most legal business through notaries, these records fill the gap left by fire losses more completely than courthouse records do in other states. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) is the starting point.
- **Use Louisiana-specific terminology in catalog searches.** Search for "successions" not "probate," "tutorships" not "guardianships," and "interdictions" not "incompetency" to find the correct record series.
- **Expect multilingual records.** French, Spanish, and English all appear in New Orleans records of this period, sometimes in the same notarial volume. A researcher must be able to read all three, or work with translations.
- **Check the Cabildo records for 1763–1803 context.** Ancestors living in New Orleans at the start of the early 1800s were governed under Spanish law during their formative years; their legal and property history may be in Spanish-era Cabildo records.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, Census, and Naming Customs all returned only generic content** (not Louisiana-specific) during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly at familysearch.org for the most current Louisiana-specific guidance, particularly for civil registration start dates and levels.
- **Do not treat an empty online search as proof a record does not exist.** Given the magnitude of un-digitized holdings at the Notarial Archives alone (30+ million pages), a negative online result for an early 1800s New Orleans ancestor is most likely a digitization gap, not an absence of records.

## Boston Port of Entry — 1840s Immigration Records

Boston was one of America's busiest ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of immigrants, especially Irish people fleeing the Great Famine. Key records and repositories include:

### Core Arrival Records
- **Federal Customs Passenger Lists** (NARA Record Group 36) — the primary arrival record series.
  - **FamilySearch** holds collection **1784312**, with a digitized volume (DGS 003345210, 389 images) covering exactly 1840–1850.
  - **Ancestry** has an indexed version.
  - ⚠️ *Important caveat:* The FamilySearch volume is full-text searchable but only ~3% name-indexed, so you'll need to use full-text search or browse page by page rather than a standard name search.
  - *What's recorded:* Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only — **no hometown or parish**.

### Finding the Specific Village or County of Origin
Since 1840s manifests don't record a hometown, these additional record types are essential:

| Record Type | Repository |
|---|---|
| Naturalization records | FamilySearch collection **1459213** |
| Catholic parish registers | **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** |
| Boston Pilot missing-persons notices | Indexed newspaper notices — a critical resource for Irish immigrants |

### Physical Holdings
- Original passenger list volumes are held at the **National Archives at Boston**, located in Waltham, Massachusetts.

---

**Suggested next step:** Build a research plan around these specific record series, starting with the passenger lists via full-text search on FamilySearch, then moving to naturalization records and the Boston Pilot notices to narrow down the place of origin.

quirks: 1840s customs passenger lists (pre-1891) record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — no hometown, village of origin, or names of traveling companions beyond the same ship. The manifest alone rarely proves where in Ireland, Germany, or elsewhere the immigrant originated.

The single FamilySearch digitized volume for Port of Boston passenger lists covering 1840-1850 (DGS 003345210, 389 images) is only 3% name-indexed — it must be searched via full-text search or browsed image by image rather than by standard name search.

Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. An immigrant who arrived in Boston in the 1840s but settled in Pennsylvania may have naturalized in a Pennsylvania court, not a Massachusetts court. Search courts in both the arrival and destination states.

Massachusetts civil vital registration began at the town level but was not comprehensive in the 1840s according to the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston). Church records are essential for this decade.

The Boston Pilot newspaper (Irish Catholic) published 'Missing Persons' notices for Irish immigrants separated from family — a unique substitute source not found in any official record series. These notices have been indexed and are searchable online.

Examine the full passenger manifest for every family member when searching for an immigrant family — passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents.
The National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA facility) holds the original customs passenger list volumes for the Port of Boston; FamilySearch and Ancestry hold digitized and indexed copies.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Port:** Port of Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Administrative context:** Boston was incorporated as a city in 1822 and was by the 1840s one of the five principal US ports of entry
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County; Commonwealth of Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** By 1850, more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston). Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major seaport, maritime trade, manufacturing, commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive Irish immigration, particularly during and after the Great Famine (1845–1852); also English, Canadian, German, and other European arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish arrivals — Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's); Methodist, Episcopal, and other Protestant denominations also present
- **Key historical events:** The Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) produced the largest single surge of immigration Boston ever received in the 1840s

## Boundary changes
- Boston's boundaries and its status as Suffolk County's county seat were stable throughout the 1840s
- No jurisdictional reorganization affecting port records during this period
- Suffolk County (the enclosing county) remained unchanged

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level at which it was created is noted.

### Passenger lists (the primary immigration record)
- **Record level:** Federal (US Customs Service)
- **Start date:** Federal customs passenger lists begin 1820 for major US ports
- **What exists:** Customs passenger lists (NARA Record Group 36) for the Port of Boston, 1820–1891, are the primary source. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) covers this period.
- **Content warning:** 1840s manifests typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not hometown or village within that country (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston). This significantly limits identifying an exact place of origin from the manifest alone.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (DGS 003345210) covering 1840–1850: 389 images, only 3% name-indexed, but **full-text searchable** — meaning the manuscript text can be searched, but standard name-search in the catalog will not surface records in this volume. Browse image by image or use full-text search.
- **Where held (originals):** National Archives at Boston, 380 Trapelo Road, Waltham, MA 02452 (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Also available:** Ancestry.com (subscription) holds an indexed passenger list collection covering this port and period

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Record level:** Town (Massachusetts registered vital events at the town level)
- **What exists:** Massachusetts civil vital registration was in place in the 1840s but was not comprehensive during this decade — church records are essential for this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston). FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) covers the 1840s and is the place to check for births, marriages, and deaths recorded in Boston after arrival.
- **Gaps:** The specific start date and completeness of Boston-level vital registration in the 1840s was not confirmed by any fetched wiki page — the FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Vital Records returned generic content rather than specific dates. Confirm registration coverage before concluding a record is absent.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below)

### Church records
- **Record level:** Parish (congregation)
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic parishes are the most important for Irish immigrants of the 1840s — the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's (Boston) are specifically named as holding baptism, marriage, and burial registers from this decade (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives (specifically named as the repository for Boston Catholic parish records); FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) covers this period
- **Language:** English (Catholic records in Boston were generally kept in English, unlike Latin-language registers in some European countries)
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection is indexed; the Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds originals and additional undigitized registers

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1840 and 1850 federal censuses bracket the target decade. The 1850 census is the first to name every individual household member; 1840 lists only the head of household with age/sex tallies for other members.
- **State census:** Massachusetts did not conduct a state census in the 1840s that supplements the federal count
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 mortality schedule records deaths occurring in the year preceding the June 1850 census — this captures immigrants who died shortly after arrival in 1849–1850
- **Access:** Both the 1840 and 1850 censuses are indexed and image-available on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Naturalization records
- **Record level:** Court (any court of record — federal, state, or local, pre-1906)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection 1459213, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) covers declarations of intention and petitions filed in Massachusetts courts during and after the 1840s
- **Critical caveat:** An immigrant who arrived in Boston in the 1840s and then moved to Pennsylvania could have naturalized in a Pennsylvania court, not a Massachusetts court. Search naturalization records in every state where the immigrant is known to have lived (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Content:** Declaration of intention ("first papers") and petition for citizenship ("second papers") may record country of origin, arrival date and port, and sometimes the specific ship name
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch collection is indexed; originals are held at the respective courthouses and the National Archives at Boston

### The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" notices
- **Description:** The Pilot, Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper, published notices placed by families seeking relatives who had emigrated and not been heard from. These cover approximately 1831–1921 and have been indexed.

- No jurisdictional reorganization affecting port records during this period

The locality guide has been recorded as **loc_001**. Here is a summary of the findings:

---

## Indian Territory (Oklahoma) — Mid-1800s to Statehood (1907)

### Context
Indian Territory was governed by the **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole) under federal oversight. There were no conventional county courts or civil vital registration during this period, so genealogical research depends almost entirely on federal and tribal records.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

| Record Type | What It Contains | Where to Find It |
|---|---|---|
| **Dawes Rolls** (1898–1914) | Definitive tribal citizenship enumeration; the anchor for all Five Tribes research | FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry; original application jackets at **National Archives, Fort Worth** (RG 75) |
| **BIA Annuity Payment Rolls** (1830s onward) | Annual payments to tribal members; pre-Dawes name evidence | FamilySearch and Fold3 (partially indexed) |
| **Indian Census Rolls** | Periodic tribal censuses ordered by the federal government | FamilySearch collection 1987432 (567,890 indexed records) |
| **Land & Allotment Records** | Land assignments under the Dawes Act | FamilySearch collection 1541872 |
| **Missionary Church Registers** | Births, marriages, deaths recorded by mission churches | FamilySearch collection 1654321 |

---

### Critical Notes
- **Freedmen vs. By-Blood rolls**: Freedmen descendants (formerly enslaved by tribal members) were enrolled in separate rolls — searching the wrong category is the most common mistake.
- **Originating-state records**: Families relocated via the **Trail of Tears** from Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, Mississippi, and Florida. Records of mid-century families may exist in those states *before* they appear in Indian Territory records.
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** holds the bulk of undigitized Bureau of Indian Affairs records (Record Group 75), including the full Dawes enrollment application jackets, which can contain family photographs, testimony, and supporting documents.

---

### Recommended Next Step
Use the **Dawes Rolls** as your anchor record, then work backward through annuity rolls and originating-state records. If you'd like, share the specific tribe and family names you're tracing and we can build a focused research plan.
