entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Present-Day Oklahoma) (1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Designated as Indian Territory by the Indian Removal Act of 1830; Oklahoma achieved statehood in 1907
- **Administrative structure:** No conventional county government during mid-1800s; governed through tribal governments (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) under federal oversight by the Bureau of Indian Affairs
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (United States), with authority passing to the State of Oklahoma in 1907
- **Population during period:** Population data from standard census tools was unavailable for Indian Territory during the target period; the territory was not included in regular federal census schedules through 1890
- **Economy:** Primarily agricultural (subsistence farming, ranching); significant disruption from forced relocation; some inter-tribal trade and commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) — relocated 1830s–1840s via Trail of Tears; Black Freedmen (formerly enslaved by tribal members); non-tribal traders and settlers; smaller tribes in separate agency areas (Osage, Quapaw, and others)
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established schools and churches beginning in the 1820s (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act 1830; Trail of Tears 1830s–1842; Civil War with tribal regiment service 1861–1865; Dawes Act 1887 (land allotment); Oklahoma Land Run 1889; Oklahoma statehood 1907

## Boundary changes
- Before 1830: the region was outside U.S. settlement jurisdiction; records for families before removal are held by originating state jurisdictions (Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, Florida)
- 1830–1907: Indian Territory under federal oversight and tribal self-governance; no standard county structure for most of the period
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory carved from the western portion of Indian Territory; the Five Civilized Tribes area in the east retained the Indian Territory designation
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma; county-level governance and civil vital registration began

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma vital records was not returned by the tools used in this survey; no precise statewide registration date can be cited from tool results. Civil registration at the state level postdates the mid-1800s target period (statehood occurred in 1907).
- **What exists for the mid-1800s:** No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory during this period. Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded (when at all) through tribal governments, missionary church registers, and BIA agency records.
- **Where held:** Missionary/church records: FamilySearch collection 1654321 ("Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"; 123,456 records, 61,728 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). BIA agency records: National Archives at Fort Worth, RG 75.
- **Gaps:** Significant. No statewide civil registration before 1907.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Missionary registers; BIA agency records; tribal court records; annuity rolls; tribal census rolls

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers, community membership lists
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 ("Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"; 123,456 records, 61,728 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Denominational archives also hold originals.
- **Digitization level: Indexed + images**
- **Language:** English; some Cherokee-language records exist in Cherokee Nation records

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory was excluded from the regular federal census through 1890; it appears as a separate enumeration in the 1900 census
- **Indian/tribal censuses:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 ("Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"; 567,890 records, 283,945 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Volume-level:** FamilySearch digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards (image group 002298871; 940 images; 99% name-indexed; full-text searchable; covering 1840–1870, Indian Territory). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Annuity rolls:** Compiled annually by BIA agents from the 1830s onward; list heads of household and sometimes family members. Held at NARA RG 75, M234; partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls). **Digitization level: Browse-only images / partial index.**

### Tribal rolls — primary genealogical record series
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Final enrollment for Five Civilized Tribes; 101,000+ individuals enrolled; lists name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes_Rolls). Held at National Archives at Fort Worth. Indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Earlier rolls:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852) — accessible through FamilySearch collection 1987432.
- **Rejected Rolls:** Claimants denied enrollment by the Dawes Commission have their own Rejected Rolls at NARA Fort Worth; genealogically significant and should not be overlooked.
- **Freedmen rolls:** Formerly enslaved persons of the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled as a separate Freedmen category, not on the By-Blood rolls; families of color or mixed ancestry must search both sets.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Five Civilized Tribes had their own tribal courts handling wills, guardianships, and estates; U.S. District Court for Indian Territory also held jurisdiction
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; NARA at Fort Worth (RG 75)
- **Digitization level:** Not confirmed from tool results; treat as physical or microfilm until verified by a direct catalog search

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory was not subject to standard federal rectangular survey during tribal government; allotment records began with the Dawes Commission after 1887
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Bureau of Indian Affairs administered allotments; tribal governments held communal lands. The BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) holds patent records for the non-tribal Oklahoma Territory area post-1889.
- **Types:** Treaty land grants; allotment schedules (post-Dawes Act); tribal land records; early settler land entries
- **FamilySearch collection:** 1541872 ("Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"; 234,567 records, 117,283 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth holds originals

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Indian Wars; Civil War (Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Seminole regiments served on both Union and Confederate sides); post-Civil War service
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files; Civil War Indian regiment muster rolls; BIA agency correspondence about military matters
- **Where held:** NARA (national service records); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries military records including Indian Territory holdings; Oklahoma Historical Society holds state-level collections

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Oklahoma cemeteries; coverage of mid-1800s rural tribal burial sites may be limited
- **Physical records:** Mission and church burial registers are included in FamilySearch collection 1654321

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Cherokee Advocate (Cherokee Nation newspaper, published from 1844) is a key mid-century source for obituaries, legal notices, and community news; published in both English and Cherokee syllabary
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for broader newspaper holdings
- **Content value:** Tribal newspapers are invaluable for community events not recorded elsewhere

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Relocation to Indian Territory was forced, not voluntary immigration; the Trail of Tears generated federal removal records in the originating state jurisdictions
- **Removal records:** NARA RG 75 holds records of the removal itself
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable for tribal members in the conventional sense; citizenship was adjudicated by tribal governments and later by the Dawes Commission
- **Declarations of intention and naturalizations for non-tribal settlers** entering Indian Territory post-1890 would be filed in federal court records at NARA

### Tax records
- **Types:** No standard county property tax in mid-1800s Indian Territory; BIA annuity payment rolls serve as the closest functional substitute
- **Date range:** Annuity rolls run from the 1830s onward (NARA RG 75, M234; FamilySearch and Fold3 partial index per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)
- **Substitute value:** Annuity rolls serve as a census substitute for off-year mid-century research

### Other record types
- **BIA agency records:** Comprehensive correspondence, school enrollment, and administrative records at NARA Fort Worth (RG 75); these often name individuals not appearing in any other record
- **Treaty documents:** Key treaties (Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek 1830 for Choctaw; Treaty of Payne's Landing 1832 for Seminole; Treaty of Pontotoc 1832 for Chickasaw; Treaty of New Echota 1835 for Cherokee) are at NARA and name signatories and affected family heads
- **Enrollment jackets (Dawes application files):** Full application files at NARA Fort Worth contain census card ancestors, family testimony, earlier roll citations, and photographs; pulled by Dawes enrollment card number

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (collection 1987432; 567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (collection 1541872; 234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (collection 1654321; 123,456 records); Tribal Enrollment Cards volume 002298871 (940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records; 1900 U.S. Federal Census Indian Territory enumeration | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records; partial index of BIA annuity rolls | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for RG 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs); online catalog at catalog.archives.gov | Free (records may require in-person visit or digitization request) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume for Indian Territory, 1830–1907. This almost certainly does not represent the complete FamilySearch microfilm holdings for this jurisdiction. The FamilySearch catalog was not separately searched with the catalog tool in this survey; a direct catalog search at FamilySearch for "Indian Territory" and each tribal name is recommended.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region) | RG 75 — Bureau of Indian Affairs: annuity rolls, agency correspondence, school records, Dawes Commission files, allotment records, tribal court records, enrollment jackets | In-person or NARA online catalog (catalog.archives.gov) |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | Tribal records, county records (post-1907), newspapers including Cherokee Advocate, photographs, local history collections | In-person; some digitized via OHS website |
| Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah) | Cherokee tribal records | Contact the Cherokee Nation directly |
| Choctaw Nation Archives (Durant) | Choctaw tribal records | Contact the Choctaw Nation directly |
| Chickasaw Nation Archives (Ada) | Chickasaw tribal records | Contact the Chickasaw Nation directly |
| Muscogee (Creek) Nation Archives (Okmulgee) | Creek tribal records | Contact the Muscogee Nation directly |
| Seminole Nation Archives (Wewoka) | Seminole tribal records | Contact the Seminole Nation directly |

## Records NOT online
- Bulk of BIA agency correspondence and administrative files (NARA RG 75) — physical or requiring a digitization request
- Tribal court records — held at Oklahoma Historical Society and NARA; not comprehensively digitized
- Cherokee Advocate newspaper from the mid-1800s — limited online; physical holdings at Oklahoma Historical Society
- Removal-era records from originating states (Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, Mississippi, Florida) tracking pre-relocation families — held at those states' archives and NARA; not aggregated in one place
- Full Dawes enrollment application jackets — referenced by card number; physical at NARA Fort Worth; some digitized but not all

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for Indian Territory mid-1800s records. The absence of county-level courthouse records (which is the common loss-type in other jurisdictions) is structural rather than loss-based: no county government existed in most of Indian Territory during this period, so those record types were never created there. Researchers should not interpret the absence of county vital records as record loss — it reflects the jurisdictional structure of a federally managed territory under tribal self-governance.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Dawes Rolls and work backward.** The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are indexed and fully accessible on FamilySearch and Ancestry; they record tribal affiliation and blood quantum, anchoring mid-century research. From a Dawes enrollment card number, pull the full enrollment jacket (application file) at NARA Fort Worth — it often contains census card ancestors, family testimony, and citations to earlier rolls. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Use annuity payment rolls for mid-century individuals.** Annual BIA annuity rolls (NARA RG 75, M234) are the closest mid-1800s equivalent to a census for Indian Territory; partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)
- **Know the tribe and the agency before searching NARA.** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes had its own BIA agency and its own record series. NARA records are organized by agency, not alphabetically across tribes; identifying the tribe (and sub-band if applicable) before searching NARA prevents searching the wrong agency record group.
- **Search Freedmen rolls separately from By-Blood rolls.** If the family included persons of African descent enslaved by tribal members, those individuals were enrolled as Freedmen in a separate roll. Freedmen descendants may appear in no By-Blood enrollment at all.
- **Look in originating states for pre-removal records.** Families relocated in the 1830s–1840s generated birth, marriage, land, and court records in Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, Mississippi, and Florida before removal; those state-level records are the research trail before Indian Territory begins.
- **Contact tribal archives directly.** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains its own archives with records not yet fully accessible through NARA or FamilySearch. Tribal citizen services offices can confirm what is held.
- **The Oklahoma Historical Society complements NARA.** For records not fully digitized, the OHS is the primary in-state repository and has extensive finding aids for both tribal and post-statehood county records.
- **The FamilySearch catalog was not fully searched in this survey.** A direct catalog search at FamilySearch for 'Indian Territory' and each tribal name is recommended to find microfilmed volumes not yet appearing in the collection or volume search results.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1830: the region was outside U.S. settlement jurisdiction; records for families before removal are held by originating state jurisdictions (Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, Florida)
- 1830–1907: Indian Territory under federal oversight and tribal self-governance; no standard county structure for most of the period
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory carved from the western portion of Indian Territory; the Five Civilized Tribes area in the east retained the Indian Territory designation
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma; county-level governance and civil vital registration began

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma vital records was not returned by the tools used in this survey; no precise statewide registration date can be cited from tool results. Civil registration at the state level postdates the mid-1800s target period (statehood occurred in 1907).
- **What exists for the mid-1800s:** No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory during this period. Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded (when at all) through tribal governments, missionary church registers, and BIA agency records.
- **Where held:** Missionary/church records: FamilySearch collection 1654321 ("Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"; 123,456 records, 61,728 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). BIA agency records: National Archives at Fort Worth, RG 75.
- **Gaps:** Significant. No statewide civil registration before 1907.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Missionary registers; BIA agency records; tribal court records; annuity rolls; tribal census rolls

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers, community membership lists
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 ("Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"; 123,456 records, 61,728 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Denominational archives also hold originals.
- **Digitization level: Indexed + images**
- **Language:** English; some Cherokee-language records exist in Cherokee Nation records

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory was excluded from the regular federal census through 1890; it appears as a separate enumeration in the 1900 census
- **Indian/tribal censuses:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 ("Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"; 567,890 records, 283,945 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Volume-level:** FamilySearch digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards (image group 002298871; 940 images; 99% name-indexed; full-text searchable; covering 1840–1870, Indian Territory). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Annuity rolls:** Compiled annually by BIA agents from the 1830s onward; list heads of household and sometimes family members. Held at NARA RG 75, M234; partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls). **Digitization level: Browse-only images / partial index.**

### Tribal rolls — primary genealogical record series
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Final enrollment for Five Civilized Tribes; 101,000+ individuals enrolled; lists name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes_Rolls). Held at National Archives at Fort Worth. Indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Earlier rolls:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852) — accessible through FamilySearch collection 1987432.
- **Rejected Rolls:** Claimants denied enrollment by the Dawes Commission have their own Rejected Rolls at NARA Fort Worth; genealogically significant and should not be overlooked.
- **Freedmen rolls:** Formerly enslaved persons of the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled as a separate Freedmen category, not on the By-Blood rolls; families of color or mixed ancestry must search both sets.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Five Civilized Tribes had their own tribal courts handling wills, guardianships, and estates; U.S. District Court for Indian Territory also held jurisdiction
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; NARA at Fort Worth (RG 75)
- **Digitization level:** Not confirmed from tool results; treat as physical or microfilm until verified by a direct catalog search

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory was not subject to standard federal rectangular survey during tribal government; allotment records began with the Dawes Commission after 1887
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Bureau of Indian Affairs administered allotments; tribal governments held communal lands. The BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) holds patent records for the non-tribal Oklahoma Territory area post-1889.
- **Types:** Treaty land grants; allotment schedules (post-Dawes Act); tribal land records; early settler land entries
- **FamilySearch collection:** 1541872 ("Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"; 234,567 records, 117,283 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872). **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth holds originals

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Indian Wars; Civil War (Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Seminole regiments served on both Union and Confederate sides); post-Civil War service
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files; Civil War Indian regiment muster rolls; BIA agency correspondence about military matters
- **Where held:** NARA (national service records); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries military records including Indian Territory holdings; Oklahoma Historical Society holds state-level collections

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Oklahoma cemeteries; coverage of mid-1800s rural tribal burial sites may be limited
- **Physical records:** Mission and church burial registers are included in FamilySearch collection 1654321

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Cherokee Advocate (Cherokee Nation newspaper, published from 1844) is a key mid-century source for obituaries, legal notices, and community news; published in both English and Cherokee syllabary
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for broader newspaper holdings
- **Content value:** Tribal newspapers are invaluable for community events not recorded elsewhere

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Relocation to Indian Territory was forced, not voluntary immigration; the Trail of Tears generated federal removal records in the originating state jurisdictions
- **Removal records:** NARA RG 75 holds records of the removal itself
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable for tribal members in the conventional sense; citizenship was adjudicated by tribal governments and later by the Dawes Commission
- **Declarations of intention and naturalizations for non-tribal settlers** entering Indian Territory post-1890 would be filed in federal court records at NARA

### Tax records
- **Types:** No standard county property tax in mid-1800s Indian Territory; BIA annuity payment rolls serve as the closest functional substitute
- **Date range:** Annuity rolls run from the 1830s onward (NARA RG 75, M234; FamilySearch and Fold3 partial index per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)
- **Substitute value:** Annuity rolls serve as a census substitute for off-year mid-century research

### Other record types
- **BIA agency records:** Comprehensive correspondence, school enrollment, and administrative records at NARA Fort Worth (RG 75); these often name individuals not appearing in any other record
- **Treaty documents:** Key treaties (Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek 1830 for Choctaw; Treaty of Payne's Landing 1832 for Seminole; Treaty of Pontotoc 1832 for Chickasaw; Treaty of New Echota 1835 for Cherokee) are at NARA and name signatories and affected family heads
- **Enrollment jackets (Dawes application files):** Full application files at NARA Fort Worth contain census card ancestors, family testimony, earlier roll citations, and photographs; pulled by Dawes enrollment card number

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (collection 1987432; 567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (collection 1541872; 234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (collection 1654321; 123,456 records); Tribal Enrollment Cards volume 002298871 (940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records; 1900 U.S. Federal Census Indian Territory enumeration | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records; partial index of BIA annuity rolls | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for RG 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs); online catalog at catalog.archives.gov | Free (records may require in-person visit or digitization request) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume for Indian Territory, 1830–1907. This almost certainly does not represent the complete FamilySearch microfilm holdings for this jurisdiction. The FamilySearch catalog was not separately searched with the catalog tool in this survey; a direct catalog search at FamilySearch for "Indian Territory" and each tribal name is recommended.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region) | RG 75 — Bureau of Indian Affairs: annuity rolls, agency correspondence, school records, Dawes Commission files, allotment records, tribal court records, enrollment jackets | In-person or NARA online catalog (catalog.archives.gov) |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | Tribal records, county records (post-1907), newspapers including Cherokee Advocate, photographs, local history collections | In-person; some digitized via OHS website |
| Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah) | Cherokee tribal records | Contact the Cherokee Nation directly |
| Choctaw Nation Archives (Durant) | Choctaw tribal records | Contact the Choctaw Nation directly |
| Chickasaw Nation Archives (Ada) | Chickasaw tribal records | Contact the Chickasaw Nation directly |
| Muscogee (Creek) Nation Archives (Okmulgee) | Creek tribal records | Contact the Muscogee Nation directly |
| Seminole Nation Archives (Wewoka) | Seminole tribal records | Contact the Seminole Nation directly |

## Records NOT online
- Bulk of BIA agency correspondence and administrative files (NARA RG 75) — physical or requiring a digitization request
- Tribal court records — held at Oklahoma Historical Society and NARA; not comprehensively digitized
- Cherokee Advocate newspaper from the mid-1800s — limited online; physical holdings at Oklahoma Historical Society
- Removal-era records from originating states (Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, Mississippi, Florida) tracking pre-relocation families — held at those states' archives and NARA; not aggregated in one place
- Full Dawes enrollment application jackets — referenced by card number; physical at NARA Fort Worth; some digitized but not all

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for Indian Territory mid-1800s records. The absence of county-level courthouse records (which is the common loss-type in other jurisdictions) is structural rather than loss-based: no county government existed in most of Indian Territory during this period, so those record types were never created there. Researchers should not interpret the absence of county vital records as record loss — it reflects the jurisdictional structure of a federally managed territory under tribal self-governance.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Dawes Rolls and work backward.** The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are indexed and fully accessible on FamilySearch and Ancestry; they record tribal affiliation and blood quantum, anchoring mid-century research. From a Dawes enrollment card number, pull the full enrollment jacket (application file) at NARA Fort Worth — it often contains census card ancestors, family testimony, and citations to earlier rolls. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Use annuity payment rolls for mid-century individuals.** Annual BIA annuity rolls (NARA RG 75, M234) are the closest mid-1800s equivalent to a census for Indian Territory; partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)
- **Know the tribe and the agency before searching NARA.** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes had its own BIA agency and its own record series. NARA records are organized by agency, not alphabetically across tribes; identifying the tribe (and sub-band if applicable) before searching NARA prevents searching the wrong agency record group.
- **Search Freedmen rolls separately from By-Blood rolls.** If the family included persons of African descent enslaved by tribal members, those individuals were enrolled as Freedmen in a separate roll. Freedmen descendants may appear in no By-Blood enrollment at all.
- **Look in originating states for pre-removal records.** Families relocated in the 1830s–1840s generated birth, marriage, land, and court records in Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, Mississippi, and Florida before removal; those state-level records are the research trail before Indian Territory begins.
- **Contact tribal archives directly.** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains its own archives with records not yet fully accessible through NARA or FamilySearch. Tribal citizen services offices can confirm what is held.
- **The Oklahoma Historical Society complements NARA.** For records not fully digitized, the OHS is the primary in-state repository and has extensive finding aids for both tribal and post-statehood county records.
- **The FamilySearch catalog was not fully searched in this survey.** A direct catalog search at FamilySearch for 'Indian Territory' and each tribal name is recommended to find microfilmed volumes not yet appearing in the collection or volume search results.

output.text_response:
Pennsylvania's Quaker communities in the late 1700s left behind some of the most systematic religious records in early America, and those records are the only practical substitute for civil vital registration, which Pennsylvania did not require statewide until 1906. Here's what to know:

---

## Key Record Types

Quaker **monthly meetings** kept registers of:
- **Births and deaths** (often recorded retroactively by relatives)
- **Marriages** (performed under the care of the meeting, with many witnesses signing)
- **Certificates of removal** (transfer letters when families moved to another meeting)
- **Disownment proceedings** (for members who violated discipline — still genealogically useful)

---

## Top Repositories

1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** — the primary repository for Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records. Holds original registers, minutes, and certificates of removal.

2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** — a major complementary collection with significant manuscript holdings.

3. **FamilySearch** — has microfilmed many monthly meeting registers; also has a browse-only digitized volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, not name-indexed). Most individual meeting records are not name-indexed online and must be browsed by film.

---

## Dense Settlement Areas

The heaviest Quaker concentration was in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties**. Identify the specific township your family lived in to determine which monthly meeting served them.

---

## Essential Finding Aid

**Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) is the most important starting tool — it abstracts meeting records and will point you to the right original volumes. Available at major genealogical libraries. Use it before browsing original registers.

---

## Recommended First Steps

1. Look up your family in **Hinshaw** to identify the monthly meeting and get extracted abstracts.
2. Use a **Quaker meeting map** (available from Friends Historical Library) to confirm which meeting served the township.
3. Contact **Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore** to determine what survives for that specific meeting and how to access it (on-site or through FamilySearch microfilm).

quirks: Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil vital registration until 1906 — for the 1760-1800 period, Quaker meeting records are the primary substitute for birth, marriage, and death documentation.
Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all attendees at the meeting, making them a secondary source naming members of a couple's wider community and kin network.

Certificates of removal (transfer letters between monthly meetings) are the key record for tracing Quaker family migration — a family that moved left behind a removal certificate in the sending meeting and generated a receiving entry at the destination meeting.
Disownment records name individuals expelled from membership, often stating the reason; the disowned person may then appear in civil or other church records for the first time.
Quaker meeting records are organized by meeting hierarchy: local monthly meeting → quarterly meeting → Philadelphia Yearly Meeting. Start at the monthly meeting level for individual events.
Dense Quaker settlement in the 1760-1800 period was concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties — search those monthly meeting records first.

FamilySearch's one digitized volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750-1800, imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images) is browse-only with 0% name indexing and no full-text search — it must be examined page by page.

The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records; the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College is the secondary major repository.
Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records and is the standard finding aid — consult it before browsing original volumes.

Quakers were pacifist; many refused military service and were disowned for participating. Military pension and bounty land files will typically not document Quaker ancestors unless they left the meeting.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Quaker Communities (1760–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Colony founded 1681 by William Penn; state from 1787
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital and center of Quaker life)

Here is the locality guide the research agent produced:

---

**Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry Boom (c. 1870–1900)**

**Key Challenge: No Statewide Vital Registration**
Pennsylvania had no statewide vital records registration during these years, so church registers are the primary substitute for birth, marriage, and death documentation.

---

### Top Sources for Tracing Mill-Worker Families

**1. Ethnic / Immigrant Parish Registers**
The Pittsburgh mills drew massive waves of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrants. Baptism and burial registers kept by ethnic parishes are often the only vital records for these families. Many are held by individual churches, local diocesan archives, or have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

**2. Federal Census Records (1870, 1880, 1900)**
Each census lists occupation — invaluable for identifying steel and iron workers. Note: the **1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed**, creating a significant gap for that decade.

**3. Pittsburgh City Directories**
Continuous runs are held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**. The 1890 directory is especially critical given the census gap. Directories list employer and address, helping you follow a family year by year.

**4. Naturalization Records**
Petitions filed at the **Allegheny County courthouse** and at the **National Archives in Philadelphia** (for federal court filings). These can reveal exact hometown of origin in Europe — essential for connecting to Old World records.

**5. Company Employment Records (Fragmentary)**
Records from Carnegie Steel and related mills survive only in fragments, held at:
- **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center), Pittsburgh
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives**, Homestead, PA

These are physical collections requiring an on-site visit or correspondence — they are not in online databases.

---

### Repositories to Contact

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| Heinz History Center | Carnegie Steel records, local newspapers, photographs |
| Rivers of Steel Archives (Homestead) | Mill employment & labor records |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories, local history collections |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Naturalization petitions, deeds, probate |
| National Archives – Philadelphia | Federal court naturalizations, census schedules |
| Ethnic parish archives / diocese | Baptism, marriage, burial registers |

---

### FamilySearch Online Collections to Search
- Pennsylvania, Allegheny County naturalization records
- U.S. Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900 (with occupation filtering)
- Pennsylvania church records (varies by denomination and parish)

For current local guidance, visit the FamilySearch wiki page directly:
👉 [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)

---

**Recommended Next Step:** Once you identify specific ancestors, use the **research-plan** skill to sequence these sources into a prioritized search strategy.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from portions of Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania (state); federal district jurisdiction: Western District of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query. Wikipedia records Pittsburgh as a rapidly expanding industrial city through this period, driven by steel production.
- **Economy:** Dominated by iron and steel manufacturing (Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin Steel, Homestead Works), glass, coal, coke, and railroad industries. The period saw Pittsburgh become the center of American steel production.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large waves of immigrants — Irish and German workers from earlier decades, followed in the 1880s–1890s by Poles, Slovaks, Croatians, Italians, and Hungarians employed in the mills. (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes), Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, Greek Catholic/Byzantine Rite (Eastern European immigrants), Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892 (Carnegie Steel vs. Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers); Great Railroad Strike of 1877 centered in Pittsburgh; rapid industrialization and urban growth 1870–1900.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were established in 1788 and were stable throughout the 1870–1900 period.
- The independent city of Allegheny (north of the Ohio River) was a separate municipality from Pittsburgh until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907 — records for families living in Allegheny City during 1870–1900 may appear under "Allegheny" rather than "Pittsburgh" in indexes.
- No other significant boundary changes affected Allegheny County during the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a specific Pennsylvania Vital Records page (all constructed-URL fetches resolved to a generic page); the earliest FamilySearch Death Certificates collection (id: 2255317) begins in 1906, consistent with statewide death registration starting around that year. The FamilySearch Wiki states: "Check whether statewide registration existed during your research period — many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). Consult the Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records for the exact level and start date.
- **What exists on FamilySearch:**
  - Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 312,045 images — **indexed + images**
  - Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957): 312,045 records, 156,023 images — **indexed + images**
  - Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909): 198,765 records, no images — **index only**
  - Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317): starts after the target period but covers persons who died after 1900 and may name family members active during 1870–1900
- **Where held:** Originals at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and Allegheny County Register of Wills.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during 1870–1900; county-level marriage registration was uneven. Church records are the primary alternative.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Baptismal and burial registers kept by individual congregations; city directory listings; federal census mortality schedules (available for 1870 and 1880).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dozens of ethnic parishes — St. Stanislaus Kostka for Polish, SS. Cyril & Methodius for Slovak, St. Nicholas for Croatian, etc.); German Lutheran and Reformed; Presbyterian; Methodist; Episcopal; Greek/Byzantine Catholic; Jewish congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, confirmations, marriages, burials, and (in some parishes) membership lists and poor relief records.
- **Where held:** Each parish's own records are the starting point. The Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds records of closed or merged Catholic parishes. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Pennsylvania church records, though access depends on the denomination and congregation. The wiki_search result notes that Catholic parish registers are often the best source for family data for Eastern European immigrant communities (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- **Language:** English for most Protestant congregations; Latin mixed with Polish, Slovak, Croatian, or Italian for Catholic parishes; German for German Lutheran/Reformed congregations.
- **Access:** Physical records at parish offices or diocesan archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch. **No comprehensive indexed online database exists for Pittsburgh Catholic parish registers of this era — physical or microfilm access is required.**

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses are available and list occupation for each person. The 1890 census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire — a critical gap for the Pittsburgh steel era.
- **1880 census:** Fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1870 and 1900:** Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1890 Veterans Schedule:** A partial substitute for 1890 — lists surviving Civil War Union veterans and their widows.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses in this period that would fill the 1890 gap.
- **Other enumerations:** State factory inspector reports (cited in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) are not a census but list workers by establishment and can place a person at a specific mill.
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses — indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, and naturalization petitions.
- **FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196): 3,200,560 images, **0 name-indexed records — browse-only**. Volume 008120441 (1,180 images, browse-only) is part of this set.
- **Naturalization records:** Volume 008120443 (Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915): 351 images, **15% name-indexed**; the remaining 85% must be browsed image by image. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including Allegheny County Common Pleas Court and the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania (National Archives at Philadelphia).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (probate originals); Allegheny County Courthouse (court records); Pennsylvania State Archives (microfilm copies); National Archives at Philadelphia (federal court naturalizations).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted by the Commonwealth, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania State Archives holds original land warrants and patents granted by the Commonwealth. County deed books are at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, sheriff's deeds (from foreclosures), and tax records. For steel-era workers, land records are less common than for rural families — most mill workers rented company housing or urban tenements — but deeds become relevant for those who bought property.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (patent records); county tax assessments at the county courthouse.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a specific Pennsylvania Land and Property page** — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865, just before the period — many workers were veterans); Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records (National Archives, indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry); Civil War draft records; 1890 Veterans Schedule (partial); Spanish-American War service records (National Archives).
- **Where held:** National Archives (Washington, D.C. and Atlanta branch for pension files); Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records for Pennsylvania regiments.
- **Access:** Civil War pension records are indexed on Fold3 (subscription) and FamilySearch (partial). These files often include detailed family and birthplace information.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, 1844 — a major repository for the era), St. Mary's Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic and Lutheran congregation cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Pittsburgh-area coverage; BillionGraves provides additional indexed headstone photographs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at each cemetery office; Allegheny Cemetery maintains its own historical records and is accessible by appointment.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (continuous since 1786), Pittsburgh Dispatch, Pittsburgh Press, and numerous ethnic-language papers (Jedność — Polish; Slovenský denník — Slovak; Unione — Italian).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) has significant Pennsylvania newspaper coverage. Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds microfilm of local papers. The ethnic-language papers are less systematically digitized — check the Library of Congress Chronicling America project and the University of Pittsburgh's archives.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor strike coverage, company announcements (including layoffs and accidents that named workers), and legal notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Eastern European steel workers arrived via New York (Ellis Island, 1892–1900; Castle Garden before 1892). Irish and German immigrants earlier in the period used New York, Baltimore, and Philadelphia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA, indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (Allegheny County courthouse and NARA Philadelphia — per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records); alien registrations (post-1940, not in this period).
- **Note on manifests:** Passenger manifests record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all traveling family members.
- **Access:** Ancestry (subscription) has the most comprehensive indexed passenger list coverage for this period; FamilySearch has a partially overlapping free collection.

### Occupational and industrial records (DISTINCTIVE TO THIS LOCALITY)
This category is the primary focus for Pittsburgh steel-era research:
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary — surviving records from Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and related firms are held at the **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel archives** (Homestead, PA). Coverage is inconsistent; many records were lost or destroyed. Contact each repository before planning a visit. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union membership lists:** The Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers maintained membership rolls; records survive fragmentarily at the United Steelworkers of America archives (Pittsburgh) and the State Historical Society of Wisconsin (which holds national union records for many AFL affiliates).
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports listing establishments, employee counts, and sometimes named employees. These are at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's Pennsylvania Room.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from 1810 onward — an unbroken run through the steel era. Directories list name, occupation, and address annually, making them the single most effective tool for tracking a mill worker year-by-year between censuses. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Accident and injury records:** Mill accidents were frequent; Pittsburgh-area coroner's inquests are at the Allegheny County Archives. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and other papers covered major accidents.
- **Homestead Strike records (1892):** Court records related to the strike, Carnegie company correspondence, and press coverage are significant for tracing worker identities. These are at the Heinz History Center and in published document collections.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessments, held at the Allegheny County Archives.
- **Date range:** Continuous from the county's formation (1788).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for 1890 can substitute for the destroyed federal census; a person taxed in a given ward can be placed at a specific address.

### Other record types

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from portions of Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania (state); federal district jurisdiction: Western District of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query. Wikipedia records Pittsburgh as a rapidly expanding industrial city through this period, driven by steel production.
- **Economy:** Dominated by iron and steel manufacturing (Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin Steel, Homestead Works), glass, coal, coke, and railroad industries. The period saw Pittsburgh become the center of American steel production.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large waves of immigrants — Irish and German workers from earlier decades, followed in the 1880s–1890s by Poles, Slovaks, Croatians, Italians, and Hungarians employed in the mills. (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes), Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, Greek Catholic/Byzantine Rite (Eastern European immigrants), Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892 (Carnegie Steel vs. Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers); Great Railroad Strike of 1877 centered in Pittsburgh; rapid industrialization and urban growth 1870–1900.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were established in 1788 and were stable throughout the 1870–1900 period.
- The independent city of Allegheny (north of the Ohio River) was a separate municipality from Pittsburgh until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907 — records for families living in Allegheny City during 1870–1900 may appear under "Allegheny" rather than "Pittsburgh" in indexes.
- No other significant boundary changes affected Allegheny County during the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a specific Pennsylvania Vital Records page (all constructed-URL fetches resolved to a generic page); the earliest FamilySearch Death Certificates collection (id: 2255317) begins in 1906, consistent with statewide death registration starting around that year. The FamilySearch Wiki states: "Check whether statewide registration existed during your research period — many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). Consult the Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records for the exact level and start date.
- **What exists on FamilySearch:**
  - Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 312,045 images — **indexed + images**
  - Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957): 312,045 records, 156,023 images — **indexed + images**
  - Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909): 198,765 records, no images — **index only**
  - Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317): starts after the target period but covers persons who died after 1900 and may name family members active during 1870–1900
- **Where held:** Originals at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and Allegheny County Register of Wills.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during 1870–1900; county-level marriage registration was uneven. Church records are the primary alternative.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Baptismal and burial registers kept by individual congregations; city directory listings; federal census mortality schedules (available for 1870 and 1880).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dozens of ethnic parishes — St. Stanislaus Kostka for Polish, SS. Cyril & Methodius for Slovak, St. Nicholas for Croatian, etc.); German Lutheran and Reformed; Presbyterian; Methodist; Episcopal; Greek/Byzantine Catholic; Jewish congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, confirmations, marriages, burials, and (in some parishes) membership lists and poor relief records.
- **Where held:** Each parish's own records are the starting point. The Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds records of closed or merged Catholic parishes. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Pennsylvania church records, though access depends on the denomination and congregation. The wiki_search result notes that Catholic parish registers are often the best source for family data for Eastern European immigrant communities (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- **Language:** English for most Protestant congregations; Latin mixed with Polish, Slovak, Croatian, or Italian for Catholic parishes; German for German Lutheran/Reformed congregations.
- **Access:** Physical records at parish offices or diocesan archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch. **No comprehensive indexed online database exists for Pittsburgh Catholic parish registers of this era — physical or microfilm access is required.**

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses are available and list occupation for each person. The 1890 census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire — a critical gap for the Pittsburgh steel era.
- **1880 census:** Fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1870 and 1900:** Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1890 Veterans Schedule:** A partial substitute for 1890 — lists surviving Civil War Union veterans and their widows.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses in this period that would fill the 1890 gap.
- **Other enumerations:** State factory inspector reports (cited in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) are not a census but list workers by establishment and can place a person at a specific mill.
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses — indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, and naturalization petitions.
- **FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196): 3,200,560 images, **0 name-indexed records — browse-only**. Volume 008120441 (1,180 images, browse-only) is part of this set.
- **Naturalization records:** Volume 008120443 (Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915): 351 images, **15% name-indexed**; the remaining 85% must be browsed image by image. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including Allegheny County Common Pleas Court and the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania (National Archives at Philadelphia).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (probate originals); Allegheny County Courthouse (court records); Pennsylvania State Archives (microfilm copies); National Archives at Philadelphia (federal court naturalizations).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted by the Commonwealth, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania State Archives holds original land warrants and patents granted by the Commonwealth. County deed books are at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, sheriff's deeds (from foreclosures), and tax records. For steel-era workers, land records are less common than for rural families — most mill workers rented company housing or urban tenements — but deeds become relevant for those who bought property.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (patent records); county tax assessments at the county courthouse.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a specific Pennsylvania Land and Property page** — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865, just before the period — many workers were veterans); Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records (National Archives, indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry); Civil War draft records; 1890 Veterans Schedule (partial); Spanish-American War service records (National Archives).
- **Where held:** National Archives (Washington, D.C. and Atlanta branch for pension files); Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records for Pennsylvania regiments.
- **Access:** Civil War pension records are indexed on Fold3 (subscription) and FamilySearch (partial). These files often include detailed family and birthplace information.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Pittsburgh-area coverage; BillionGraves provides additional indexed headstone photographs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at each cemetery office; Allegheny Cemetery maintains its own historical records and is accessible by appointment.

- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) has significant Pennsylvania newspaper coverage. Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds microfilm of local papers. The ethnic-language papers are less systematically digitized — check the Library of Congress Chronicling America project and the University of Pittsburgh's archives.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor strike coverage, company announcements (including layoffs and accidents that named workers), and legal notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Eastern European steel workers arrived via New York (Ellis Island, 1892–1900; Castle Garden before 1892). Irish and German immigrants earlier in the period used New York, Baltimore, and Philadelphia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA, indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (Allegheny County courthouse and NARA Philadelphia — per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records); alien registrations (post-1940, not in this period).
- **Note on manifests:** Passenger manifests record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all traveling family members.
- **Access:** Ancestry (subscription) has the most comprehensive indexed passenger list coverage for this period; FamilySearch has a partially overlapping free collection.

### Occupational and industrial records (DISTINCTIVE TO THIS LOCALITY)
This category is the primary focus for Pittsburgh steel-era research:
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary — surviving records from Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and related firms are held at the **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel archives** (Homestead, PA). Coverage is inconsistent; many records were lost or destroyed. Contact each repository before planning a visit. - **Union membership lists:** The Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers maintained membership rolls; records survive fragmentarily at the United Steelworkers of America archives (Pittsburgh) and the State Historical Society of Wisconsin (which holds national union records for many AFL affiliates).
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports listing establishments, employee counts, and sometimes named employees. These are at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's Pennsylvania Room.

- **Homestead Strike records (1892):** Court records related to the strike, Carnegie company correspondence, and press coverage are significant for tracing worker identities. These are at the Heinz History Center and in published document collections.

Here is what the locality-guide found for tracing families affected by the 1793 Philadelphia yellow fever epidemic:

---

**Locality Guide — Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810; Yellow Fever Epidemic Focus)**

Because Pennsylvania had **no civil registration** in 1793, the records that matter most fall into two categories:

### 1. Church Burial Registers
The pace of dying (August–November 1793) overwhelmed normal record-keeping, but key congregations that documented epidemic burials include:
- **Christ Church** — Episcopal; the FamilySearch Wiki specifically names it for epidemic burials
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)** — Lutheran/Episcopal; likewise cited for 1793 burials
- Other Philadelphia congregations (Quaker, Presbyterian, Catholic) kept their own registers; the degree of completeness varies

### 2. Epidemic-Specific Manuscript Sources
These are the most targeted resources for this particular event:
- **Mathew Carey's published list of the dead** — a printed name list of victims; the first stop for any name search
- **Committee of Citizens minutes** — records of the citizen-relief committee that organized the response
- **Bush Hill hospital records** — patient and death records from the emergency hospital

### Key Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Committee minutes, municipal records, some hospital records |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Carey list, manuscript collections, church register microfilm |
| **FamilySearch** | Indexed and microfilmed church burial registers (searchable online) |

### Flanking Records (Before & After the Epidemic)
- **1790 & 1800 U.S. Federal Census** — bracket the epidemic; useful for household reconstruction
- **Philadelphia County Probate Records (1793–1794)** — estates filed shortly after a death; a strong indicator of epidemic victims
- **Pennsylvania Gazette and other Philadelphia newspapers** — obituaries and death notices from the epidemic period

### Important Caveat
Many deaths in this period were **never entered in any register** — the documentation gap is a *creation* gap, not a loss of records that once existed. Absence of a record for a specific person does not mean the records are lost.

---

The agent notes that a good next step would be a sequenced research plan: Carey name list → church burial registers → probate filings (late 1793–1794) → 1790/1800 censuses. Let me know if you'd like that plan built, or if you have a specific person to search for.
