entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810; Focus: 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682; the city of Philadelphia chartered 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county were coterminous for this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 at the time of the 1793 epidemic (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). No population tool data was returned for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; mercantile trade, shipping, artisan crafts; served as the national capital 1790–1800
- **Ethnic composition:** English and Welsh Quakers (founding generation); by 1793 also substantial German, Irish, Scots-Irish, and free and enslaved African American communities; Haitian refugees arrived alongside the Saint-Domingue origin of the epidemic
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quaker), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist; African Methodist Episcopal congregation founded in Philadelphia during this era
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed approximately 5,000 of ~50,000 residents, August–November 1793 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793); Philadelphia was the nation's largest city and its capital

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia city and county were coterminous during this period
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 formally merged city and county — outside the target period and does not affect 1793 records
- No historical boundary changes were returned by `place_search_all` (empty result set)
- Records from the 1780s–1810s were created and held under Philadelphia County jurisdiction

## Available record types

Note on jurisdictional level: Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration in 1793. The earliest statewide death certificate collection on FamilySearch begins in 1906. All vital event documentation for 1793 is at the congregation (church) level — not county, not state.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Pennsylvania Vital Records page in this survey (all four constructed-URL reads redirected to a generic page). The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317) confirms statewide death registration began no earlier than 1906. No start date for an earlier local or county-level registration requirement can be stated from the tool results of this survey.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registration at state or county level. Church registers are the sole systematic vital record source.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil registration in this period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see Church Records below) and epidemic-specific records (see below)

### Epidemic-specific records (1793 yellow fever)
The FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793 identifies these as the key genealogical sources for the 1793 outbreak:

- **Mathew Carey's published account:** A contemporary printed list naming the dead, published in multiple editions in 1793. Widely held in research libraries and available in facsimile. The most direct single source for identifying a victim of the epidemic.
- **Committee of Citizens minutes and reports:** The committee appointed to coordinate epidemic relief produced minutes and reports documenting the dead and relief efforts. Repository: Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** The emergency hospital established during the epidemic generated patient records. Repository: Historical Society of Pennsylvania and/or Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Church burial registers:** Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church) are specifically named by the FamilySearch Wiki for epidemic burials. See Church Records.

### Church records
- **Primary source for the period.** Church registers are the only systematic vital documentation before civil registration.
- **Denominations and key sources:** Society of Friends (Quaker), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church burial register named for epidemic burials), Swedish Lutheran — Gloria Dei/Old Swedes' (named for epidemic burials), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793 and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; confirmation registers for some denominations
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (Quaker), 1750–1800. Image group 001188322, 145 images. **Browse-only (digitization level: browse-only images)** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be examined image by image.
- **Indexes:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records). Consult their publications before attempting to browse unindexed registers.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; German Lutheran and German Reformed registers may be in German — the researcher must read the original language.
- **Where held:** Originals at individual churches; Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center (Catholic); Presbyterian Historical Society; Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds transcriptions and some originals. FamilySearch holds the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes digitally.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 census (3 years before the epidemic) and the 1800 census (7 years after) bracket the event. Both are indexed and available online. A family present in 1790 but absent or diminished in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct separate state censuses during this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available only from 1850 onward; do not cover 1793.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal census indexed and available via Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch. Digitization level: **indexed + images**.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories, guardianships. A substantial surge in probate filings is expected in late 1793 and 1794 following a death toll of ~5,000.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** If the ancestor left a will, search the will books; if they died intestate, search administration dockets.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196) — 3,200,560 images, **0 name-indexed records**, not full-text searchable. Digitization level: **browse-only images.** Must be navigated by date (late 1793–1794) and county (Philadelphia) within the volumes. URL: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **Where held:** FamilySearch images (browse-only); originals at the Philadelphia Register of Wills.
- **Orphans' Court:** Children orphaned by the epidemic came before the Orphans' Court for guardianship appointments. These records can reveal both parents' deaths and name surviving relatives who assumed custody. Held at the Philadelphia Register of Wills; not confirmed as digitized in this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages; property may have changed hands rapidly following epidemic deaths
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (Recorder of Deeds deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (warrants and surveys)
- **Access:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Pennsylvania Land and Property page in this survey (generic redirect). Confirm specific holdings by contacting the Philadelphia City Archives. Digitization level for 1793 deed books: **physical only** (not confirmed as digitized)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (ended 1783; pension files for veterans living in Philadelphia in 1793) and the Quasi-War with France (1798–1800)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA); Quasi-War service records (NARA); Pennsylvania militia records (Pennsylvania State Archives)
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files — **indexed + images** on Fold3 and Ancestry

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Mikveh Israel Cemetery (Jewish), African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas burial ground, and others. Mass burials during the epidemic may not have received individual marked graves.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Philadelphia grave inscriptions. Digitization level: **indexed** (transcriptions; no images of all markers)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual churches or their archives; not confirmed as fully digitized in this survey

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers active in 1793:** General Advertiser (later the Aurora General Advertiser), Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, Federal Gazette. These published death notices, estate sale announcements, legal notices, and epidemic-specific lists of the dead and the sick.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds runs of major Philadelphia papers; Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value for epidemic research:** Death notices August–November 1793; estate auction notices (identifying heirs and property); legal notices of administrations

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a primary Atlantic port of entry in the 1790s. Ships from Saint-Domingue (Haiti) in summer 1793 are believed to have brought the epidemic.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at the port of Philadelphia; naturalization declarations in local courts (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists; Ancestry holds indexed versions
- **Note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest when researching traveling families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania assessment lists; 1798 Federal Direct Tax (the "glass and windows" tax)
- **The 1798 Federal Direct Tax** enumerated all Philadelphia households and property — a near-census substitute between the 1790 and 1800 federal enumerations. It can confirm a household's survival and composition five years after the epidemic.
- **Where held:** NARA holds the 1798 Federal Direct Tax; some indexes on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for the non-existent 1790–1800 intercensal census years

### Other record types
- **Almshouse / Overseers of the Poor:** Philadelphia's Overseers of the Poor maintained records of indigent residents, including epidemic survivors who lost breadwinners. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives. Not confirmed as digitized in this survey.
- **Free African Society records:** The Free African Society (founded Philadelphia, 1787) mobilized its members to nurse the sick during the epidemic. Their records may document African American families. Contact the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Published histories and contemporary accounts:** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) is the primary contemporary source listing the dead. The Committee of Citizens also published reports. Both are held at research libraries and reprinted in modern editions.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 — 3.2M browse-only images (collection 1999196); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 — 312,045 records (collection 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 — 198,765 records (collection 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750-1800 — 145 browse-only images (image group 001188322) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1790 and 1800 (indexed + images); Philadelphia passenger lists; 1798 Federal Direct Tax | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers from the 1790s | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records; Quasi-War records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Philadelphia cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, military records, 1798 Federal Direct Tax | Free (some online; some in-person) |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Digitized historic American newspapers including Philadelphia papers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia, 1780-1810 (totalResults: 1) — the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, image group 001188322. This represents the complete result set for the city-level standardPlace. Additional volumes may exist under the county-level standardPlace "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States" — that search was not run in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Committee of 1793 minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, deed books, Overseers of the Poor records | In-person; contact for appointments |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript epidemic sources; Mathew Carey papers; church record transcriptions; Philadelphia newspaper runs | In-person; some digitized materials online |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person; publications available in libraries |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills | Probate records including wills, administration dockets, Orphans' Court | In-person; some records browsable on FamilySearch |
| Presbyterian Historical Society | Presbyterian congregation records for Philadelphia churches | In-person; contact for access |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Warrants, surveys, state-level records | In-person; online catalog |
| Individual church offices | Baptism, marriage, and burial registers not yet microfilmed or digitized | Contact individual churches or their diocesan archives |

## Records NOT online
- Bush Hill hospital records (epidemic-specific): physical at Philadelphia City Archives and/or Historical Society of Pennsylvania only; not confirmed as digitized
- Committee of the Citizens of Philadelphia (1793) minutes: physical at Philadelphia City Archives / Historical Society of Pennsylvania; not confirmed as digitized
- Overseers of the Poor / almshouse records: physical at Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as digitized
- Orphans' Court / guardianship records (epidemic aftermath): physical at Philadelphia Register of Wills; not confirmed as digitized
- Most congregation-level baptism, marriage, and burial registers beyond the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume: held at individual churches or their archives; microfilm may exist at FamilySearch but was not returned as digitized online images in this survey
- Philadelphia deed books for the 1793 period: physical at Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as digitized
- Pennsylvania assessment lists: not returned as digitized in this survey

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that specific Philadelphia record sets from the 1793 period were destroyed or lost. A documentation gap does exist for the epidemic period itself: the pace of death (up to 100 per day at the peak) outstripped normal record-keeping, and some burials were mass interments without individual entries in surviving registers. This is a creation gap, not a documentary loss — the events occurred but were not recorded. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793), Mathew Carey's published name list and surviving church burial registers are the key documentation that does survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's name list.** His "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (multiple 1793 editions) named many of the dead and is the most direct single source for identifying epidemic victims. It has been reprinted and is accessible in research libraries.
- **Search church burial registers before anything else.** With no civil death registration in 1793, church burial registers are the only systematic death record. The FamilySearch Wiki names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') specifically as sources for epidemic burials (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793). Contact those churches or the Historical Society of Pennsylvania for access.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 censuses in tandem.** A family present in 1790 but absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths. The 1798 Federal Direct Tax provides a mid-decade household snapshot.
- **Search probate records for late 1793 and 1794.** A probate wave followed the epidemic. FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Probate Records (collection 1999196) has 3.2 million browse-only images — navigate by date and county within the volumes.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810; Focus: 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682; the city of Philadelphia chartered 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county were coterminous for this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 at the time of the 1793 epidemic (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). No population tool data was returned for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; mercantile trade, shipping, artisan crafts; served as the national capital 1790–1800
- **Ethnic composition:** English and Welsh Quakers (founding generation); by 1793 also substantial German, Irish, Scots-Irish, and free and enslaved African American communities; Haitian refugees arrived alongside the Saint-Domingue origin of the epidemic
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quaker), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist; African Methodist Episcopal congregation founded in Philadelphia during this era
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed approximately 5,000 of ~50,000 residents, August–November 1793 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793); Philadelphia was the nation's largest city and its capital

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia city and county were coterminous during this period
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 formally merged city and county — outside the target period and does not affect 1793 records
- No historical boundary changes were returned by `place_search_all` (empty result set)
- Records from the 1780s–1810s were created and held under Philadelphia County jurisdiction

## Available record types

Note on jurisdictional level: Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration in 1793. The earliest statewide death certificate collection on FamilySearch begins in 1906. All vital event documentation for 1793 is at the congregation (church) level — not county, not state.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Pennsylvania Vital Records page in this survey (all four constructed-URL reads redirected to a generic page). The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317) confirms statewide death registration began no earlier than 1906. No start date for an earlier local or county-level registration requirement can be stated from the tool results of this survey.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registration at state or county level. Church registers are the sole systematic vital record source.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil registration in this period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see Church Records below) and epidemic-specific records (see below)

### Epidemic-specific records (1793 yellow fever)
The FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793 identifies these as the key genealogical sources for the 1793 outbreak:

- **Mathew Carey's published account:** A contemporary printed list naming the dead, published in multiple editions in 1793. Widely held in research libraries and available in facsimile. The most direct single source for identifying a victim of the epidemic.
- **Committee of Citizens minutes and reports:** The committee appointed to coordinate epidemic relief produced minutes and reports documenting the dead and relief efforts. Repository: Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** The emergency hospital established during the epidemic generated patient records. Repository: Historical Society of Pennsylvania and/or Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Church burial registers:** Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church) are specifically named by the FamilySearch Wiki for epidemic burials. See Church Records.

### Church records
- **Primary source for the period.** Church registers are the only systematic vital documentation before civil registration.
- **Denominations and key sources:** Society of Friends (Quaker), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church burial register named for epidemic burials), Swedish Lutheran — Gloria Dei/Old Swedes' (named for epidemic burials), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793 and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; confirmation registers for some denominations
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (Quaker), 1750–1800. Image group 001188322, 145 images. **Browse-only (digitization level: browse-only images)** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be examined image by image.
- **Indexes:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records). Consult their publications before attempting to browse unindexed registers.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; German Lutheran and German Reformed registers may be in German — the researcher must read the original language.
- **Where held:** Originals at individual churches; Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center (Catholic); Presbyterian Historical Society; Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds transcriptions and some originals. FamilySearch holds the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes digitally.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 census (3 years before the epidemic) and the 1800 census (7 years after) bracket the event. Both are indexed and available online. A family present in 1790 but absent or diminished in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct separate state censuses during this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available only from 1850 onward; do not cover 1793.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal census indexed and available via Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch. Digitization level: **indexed + images**.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories, guardianships. A substantial surge in probate filings is expected in late 1793 and 1794 following a death toll of ~5,000.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** If the ancestor left a will, search the will books; if they died intestate, search administration dockets.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196) — 3,200,560 images, **0 name-indexed records**, not full-text searchable. Digitization level: **browse-only images.** Must be navigated by date (late 1793–1794) and county (Philadelphia) within the volumes. URL: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **Where held:** FamilySearch images (browse-only); originals at the Philadelphia Register of Wills.
- **Orphans' Court:** Children orphaned by the epidemic came before the Orphans' Court for guardianship appointments. These records can reveal both parents' deaths and name surviving relatives who assumed custody. Held at the Philadelphia Register of Wills; not confirmed as digitized in this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages; property may have changed hands rapidly following epidemic deaths
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (Recorder of Deeds deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (warrants and surveys)
- **Access:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Pennsylvania Land and Property page in this survey (generic redirect). Confirm specific holdings by contacting the Philadelphia City Archives. Digitization level for 1793 deed books: **physical only** (not confirmed as digitized)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (ended 1783; pension files for veterans living in Philadelphia in 1793) and the Quasi-War with France (1798–1800)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA); Quasi-War service records (NARA); Pennsylvania militia records (Pennsylvania State Archives)
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files — **indexed + images** on Fold3 and Ancestry

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Mikveh Israel Cemetery (Jewish), African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas burial ground, and others. Mass burials during the epidemic may not have received individual marked graves.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Philadelphia grave inscriptions. Digitization level: **indexed** (transcriptions; no images of all markers)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual churches or their archives; not confirmed as fully digitized in this survey

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers active in 1793:** General Advertiser (later the Aurora General Advertiser), Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, Federal Gazette. These published death notices, estate sale announcements, legal notices, and epidemic-specific lists of the dead and the sick.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds runs of major Philadelphia papers; Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value for epidemic research:** Death notices August–November 1793; estate auction notices (identifying heirs and property); legal notices of administrations

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a primary Atlantic port of entry in the 1790s. Ships from Saint-Domingue (Haiti) in summer 1793 are believed to have brought the epidemic.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at the port of Philadelphia; naturalization declarations in local courts (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists; Ancestry holds indexed versions
- **Note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest when researching traveling families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania assessment lists; 1798 Federal Direct Tax (the "glass and windows" tax)
- **The 1798 Federal Direct Tax** enumerated all Philadelphia households and property — a near-census substitute between the 1790 and 1800 federal enumerations. It can confirm a household's survival and composition five years after the epidemic.
- **Where held:** NARA holds the 1798 Federal Direct Tax; some indexes on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for the non-existent 1790–1800 intercensal census years

### Other record types
- **Almshouse / Overseers of the Poor:** Philadelphia's Overseers of the Poor maintained records of indigent residents, including epidemic survivors who lost breadwinners. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives. Not confirmed as digitized in this survey.
- **Free African Society records:** The Free African Society (founded Philadelphia, 1787) mobilized its members to nurse the sick during the epidemic. Their records may document African American families. Contact the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Published histories and contemporary accounts:** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) is the primary contemporary source listing the dead. The Committee of Citizens also published reports. Both are held at research libraries and reprinted in modern editions.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 — 3.2M browse-only images (collection 1999196); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 — 312,045 records (collection 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 — 198,765 records (collection 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750-1800 — 145 browse-only images (image group 001188322) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1790 and 1800 (indexed + images); Philadelphia passenger lists; 1798 Federal Direct Tax | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers from the 1790s | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records; Quasi-War records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Philadelphia cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, military records, 1798 Federal Direct Tax | Free (some online; some in-person) |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Digitized historic American newspapers including Philadelphia papers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia, 1780-1810 (totalResults: 1) — the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, image group 001188322. This represents the complete result set for the city-level standardPlace. Additional volumes may exist under the county-level standardPlace "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States" — that search was not run in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Committee of 1793 minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, deed books, Overseers of the Poor records | In-person; contact for appointments |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript epidemic sources; Mathew Carey papers; church record transcriptions; Philadelphia newspaper runs | In-person; some digitized materials online |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person; publications available in libraries |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills | Probate records including wills, administration dockets, Orphans' Court | In-person; some records browsable on FamilySearch |
| Presbyterian Historical Society | Presbyterian congregation records for Philadelphia churches | In-person; contact for access |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Warrants, surveys, state-level records | In-person; online catalog |
| Individual church offices | Baptism, marriage, and burial registers not yet microfilmed or digitized | Contact individual churches or their diocesan archives |

## Records NOT online
- Bush Hill hospital records (epidemic-specific): physical at Philadelphia City Archives and/or Historical Society of Pennsylvania only; not confirmed as digitized
- Committee of the Citizens of Philadelphia (1793) minutes: physical at Philadelphia City Archives / Historical Society of Pennsylvania; not confirmed as digitized
- Overseers of the Poor / almshouse records: physical at Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as digitized
- Orphans' Court / guardianship records (epidemic aftermath): physical at Philadelphia Register of Wills; not confirmed as digitized
- Most congregation-level baptism, marriage, and burial registers beyond the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume: held at individual churches or their archives; microfilm may exist at FamilySearch but was not returned as digitized online images in this survey
- Philadelphia deed books for the 1793 period: physical at Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as digitized
- Pennsylvania assessment lists: not returned as digitized in this survey

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that specific Philadelphia record sets from the 1793 period were destroyed or lost. A documentation gap does exist for the epidemic period itself: the pace of death (up to 100 per day at the peak) outstripped normal record-keeping, and some burials were mass interments without individual entries in surviving registers. This is a creation gap, not a documentary loss — the events occurred but were not recorded. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793), Mathew Carey's published name list and surviving church burial registers are the key documentation that does survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's name list.** His "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (multiple 1793 editions) named many of the dead and is the most direct single source for identifying epidemic victims. It has been reprinted and is accessible in research libraries.
- **Search church burial registers before anything else.** With no civil death registration in 1793, church burial registers are the only systematic death record. The FamilySearch Wiki names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') specifically as sources for epidemic burials (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793). Contact those churches or the Historical Society of Pennsylvania for access.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 censuses in tandem.** A family present in 1790 but absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths. The 1798 Federal Direct Tax provides a mid-decade household snapshot.
- **Search probate records for late 1793 and 1794.** A probate wave followed the epidemic. FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Probate Records (collection 1999196) has 3.2 million browse-only images — navigate by date and county within the volumes.
- **Check Orphans' Court records.** Children orphaned by the epidemic came before the Orphans' Court. These files can document both parents' deaths and name the relatives who assumed custody.
- **Consult the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** for compiled church record indexes before attempting to browse unindexed registers (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Newspaper death notices are substantive.** Philadelphia papers published extensive daily death lists August–November 1793. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) hold searchable runs.
- **African American families:** The Free African Society mobilized to nurse the sick; their records and those of the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas may document Black Philadelphia families. Contact the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Cross-border and cross-county research:** Thousands fled Philadelphia during the epidemic into Chester, Montgomery, Bucks, and Delaware counties in Pennsylvania, and into Gloucester and Burlington counties in New Jersey. Church and court records in those jurisdictions may document refugee families who did not return.
- **German-language records:** German Lutheran and German Reformed congregation registers may be in German — the researcher should be prepared to work with the original language or commission a translation.
- **The 1793 FamilySearch wiki_place_page results for Pennsylvania** returned only a generic guide, not Pennsylvania-specific content. For Pennsylvania-specific research guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy.

**Chicago & Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire (1871) Research Guide**

The single most important thing to understand when researching families affected by the Great Chicago Fire of **October 8–10, 1871** is that the fire destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, wiping out virtually all official records created before that date — deeds, court records, tax rolls, birth and death registers, and many church registers. Because so much was lost locally, you must lean on records held outside Chicago:

| Record Type | Repository |

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago / Cook County, Illinois (1855–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago (city and county seat of Cook County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools for this query; the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire notes more than 100,000 residents were left homeless by the fire, indicating a city of substantial size by 1871.
- **Economy:** Chicago was a major inland commercial hub in this period — railroad terminus, meatpacking, lumber, and manufacturing. Its character as an immigrant-receiving city is directly relevant to which records exist and in which languages.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish and German immigrant communities predominated in the 1860s–1870s, with growing Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian) and smaller Czech and Polish populations. This directly affects which church records and newspapers exist.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant for Irish and German communities), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Baptist. Denominational archives, not just the county courthouse, hold the majority of vital records for the pre-fire period.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871. It killed approximately 300 people, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with most of the city's official records (per Wikipedia, [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)). This event defines the entire record landscape for this locality and period — records fall into a sharp before/after division at October 1871.

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change data was returned by `place_search_all` for this query. The guide treats Cook County and the City of Chicago as the research jurisdictions throughout the 1855–1885 window.
- Cook County held authority over the city throughout this period; records from before the city's own civil registration systems are found at the county level.

## The 1871 record divide — critical context for all research

Every record type below must be evaluated against this divide. The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most of the city's early records, including deeds, probate files, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. A negative search result for any record type before October 1871 is almost certainly a record loss, not an indexing gap — the records no longer exist in most categories. Sources that survived did so because their originals were stored outside the burned district or had already been transmitted elsewhere.

The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)) lists the primary substitute sources: reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act (1872), surviving or re-established church registers, insurance company records (especially Chicago Title and Trust Company at the Chicago History Museum), the 1870 federal census (which survived because originals were in Washington), and city directories at the Newberry Library.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists on FamilySearch:** Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (collection 2024189, 1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (collection 1913456, 980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (collection 1756321, 620,000 records). All three collections begin at 1871, consistent with the fire destroying earlier civil records.
- **Holding level:** County (Cook County Clerk's office). The FamilySearch Wiki notes the Cook County Clerk holds vital records from 1871 onward ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- **Pre-1871 vital events:** Civil registration records for events before October 1871 are largely destroyed. The FamilySearch Wiki states the specific start date for any earlier statewide or local registration system was not confirmed by the pages returned in this survey — the Vital Records and Chicago Genealogy wiki pages did not resolve to place-specific content. Church registers are the primary alternative for pre-fire vital events.
- **Gaps:** Births, marriages, and deaths occurring before October 1871 have no surviving civil record in most cases. Events in the days and weeks around the fire itself may also be incompletely recorded.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collections).

### Church records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (collection 1803978, 285,000 records). This collection covers both pre- and post-fire periods, meaning some pre-fire registers survived.
- **Repository for Catholic families:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. This is especially important for Irish and German immigrant families who make up a large share of Chicago's 1871 population ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Language:** Catholic registers for German-speaking parishes may be in German or Latin; Scandinavian Lutheran registers may be in Swedish or Norwegian.
- **Note on losses:** Many church registers were destroyed in the fire, though parishes that survived or were re-established created new registers and sometimes reconstructed earlier ones. Do not assume all church records for a given parish are lost without checking the parish archive or the Bernardin Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1803978). Archives-held registers not in this collection are physical only.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 are the relevant enumerations. The 1870 census for Chicago survived the fire because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. — this is the single most important pre-fire population record for Chicago families ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)). The 1880 census captures the rebuilt city and its population nine years after the fire.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules exist for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 (deaths in the year preceding the census). The 1870 mortality schedule may record some deaths related to the fire's aftermath, and would be held as part of the 1870 federal census holdings.
- **State census:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Census page did not resolve to a place-specific page in this survey; no Illinois state census data was confirmed by the tools. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Illinois state census information.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and searchable on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). The 1880 and 1870 censuses for Illinois are widely indexed.

### Probate and court records
- **Status:** Pre-fire probate records are largely destroyed along with the Courthouse. Post-fire probate and court records for Cook County are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- **Reconstructed pre-fire records:** FamilySearch has one digitized volume of reconstructed pre-fire County Court Records (DGS 009982110, 38 images, date range 1865–1871). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be examined image by image with no search capability.
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianship files, naturalizations (pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record), civil suits.
- **Digitization level:** Reconstructed pre-fire records: browse-only images (DGS 009982110). Post-fire records: physical at IRAD; some may be microfilmed at FamilySearch.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal land state; original federal land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website. These predate the fire and survived in Washington.
- **Pre-fire deeds:** County deed books were destroyed in the Courthouse fire.
- **Post-fire re-recordings:** The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Post-fire Property Re-recordings (DGS 009982111, 112 images, 1871–1880). This volume is **41% name-indexed** and not full-text searchable — approximately 41% of entries are reachable by name search; the remaining ~59% must be browsed.
- **Insurance records as land substitute:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum contains pre-fire property ownership documentation that survived because it was held by the insurance company, not the courthouse.
- **Digitization level:** Post-fire re-recordings: partially indexed + images (DGS 009982111). Federal patents: indexed online at BLM GLO.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) is the primary military event affecting Chicago families in this period. Many men who appear in the 1870 and 1880 censuses served.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, draft registrations (1863 Civil War draft), and unit rosters.
- **Where held:** NARA (National Archives and Records Administration) at archives.gov; Fold3 (subscription, indexed Civil War records). State adjutant general records may be at the Illinois State Archives in Springfield.
- **Survival:** Military records were held at federal repositories in Washington, D.C. — not in the Cook County Courthouse — so they were unaffected by the 1871 fire. Civil War pension files are particularly valuable because they often contain extensive family information including birth places, marriage dates, and children's names.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription); NARA records vary by series.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online cemetery index. Major Chicago-area cemeteries (Graceland, Rosehill, Calvary, Mount Carmel) have substantial FindAGrave coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records at individual cemeteries. The major cemeteries were located outside the burned district and largely survived the fire intact.
- **Denominational cemeteries:** Catholic, Jewish, and other denominational cemeteries each maintained their own burial registers. Catholic cemeteries' records may be at the Bernardin Archives or individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (founded 1847) and Chicago Times (founded 1854) both covered the period. These papers survived the fire and carried extensive coverage of victims, displaced families, charity relief, property losses, and deaths in the fire's aftermath — making them a primary source for 1871 fire-affected families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) holds digitized historical newspapers. The Newberry Library in Chicago holds local and ethnic papers on microfilm and in its collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (sheriff's sales, probate announcements), fire relief lists, and subscriber lists for the Burnt Record Act re-registrations all appear in newspapers of this period.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Chicago in 1871 had a very large immigrant population — Irish, German, and Scandinavian families predominate in the record losses. Many had arrived in the 1840s–1860s.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests (arrival at Great Lakes ports and eastern seaboard ports), declarations of intent and naturalization petitions filed in any court of record before 1906. Naturalization petitions for the Cook County area may be at IRAD or NARA's Great Lakes Regional facility.
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Ancestry census and immigration collections; FamilySearch (naturalization records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family's arrival, examine the full manifest for all family members, not only the household head.
- **Note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in a wide variety of courts (federal district courts, state courts, local courts of record). Many Cook County naturalization records may have been destroyed in the 1871 fire. NARA Great Lakes Region may hold surviving federal court naturalizations.

### Tax records
- **Status:** Pre-fire tax rolls were held in the courthouse and were destroyed in the 1871 fire. No pre-fire property or poll tax records were confirmed as surviving in the survey tools.
- **Substitute value:** City directories (Newberry Library) substitute for tax lists in terms of locating a person in the city in a given year. The BLM GLO federal land patent records confirm land ownership independently of destroyed local tax rolls.

### Insurance records (special substitute source)
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection:** The Chicago History Museum holds insurance company records that document pre-fire property ownership. This collection survived because it was held by a private company, not in the courthouse. It is a critical and often-overlooked substitute for destroyed deed and property records. ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- **Access:** Physical, at the Chicago History Museum. Consult the Museum's finding aids before visiting.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); 2 digitized volumes (reconstructed pre-fire court records and post-fire property re-recordings) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military Records (Civil War service and pension) | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives records, passenger lists | Free to request |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents (pre-fire, unaffected by disaster) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes were returned by `volume_search` for this place and period, and the total results count was 2 — this is the complete set for the queried date range.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories (1840s onward), maps, manuscripts, ethnic newspapers | In-person; consult website for hours |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records, photographs, personal papers | In-person; finding aids on website |
| IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County court and probate records post-1871 | In-person or contact IRAD |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives for access procedures |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person or written request |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | State-level records, adjutant general (military) | In-person or online finding aids |
| NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago | Federal records including federal court naturalizations | In-person or online request |

## Records NOT online
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum, physical only)
- Most church registers not captured in FamilySearch collection 1803978, including many Catholic parish registers at the Bernardin Archives
- IRAD Cook County probate and court records (physical at Northeastern Illinois University)
- Pre-fire records that survived in isolated form (individual parish archives, private family papers)
- The reconstructed pre-fire court records volume (DGS 009982110) is digitized on FamilySearch but is browse-only with no name index — it requires image-by-image examination

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, eliminating most of the city's official records including deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia, [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire); FamilySearch Wiki, [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)). Many church registers were also destroyed. No tool result in this survey confirms the survival or loss of any specific individual record set beyond these general categories — an empty search result for a pre-1871 record in any online database should be assumed to reflect record destruction, not indexing absence.

**Surviving pre-fire records confirmed by this survey:**
- 1870 federal census (originals in Washington, D.C.)
- Federal land patents at BLM GLO
- Military records at NARA (held federally, not in the Courthouse)
- City directories at the Newberry Library
- Some church registers (FamilySearch collection 1803978 covers 1833–1925, spanning the fire)
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum)

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1870 census.** It predates the fire and is fully indexed. It anchors the family — names, ages, birthplaces, neighbors — before the October 1871 destruction. The 1880 census then shows where family members ended up after the fire. ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- **Search newspapers for fire relief and aftermath notices.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of victims, displaced families, and charity relief recipients in late October and November 1871. These lists name individuals who appear in no official record of the disaster.
- **For land ownership before the fire, go to insurance records first.** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum documents pre-fire property ownership and is the most direct substitute for destroyed courthouse deed books.
- **Burnt Record Act re-recordings fill the land gap.** After 1872, property owners were legally required to re-file deeds. The FamilySearch volume DGS 009982111 (112 images, 41% name-indexed, 1871–1880) captures these. Search the indexed portion first, then browse the un-indexed images.
- **Church records bridge the fire divide.** Even for denominations whose registers burned, parishes were quickly re-established and often reconstructed earlier events from memory, family bibles, and other sources. The Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives holds Catholic registers; contact denominational archives for Protestant churches.
- **City directories substitute for destroyed tax and voter rolls.** The Newberry Library holds Chicago directories from the 1840s onward. A directory entry places a person at a specific address and occupation in a given year and can substitute for census years and lost tax records alike.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations may be lost.** Cook County court naturalizations filed before October 1871 were likely destroyed. However, federal courts (also holding naturalizations) were not in the Courthouse. Check NARA Great Lakes Region for federal court naturalizations that may survive.
- **FamilySearch wiki pages for Cook County, Illinois and for Illinois vital records did not return place-specific content in this survey** — all four `wiki_place_page` sections and all constructed-URL `wiki_read` calls returned the generic fallback page. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records directly for current, jurisdiction-specific guidance.
- **Do not limit the search to Cook County alone.** Families displaced by the fire relocated to DuPage, Kane, Lake, and Will Counties in Illinois, and to Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Records created after October 1871 for fire-affected families may be in the surrounding jurisdictions.

- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools for this query; the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire notes more than 100,000 residents were left homeless by the fire, indicating a city of substantial size by 1871.
- **Economy:** Chicago was a major inland commercial hub in this period — railroad terminus, meatpacking, lumber, and manufacturing. Its character as an immigrant-receiving city is directly relevant to which records exist and in which languages.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish and German immigrant communities predominated in the 1860s–1870s, with growing Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian) and smaller Czech and Polish populations. This directly affects which church records and newspapers exist.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant for Irish and German communities), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Baptist. Denominational archives, not just the county courthouse, hold the majority of vital records for the pre-fire period.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871. It killed approximately 300 people, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with most of the city's official records (per Wikipedia, [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)). This event defines the entire record landscape for this locality and period — records fall into a sharp before/after division at October 1871.

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change data was returned by `place_search_all` for this query. The guide treats Cook County and the City of Chicago as the research jurisdictions throughout the 1855–1885 window.
- Cook County held authority over the city throughout this period; records from before the city's own civil registration systems are found at the county level.

## The 1871 record divide — critical context for all research

Every record type below must be evaluated against this divide. The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most of the city's early records, including deeds, probate files, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. A negative search result for any record type before October 1871 is almost certainly a record loss, not an indexing gap — the records no longer exist in most categories. Sources that survived did so because their originals were stored outside the burned district or had already been transmitted elsewhere.

The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)) lists the primary substitute sources: reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act (1872), surviving or re-established church registers, insurance company records (especially Chicago Title and Trust Company at the Chicago History Museum), the 1870 federal census (which survived because originals were in Washington), and city directories at the Newberry Library.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists on FamilySearch:** Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (collection 2024189, 1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (collection 1913456, 980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (collection 1756321, 620,000 records). All three collections begin at 1871, consistent with the fire destroying earlier civil records.
- **Holding level:** County (Cook County Clerk's office). The FamilySearch Wiki notes the Cook County Clerk holds vital records from 1871 onward ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- **Pre-1871 vital events:** Civil registration records for events before October 1871 are largely destroyed. The FamilySearch Wiki states the specific start date for any earlier statewide or local registration system was not confirmed by the pages returned in this survey — the Vital Records and Chicago Genealogy wiki pages did not resolve to place-specific content. Church registers are the primary alternative for pre-fire vital events.
- **Gaps:** Births, marriages, and deaths occurring before October 1871 have no surviving civil record in most cases. Events in the days and weeks around the fire itself may also be incompletely recorded.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collections).

### Church records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (collection 1803978, 285,000 records). This collection covers both pre- and post-fire periods, meaning some pre-fire registers survived.
- **Repository for Catholic families:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. This is especially important for Irish and German immigrant families who make up a large share of Chicago's 1871 population ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Language:** Catholic registers for German-speaking parishes may be in German or Latin; Scandinavian Lutheran registers may be in Swedish or Norwegian.
- **Note on losses:** Many church registers were destroyed in the fire, though parishes that survived or were re-established created new registers and sometimes reconstructed earlier ones. Do not assume all church records for a given parish are lost without checking the parish archive or the Bernardin Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1803978). Archives-held registers not in this collection are physical only.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 are the relevant enumerations. The 1870 census for Chicago survived the fire because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. — this is the single most important pre-fire population record for Chicago families ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)). The 1880 census captures the rebuilt city and its population nine years after the fire.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules exist for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 (deaths in the year preceding the census). The 1870 mortality schedule may record some deaths related to the fire's aftermath, and would be held as part of the 1870 federal census holdings.
- **State census:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Census page did not resolve to a place-specific page in this survey; no Illinois state census data was confirmed by the tools. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Illinois state census information.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and searchable on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). The 1880 and 1870 censuses for Illinois are widely indexed.

### Probate and court records
- **Status:** Pre-fire probate records are largely destroyed along with the Courthouse. Post-fire probate and court records for Cook County are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- **Reconstructed pre-fire records:** FamilySearch has one digitized volume of reconstructed pre-fire County Court Records (DGS 009982110, 38 images, date range 1865–1871). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be examined image by image with no search capability.
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianship files, naturalizations (pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record), civil suits.
- **Digitization level:** Reconstructed pre-fire records: browse-only images (DGS 009982110). Post-fire records: physical at IRAD; some may be microfilmed at FamilySearch.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal land state; original federal land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website. These predate the fire and survived in Washington.
- **Pre-fire deeds:** County deed books were destroyed in the Courthouse fire.
- **Post-fire re-recordings:** The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Post-fire Property Re-recordings (DGS 009982111, 112 images, 1871–1880). This volume is **41% name-indexed** and not full-text searchable — approximately 41% of entries are reachable by name search; the remaining ~59% must be browsed.
- **Insurance records as land substitute:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum contains pre-fire property ownership documentation that survived because it was held by the insurance company, not the courthouse.
- **Digitization level:** Post-fire re-recordings: partially indexed + images (DGS 009982111). Federal patents: indexed online at BLM GLO.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) is the primary military event affecting Chicago families in this period. Many men who appear in the 1870 and 1880 censuses served.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, draft registrations (1863 Civil War draft), and unit rosters.
- **Where held:** NARA (National Archives and Records Administration) at archives.gov; Fold3 (subscription, indexed Civil War records). State adjutant general records may be at the Illinois State Archives in Springfield.
- **Survival:** Military records were held at federal repositories in Washington, D.C. — not in the Cook County Courthouse — so they were unaffected by the 1871 fire. Civil War pension files are particularly valuable because they often contain extensive family information including birth places, marriage dates, and children's names.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription); NARA records vary by series.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online cemetery index. Major Chicago-area cemeteries (Graceland, Rosehill, Calvary, Mount Carmel) have substantial FindAGrave coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records at individual cemeteries. The major cemeteries were located outside the burned district and largely survived the fire intact.
- **Denominational cemeteries:** Catholic, Jewish, and other denominational cemeteries each maintained their own burial registers. Catholic cemeteries' records may be at the Bernardin Archives or individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (founded 1847) and Chicago Times (founded 1854) both covered the period. These papers survived the fire and carried extensive coverage of victims, displaced families, charity relief, property losses, and deaths in the fire's aftermath — making them a primary source for 1871 fire-affected families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) holds digitized historical newspapers. The Newberry Library in Chicago holds local and ethnic papers on microfilm and in its collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (sheriff's sales, probate announcements), fire relief lists, and subscriber lists for the Burnt Record Act re-registrations all appear in newspapers of this period.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Chicago in 1871 had a very large immigrant population — Irish, German, and Scandinavian families predominate in the record losses. Many had arrived in the 1840s–1860s.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests (arrival at Great Lakes ports and eastern seaboard ports), declarations of intent and naturalization petitions filed in any court of record before 1906. Naturalization petitions for the Cook County area may be at IRAD or NARA's Great Lakes Regional facility.
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Ancestry census and immigration collections; FamilySearch (naturalization records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family's arrival, examine the full manifest for all family members, not only the household head.
- **Note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in a wide variety of courts (federal district courts, state courts, local courts of record). Many Cook County naturalization records may have been destroyed in the 1871 fire. NARA Great Lakes Region may hold surviving federal court naturalizations.

### Tax records
- **Status:** Pre-fire tax rolls were held in the courthouse and were destroyed in the 1871 fire. No pre-fire property or poll tax records were confirmed as surviving in the survey tools.
- **Substitute value:** City directories (Newberry Library) substitute for tax lists in terms of locating a person in the city in a given year. The BLM GLO federal land patent records confirm land ownership independently of destroyed local tax rolls.

### Insurance records (special substitute source)
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection:** The Chicago History Museum holds insurance company records that document pre-fire property ownership. This collection survived because it was held by a private company, not in the courthouse. It is a critical and often-overlooked substitute for destroyed deed and property records. ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- **Access:** Physical, at the Chicago History Museum. Consult the Museum's finding aids before visiting.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); 2 digitized volumes (reconstructed pre-fire court records and post-fire property re-recordings) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military Records (Civil War service and pension) | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives records, passenger lists | Free to request |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents (pre-fire, unaffected by disaster) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes were returned by `volume_search` for this place and period, and the total results count was 2 — this is the complete set for the queried date range.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories (1840s onward), maps, manuscripts, ethnic newspapers | In-person; consult website for hours |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records, photographs, personal papers | In-person; finding aids on website |
| IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County court and probate records post-1871 | In-person or contact IRAD |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives for access procedures |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person or written request |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | State-level records, adjutant general (military) | In-person or online finding aids |
| NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago | Federal records including federal court naturalizations | In-person or online request |

## Records NOT online
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum, physical only)
- Most church registers not captured in FamilySearch collection 1803978, including many Catholic parish registers at the Bernardin Archives
- IRAD Cook County probate and court records (physical at Northeastern Illinois University)
- Pre-fire records that survived in isolated form (individual parish archives, private family papers)
- The reconstructed pre-fire court records volume (DGS 009982110) is digitized on FamilySearch but is browse-only with no name index — it requires image-by-image examination

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, eliminating most of the city's official records including deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia, [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire); FamilySearch Wiki, [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)). Many church registers were also destroyed. No tool result in this survey confirms the survival or loss of any specific individual record set beyond these general categories — an empty search result for a pre-1871 record in any online database should be assumed to reflect record destruction, not indexing absence.

**Surviving pre-fire records confirmed by this survey:**
- 1870 federal census (originals in Washington, D.C.)
- Federal land patents at BLM GLO
- Military records at NARA (held federally, not in the Courthouse)
- City directories at the Newberry Library
- Some church registers (FamilySearch collection 1803978 covers 1833–1925, spanning the fire)
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum)

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1870 census.** It predates the fire and is fully indexed. It anchors the family — names, ages, birthplaces, neighbors — before the October 1871 destruction. The 1880 census then shows where family members ended up after the fire. ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- **Search newspapers for fire relief and aftermath notices.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of victims, displaced families, and charity relief recipients in late October and November 1871. These lists name individuals who appear in no official record of the disaster.
- **For land ownership before the fire, go to insurance records first.** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum documents pre-fire property ownership and is the most direct substitute for destroyed courthouse deed books.
- **Burnt Record Act re-recordings fill the land gap.** After 1872, property owners were legally required to re-file deeds. The FamilySearch volume DGS 009982111 (112 images, 41% name-indexed, 1871–1880) captures these. Search the indexed portion first, then browse the un-indexed images.
- **Church records bridge the fire divide.** Even for denominations whose registers burned, parishes were quickly re-established and often reconstructed earlier events from memory, family bibles, and other sources. The Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives holds Catholic registers; contact denominational archives for Protestant churches.
- **City directories substitute for destroyed tax and voter rolls.** The Newberry Library holds Chicago directories from the 1840s onward. A directory entry places a person at a specific address and occupation in a given year and can substitute for census years and lost tax records alike.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations may be lost.** Cook County court naturalizations filed before October 1871 were likely destroyed. However, federal courts (also holding naturalizations) were not in the Courthouse. Check NARA Great Lakes Region for federal court naturalizations that may survive.
- **FamilySearch wiki pages for Cook County, Illinois and for Illinois vital records did not return place-specific content in this survey** — all four `wiki_place_page` sections and all constructed-URL `wiki_read` calls returned the generic fallback page. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records directly for current, jurisdiction-specific guidance.
- **Do not limit the search to Cook County alone.** Families displaced by the fire relocated to DuPage, Kane, Lake, and Will Counties in Illinois, and to Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Records created after October 1871 for fire-affected families may be in the surrounding jurisdictions.

---

**French Colonial Louisiana, 1700s — Key Records & Repositories**

**Primary Record Type: Catholic Sacramental Registers**

**What's Available Online (FamilySearch)**

- **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** — an indexed collection that covers the colonial period.
- **Orleans Parish Sacramental Registers (from 1720)** — digitized but browse-only; no name index, no full-text search.
