> ⚠️ All colonial records are in **18th-century French script**. Translation and paleography assistance will be needed.

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Colonial census rolls, French military correspondence |

| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | Company of the Indies emigration lists, French colonial administration records |

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Period covered:** 1699–1769 (French Louisiana; Spain formally took control 1769)
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French empire)
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by tools for this pre-statehood period. Colonists, enslaved Africans, indigenous peoples, and free people of color all present throughout.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo cultivation, tobacco, rice; New Orleans became a major port on the Mississippi River
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, German settlers (along the "German Coast," upriver from New Orleans), Acadian refugees (arriving from 1755 onward), African enslaved population (Code Noir-regulated), Native American groups, and a growing free people of color community
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the sole legally recognized church under French colonial law (Code Noir). No Protestant churches were permitted to maintain official records.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); adoption and enforcement of the Code Noir; Seven Years' War; Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762) ceding Louisiana to Spain; Acadian deportation and resettlement (1755–1769); Spain's assumption of actual administrative control (1769)

## Boundary changes
- French Louisiana (1699–1762) encompassed the entire Mississippi River basin, far larger than the modern state. Records for this era were created under French colonial authority.
- By the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain and the eastern portion to Britain — but Spain did not take actual administrative control of the western (modern Louisiana) territory until 1769. Records created between 1762 and 1769 may appear under either French colonial or early Spanish administrative structures; search both.
- The modern state of Louisiana (admitted 1812) is a subset of the French colonial territory. Researchers tracing families from the colonial era must be aware that many records were created under French colonial administration and are not organized by the later county or parish structure.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did **not** exist during the French colonial period. The Catholic Church was the legally mandated institution for recording vital events.
- **What exists:** No state or colonial government vital registration for this period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content when fetched; no Louisiana-specific civil registration start date is reported by the tools.
- **Pre-registration source:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) — the sole source for vital events. See **Church records** below.

### Church records
- **Denomination present:** Roman Catholic (only legally recognized church in French Louisiana)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, and confirmations
- **Date range:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — covers 1718 onward and overlaps the French colonial period
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 004330991, 264 images, covering Orleans Parish 1720–1803 — **browse-only; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**; must be examined image by image; records are in **French and Spanish**
- **Where held (originals):** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans
- **Language:** French throughout the colonial period; Spanish entries may appear after 1769
- **Code Noir note:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Church registers are therefore a primary source for researching enslaved and free people of color, not only European colonists.

### Census records
- **Colonial enumerations:** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds colonial census rolls for French Louisiana, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records. These are physical holdings at ANOM — not online.
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 (post-statehood). No federal census applies to the 1699–1769 period.
- **State/territorial censuses:** Not applicable to the French colonial period.

### Probate and court records
- **Superior Council records:** The Conseil Supérieur (Superior Council) was the governing administrative and judicial body of French colonial Louisiana. Its records include land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories. Held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 004330992, 149 images, covering Louisiana 1699–1769, described as "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)" — **browse-only; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**; must be examined image by image; records are in **French and Spanish**
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — covers from 1756, overlapping the final years of the French colonial period
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, court proceedings, guardianships, contracts
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Look for both will filings and administration proceedings; the Superior Council handled both
- **Legal tradition:** Louisiana civil law (derived from French and Spanish legal traditions) — not English common law. Forms, terminology, and inheritance rules differ substantially from other U.S. jurisdictions.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French concession system (not the U.S. rectangular survey system). Land was granted in long, narrow lots ("arpents") fronting rivers.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial concessions were granted by the French Crown via the Superior Council and the Company of the Indies. Per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants, French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and in records at the **Louisiana State Land Office**.
- **Notarial archives:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants. This is a physical repository with public access.
- **Types:** Land concessions, notarial contracts, marriage settlements (contrats de mariage), property transactions
- **Language:** French

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King William's War, Queen Anne's War, various conflicts with Native American groups, French and Indian War (Seven Years' War, 1754–1763)
- **Record types:** French colonial military muster rolls and correspondence
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France, holds administrative and military correspondence for the colony. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds some colonial-era records acquired after U.S. sovereignty.
- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) covers primarily U.S.-era military records; pre-1769 French colonial military records are not typically found there.

### Cemetery records
- **Context:** Formal cemetery records for the colonial period are sparse. Catholic burial registers (see Church records) are the primary source for deaths.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Louisiana cemeteries but coverage of colonial-era burials is limited.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No Louisiana newspapers were published during the French colonial period (1699–1769). The earliest Louisiana newspaper, the *Moniteur de la Louisiane*, began in 1794 — outside this period.
- **Not applicable** as a primary source for the 1699–1769 period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for the colony
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists, Company of the Indies emigration records, Acadian deportation and resettlement lists (1755–1769)
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France) holds company and administrative emigration records. Acadian deportation lists have been published and are available in genealogical databases.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute records were maintained by the Superior Council
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Superior Council records) and ANOM (France)
- **Substitute value:** Can partially substitute for missing census records to establish presence and landholding

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical access) holds notarial contracts from the 1730s — marriage settlements, property sales, manumissions, apprenticeship records, and wills. These are among the richest sources for family and social history in the colonial period.
- **Company of the Indies records:** The Company of the Indies (Compagnie des Indes) administered Louisiana from 1717 to 1731 and generated emigration, labor, and administrative records — held at ANOM.
- **Code Noir records:** Church baptism registers documenting enslaved persons are the primary genealogical source for African-descended families; some manumission documents are in notarial records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341); DGS 004330991 (Orleans Parish sacramental registers, 1720-1803, browse-only); DGS 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699-1769, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ — some colonial-era and post-Purchase records | Free/fee varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes match this place and period in FamilySearch volume search; both are detailed above. This is the complete result set (totalResults: 2, no nextPageToken). The FamilySearch collections_search returned 4 total collections for Louisiana; 2 overlap the 1699–1769 period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, estate inventories, notarial acts, 1699–1769); partially digitized at FamilySearch | In-person; contact Louisiana State Museum |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial contracts, marriage settlements, wills, property transactions, from 1730s | In-person; public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Catholic parish registers, diocesan records | Contact archives for access |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person/mail |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls, military records, Company of the Indies records | In-person (France) or via paid researcher; some finding aids online at anom.archivesdefrance.culture.gouv.fr |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (held at ANOM, France)
- Most Superior Council records beyond the partial digitization in DGS 004330992
- New Orleans Notarial Archives (physical access only)
- Company of the Indies emigration and administrative records (ANOM)
- French colonial military records (ANOM)
- Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (beyond what FamilySearch has microfilmed)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Louisiana colonial record set was destroyed or lost. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana-specific topics returned only generic content and did not address losses. The absence of online records reflects the digitization state of a very old colonial archive, not confirmed destruction. Contact the Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM directly to assess survival and extent of any specific series.

## Research tips
- **Church registers are the vital records.** There was no civil registration in French Louisiana. Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the only official record of vital events. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) is the starting point, supplemented by in-person research at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **The two digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period are browse-only.** DGS 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720–1803) and DGS 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Budget significant time to browse image by image.
- **Records are in French (and Spanish after 1769).** You will need to read 18th-century French script, or engage a translator/professional researcher familiar with French paleography.
- **The transition period 1762–1769 is administratively ambiguous.** France signed Louisiana over to Spain in 1762 but Spain did not take control until 1769. Records from this period may appear under either colonial authority — search both French and early Spanish administrative series.
- **Go to the notarial archives for contracts and property.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical access) holds records from the 1730s and is the richest source for property transactions, marriage contracts, and manumissions that do not appear in church or government administrative series. Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **For Acadian families:** The deportation of the Acadians from Nova Scotia (1755) and their settlement in Louisiana are well-documented in dedicated finding aids and genealogical databases. Search specifically for Acadian deportation lists if your family arrived mid-century.
- **ANOM is essential for the colonial period.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for French Louisiana that have no equivalent online. Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Research enslaved ancestors through church registers.** The Code Noir mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, making church registers the primary source for African-descended families in this period. Some manumissions and testamentary provisions for enslaved and free persons of color also appear in notarial records.
- **Louisiana civil law differs from common law.** Probate, inheritance, and land records use civil law forms and terminology. Consult a guide to French and Spanish colonial law before interpreting estate inventories or land concession documents.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Census, Genealogy) returned only generic content when fetched during this survey. Consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki for any updates.

- **Notarial archives:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants. This is a physical repository with public access.
- **Types:** Land concessions, notarial contracts, marriage settlements (contrats de mariage), property transactions
- **Language:** French

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King William's War, Queen Anne's War, various conflicts with Native American groups, French and Indian War (Seven Years' War, 1754–1763)
- **Record types:** French colonial military muster rolls and correspondence
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France, holds administrative and military correspondence for the colony. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds some colonial-era records acquired after U.S. sovereignty.
- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) covers primarily U.S.-era military records; pre-1769 French colonial military records are not typically found there.

### Cemetery records
- **Context:** Formal cemetery records for the colonial period are sparse. Catholic burial registers (see Church records) are the primary source for deaths.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Louisiana cemeteries but coverage of colonial-era burials is limited.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No Louisiana newspapers were published during the French colonial period (1699–1769). The earliest Louisiana newspaper, the *Moniteur de la Louisiane*, began in 1794 — outside this period.
- **Not applicable** as a primary source for the 1699–1769 period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for the colony
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists, Company of the Indies emigration records, Acadian deportation and resettlement lists (1755–1769)
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France) holds company and administrative emigration records. Acadian deportation lists have been published and are available in genealogical databases.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute records were maintained by the Superior Council
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Superior Council records) and ANOM (France)
- **Substitute value:** Can partially substitute for missing census records to establish presence and landholding

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical access) holds notarial contracts from the 1730s — marriage settlements, property sales, manumissions, apprenticeship records, and wills. These are among the richest sources for family and social history in the colonial period.
- **Company of the Indies records:** The Company of the Indies (Compagnie des Indes) administered Louisiana from 1717 to 1731 and generated emigration, labor, and administrative records — held at ANOM.
- **Code Noir records:** Church baptism registers documenting enslaved persons are the primary genealogical source for African-descended families; some manumission documents are in notarial records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341); DGS 004330991 (Orleans Parish sacramental registers, 1720-1803, browse-only); DGS 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699-1769, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ — some colonial-era and post-Purchase records | Free/fee varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes match this place and period in FamilySearch volume search; both are detailed above. This is the complete result set (totalResults: 2, no nextPageToken). The FamilySearch collections_search returned 4 total collections for Louisiana; 2 overlap the 1699–1769 period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, estate inventories, notarial acts, 1699–1769); partially digitized at FamilySearch | In-person; contact Louisiana State Museum |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial contracts, marriage settlements, wills, property transactions, from 1730s | In-person; public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Catholic parish registers, diocesan records | Contact archives for access |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person/mail |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls, military records, Company of the Indies records | In-person (France) or via paid researcher; some finding aids online at anom.archivesdefrance.culture.gouv.fr |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (held at ANOM, France)
- Most Superior Council records beyond the partial digitization in DGS 004330992
- New Orleans Notarial Archives (physical access only)
- Company of the Indies emigration and administrative records (ANOM)
- French colonial military records (ANOM)
- Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (beyond what FamilySearch has microfilmed)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Louisiana colonial record set was destroyed or lost. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana-specific topics returned only generic content and did not address losses. The absence of online records reflects the digitization state of a very old colonial archive, not confirmed destruction. Contact the Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM directly to assess survival and extent of any specific series.

## Research tips
- **Church registers are the vital records.** There was no civil registration in French Louisiana. Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the only official record of vital events. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) is the starting point, supplemented by in-person research at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **The two digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period are browse-only.** DGS 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720–1803) and DGS 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Budget significant time to browse image by image.
- **Records are in French (and Spanish after 1769).** You will need to read 18th-century French script, or engage a translator/professional researcher familiar with French paleography.
- **The transition period 1762–1769 is administratively ambiguous.** France signed Louisiana over to Spain in 1762 but Spain did not take control until 1769. Records from this period may appear under either colonial authority — search both French and early Spanish administrative series.
- **Go to the notarial archives for contracts and property.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical access) holds records from the 1730s and is the richest source for property transactions, marriage contracts, and manumissions that do not appear in church or government administrative series. Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **For Acadian families:** The deportation of the Acadians from Nova Scotia (1755) and their settlement in Louisiana are well-documented in dedicated finding aids and genealogical databases. Search specifically for Acadian deportation lists if your family arrived mid-century.
- **ANOM is essential for the colonial period.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for French Louisiana that have no equivalent online. Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Research enslaved ancestors through church registers.** The Code Noir mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, making church registers the primary source for African-descended families in this period. Some manumissions and testamentary provisions for enslaved and free persons of color also appear in notarial records.
- **Louisiana civil law differs from common law.** Probate, inheritance, and land records use civil law forms and terminology. Consult a guide to French and Spanish colonial law before interpreting estate inventories or land concession documents.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Census, Genealogy) returned only generic content when fetched during this survey. Consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki for any updates.

**Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide (Schuylkill County, 1870–1900)**

This survey focuses on **Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania** (formed 1811, county seat Pottsville) — the heart of Pennsylvania's **anthracite coal region** during the late 1800s.

---

### Key Finding: No Statewide Civil Vital Records

Pennsylvania did **not require statewide birth or death registration** for most of this period, so **church registers** from the specific ethnic parish are the primary vital-record substitute. Look for:

- **Irish Catholic** parishes
- **Welsh Congregational** congregations
- **Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak Catholic** parishes (growing rapidly after 1880)

---

### Best Starting Point: Mine Worker Employment Cards

A **FamilySearch digitized volume** of Mine Worker Employment Cards for Schuylkill County (1870–1900) is **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the single best starting point for a mining ancestor.

---

### Record Types & Repositories

| Record Type | Where Held | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mine Worker Employment Cards** (1870–1900) | FamilySearch (online, indexed) | Best first search |
| **Marriage records** | FamilySearch — 3 overlapping PA collections | Indexed, online |
| **Probate records** | FamilySearch (3.2 million images) | Browse-only, no name index |
| **Mine Inspector Reports** (1870+) | Pennsylvania State Archives | List fatal accidents by name, age, nationality |
| **Naturalization records** (1840s–1906) | Pennsylvania State Archives | Schuylkill County records held here |
| **Church registers** | Individual parishes; some on FamilySearch/Ancestry | Critical vital-record substitute |

---

### Important Cautions

1. **The 1890 federal census is largely destroyed.** Substitute with tax lists, city directories, and state census records.
2. **FamilySearch Wiki content for Pennsylvania is generic** — some parish assignments and registration dates could not be confirmed from wiki sources alone.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Search the **Mine Worker Employment Cards** on FamilySearch first.
2. Identify the ancestor's **ethnic/religious background** to pinpoint the correct parish.
3. Check **Pennsylvania State Archives** for naturalization records (especially post-1880 immigration waves) and Mine Inspector Reports if an accident death is suspected.
4. Use a **research plan** (the `research-plan` agent) to build a prioritized search sequence once the locality guide is in place — it can draw on this guide (saved as `loc_001`) directly.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Coal Mining Region (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 (the parent jurisdiction is not stated in the tool results returned for this survey).
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated. Schuylkill County was the heart of Pennsylvania's Hard Coal region, with hundreds of collieries operating 1870–1900. Ancillary trades (blacksmithing, rail transport, timbering, company store retail) appear in the same records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic immigrant population (especially post-Famine), Welsh and English miners, and by the 1880s–1890s significant Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Italian immigration. The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining identifies Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, and Lithuanian Catholic as the principal ethnic-parish denominations.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple national parishes), Welsh Congregational, Anglican/Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, and later Eastern European Catholic and Greek Catholic congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875–1879), major labor strikes, growth of the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad (central to mine operations), formation of the United Mine Workers of America (1890).

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its 1811 formation during the target period.
- Neighboring Luzerne County gave rise to Lackawanna County in 1878, which is directly relevant if research extends north — Mine Accident Reports covering 1870–1895 span both county names. For events in what is now Lackawanna County before 1878, search Luzerne County records.
- The counties adjoining Schuylkill were not listed in a Neighboring Counties table because the FamilySearch Wiki county page returned only generic content; consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for that table.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and did not state a jurisdiction-specific registration date. - **Start with the Mine Worker Employment Cards** (FamilySearch volume 002240015 — Schuylkill County, 1870–1900, 95% indexed): this is the most accessible mining-specific record confirmed by this survey and may directly name and date employment.
- **Identify the ethnic parish first.** The coal-region ethnic parishes (Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic) served specific national communities and their registers contain the most detailed family data, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining. Do not search a generic 'Catholic' collection without knowing which national parish served the specific colliery or patch town.
- **Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (annual from 1870)** list fatal accidents by name, age, nationality, and cause — consult for any ancestor who may have died in a mining accident; source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining.
- **For deaths before 1906**, there are no statewide civil death certificates. Use church burial registers, newspaper obituaries (especially the Miners' Journal), mine accident reports, and cemetery records.
- **Naturalization records** for Schuylkill County (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any Pennsylvania court of record, not only the county of residence — broaden the search if the county court records turn up nothing.
- **For the 1890 gap**, use county tax lists and city/borough directories to bridge the decade between the 1880 and 1900 census enumerations.
- **Check both Luzerne and Lackawanna counties** if research touches the northern anthracite region, because Lackawanna was carved from Luzerne in 1878 — records before that split are under Luzerne.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania pages** returned only generic content during this survey. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy for Pennsylvania-specific articles on vital records dates, church record locations, and land record systems once those pages are accessible.
- **20 additional digitized volumes** beyond the 3 examined remain from the volume_search result set (total: 23). Retrieve them with a follow-up search using nextPageToken PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2 to identify additional census, vital, land, or church record volumes for this county and period.

Locality guide written as **loc_001** in the project file. Here's the summary:

---

**Massachusetts Colonial Records, 1620–1700**

Two separate colonies produced records during most of this period that must be searched independently until their 1691 merger:

- **Plymouth Colony** (1620–1691) — its own court, land, probate, and vital records
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628–1691) — likewise separate series

**Key things to know:**

- **Vital registration was town-level**, mandated in 1639. You must search the specific town, not just the county or state.
- The **"Great Migration" study series** (New England Historic Genealogical Society) reconstructs every known settler arriving 1620–1643 — this is the single best starting point before touching individual record sets.
- **FamilySearch** holds three indexed collections covering this period: town vital records, church records, and probate records going back to the 1630s. Two additional browse-only digitized volumes exist: town meeting/proprietors' records (image-by-image) and Suffolk County Congregational church admissions (full-text searchable but not name-indexed).
- **County deed and probate records** survive from the 1630s in remarkably complete runs.
- No federal census or passenger list records apply to 1620–1700.

**Recommended next step:** Identify the specific town(s) where your ancestor settled, then search the town vital records and Congregational church records for that place, followed by the county-level probate and land series.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628 with major settlement beginning 1630; the two merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630-1640 (Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony). No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, timber, trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers, with small Indigenous populations
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church; some Quaker, Anglican, and Baptist congregations by the late 1600s
- **Key historical events:** The Great Migration (1630-1640, ~20,000 settlers); King Philip's War (1675-1676), which displaced many communities and destroyed some early records; the 1691 merger of Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony into the Province of Massachusetts Bay

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) were separate jurisdictions with distinct record series throughout the target period. **Records for Plymouth Colony must be searched separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records** — they were published and indexed separately (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- In 1691 the two colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay, so records after 1691 fall under the unified province.
- County governments were established within Massachusetts Bay Colony beginning in 1643 (Middlesex, Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk). Land and probate records follow county lines from their founding dates.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the colony in 1639 — this is a **town-level** system, not county or statewide. No statewide civil registration existed until the 1840s. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** Town vital records from 1620 (some towns) through 1890 are collected in the FamilySearch indexed collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550). This collection is name-indexed with images.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town clerk offices; transcriptions in the Tanner-Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" published series (abstracts for over 200 towns); digitized and indexed at FamilySearch (collection 2061550)
- **Gaps:** Not every town recorded diligently from 1639; recording quality varies by town and clerk. Plymouth Colony records before 1691 require a separate search.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptisms, marriages, and burial records — the primary vital source for many families

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church and kept the most complete records throughout the period. Quaker meetings, Anglican churches, and some Baptist congregations appear by the 1670s-1680s.
- **Record types:** Membership admission lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — name-indexed with images
  - FamilySearch digitized volume 007612045: Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700, 121 images — **full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed** (accessible via fulltext_search but not name search)
  - New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston — manuscript church records and published compilations
- **Language:** English
- **Note:** Church membership admission was a formal event separate from baptism, and the admission date can appear years after arrival in a community — both series (admissions and baptisms) should be searched.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790 — well after the target period of 1620-1700. No federal census records apply to this period.
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** No formal periodic census existed during this period. Tax lists and militia musters functioned as partial population enumerations.
- **State/provincial census:** None for the 1620-1700 period.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting records and proprietors' records serve as partial enumerations — see the town meeting volumes below.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions
- **Date range:** County probate courts began in the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — name-indexed with images. Original records at county probate courts and the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Testate or intestate:** If an ancestor left a will, search the will series; if they died without one, search the administration series. The probate collection covers both.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial governments granted land; county registries of deeds recorded transfers from the 1630s onward
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, proprietors' records, town allotments
- **Date range:** County deed records begin in the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (held at county level, not town or state). FamilySearch has microfilmed many county deed books but the tool did not return a specific indexed collection for colonial-era deeds — consult the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific county name.
- **Town meeting and proprietors' records:** FamilySearch digitized volume 007612044 covers Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698, 188 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be reviewed image by image)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675-1676); earlier Pequot War (1636-1637); various militia musters throughout the period
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colonial military service records, pension records (pensions postdate this period)
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial military records. The FamilySearch collection Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some colonial-era military records, but its primary holdings for this period are limited.
- **Note:** No federal military pension or draft records apply to this pre-federal period. Bounty land records also postdate this era.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Many 17th-century burying grounds survive in Massachusetts towns (e.g., King's Chapel Burying Ground, Boston, 1630; Granary Burying Ground, Boston, 1660; Plymouth Burial Hill)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has broad Massachusetts coverage including colonial-era stones. However, many 17th-century stones are weathered or missing.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this period; most burials are documented through surviving headstones, transcription projects, and town records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in Massachusetts was Publick Occurrences (1690, single issue) and the Boston News-Letter (1704). No newspapers survive for most of the 1620-1700 target period.
- **Access:** Not applicable as a primary source for 1620-1700.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston was the primary port of entry for the Great Migration. Plymouth received the Mayflower passengers (1620) and subsequent ships.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial arrivals, though formal manifests as required later did not exist. Published ship lists and reconstructed passenger records from the Great Migration era are the primary finding aids.
- **Where held:** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series (https://www.nehgs.org) documents every known settler who arrived 1620-1643, reconstructed from multiple colonial sources — the single most important finding aid for this period. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) begins in 1820 and does NOT cover colonial arrivals.
- **Note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) for the colonial period were not uniformly kept. The Great Migration series and published works such as Banks's "Planters of the Commonwealth" reconstruct arrivals from church, court, and land records.
  - Content note: For the colonial period, family groups are reconstructed from multiple sources — children as young as infants traveled with parents, and siblings may appear in church, land, or probate records rather than passenger lists.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rate lists (property/poll tax), colony tax lists
- **Date range:** Tax lists begin in the 1630s at the town and colony level
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); some published in local histories. No specific FamilySearch indexed collection was returned for colonial-era tax records.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census records and can place a man in a town in a given year.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Town meeting records document who held office, who owned property, who was responsible for roads, and who received poor relief — naming ordinary people not found elsewhere. Volume 007612044 (FamilySearch, 1620-1698, browse-only) is the digitized example.
- **Court records:** The Massachusetts General Court and county courts handled civil suits, criminal cases, and community disputes. The Massachusetts Archives holds the original colony court records from the 1620s onward.
- **Published local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories often reprint early records and carry biographical sketches of founding families. These are a major finding aid for this period.
- **The "Great Migration" study series (NEHGS):** Encyclopedic, multi-volume series covering every known settler 1620-1643 with source citations. Essential first stop.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (collection 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection 1678901); digitized volumes 007612044 (town meeting/proprietors' records, browse-only) and 007612045 (Suffolk Congregational admissions, full-text searchable) | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection and additional Massachusetts record sets | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records including colonial burying grounds | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Federal records (limited applicability to 1620-1700 colonial period) | Free/Fee |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` tool returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts, 1620-1700 (totalResults: 2); both are detailed above. This appears to be the complete set for this query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward, colonial military records | In-person; some records available via microfilm |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript church records; published genealogies | In-person; some records online via AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| County registries of deeds | Colonial-era deed books from the 1630s, in remarkably complete runs | In-person or county website |
| County probate courts | Colonial probate files, wills, administrations from the 1630s | In-person or via FamilySearch collection 1678901 |
| Individual town clerk offices | Original town vital records from 1639 | In-person or via FamilySearch collection 2061550 |
| Plymouth Colony records | Published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records | Published in print; NEHGS and Massachusetts Archives |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial-era land deed books (beyond what FamilySearch has microfilmed at the county level — the specific county-level deed collections were not returned in this survey; consult the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific county)
- Most town meeting minutes beyond the two volumes returned (007612044 is browse-only and covers only one batch of records)
- Colonial tax lists and rate books (held at Massachusetts Archives and in town records; not returned as an indexed online collection)
- Congregational church disciplinary records (excommunications, admonishments) for most churches outside Suffolk County in this period
- Many local and county histories (WorldCat and NEHGS catalog are the finding aids; physical copies at NEHGS and state libraries)

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed several frontier Massachusetts towns and their records. No tool result named a specific record set destroyed; the Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS are the repositories to consult for confirmation of any individual town's record survival.
- No other specific record losses were returned by tool results for this period.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Great Migration series (NEHGS):** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series documents every known settler who arrived 1620-1643, reconstructed from church, court, land, and probate records. # Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628 with major settlement beginning 1630; the two merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630-1640 (Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony). No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, timber, trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers, with small Indigenous populations
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church; some Quaker, Anglican, and Baptist congregations by the late 1600s
- **Key historical events:** The Great Migration (1630-1640, ~20,000 settlers); King Philip's War (1675-1676), which displaced many communities and destroyed some early records; the 1691 merger of Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony into the Province of Massachusetts Bay

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) were separate jurisdictions with distinct record series throughout the target period. **Records for Plymouth Colony must be searched separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records** — they were published and indexed separately (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- In 1691 the two colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay, so records after 1691 fall under the unified province.
- County governments were established within Massachusetts Bay Colony beginning in 1643 (Middlesex, Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk). Land and probate records follow county lines from their founding dates.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the colony in 1639 — this is a **town-level** system, not county or statewide. No statewide civil registration existed until the 1840s. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** Town vital records from 1620 (some towns) through 1890 are collected in the FamilySearch indexed collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550). This collection is name-indexed with images.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town clerk offices; transcriptions in the Tanner-Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" published series (abstracts for over 200 towns); digitized and indexed at FamilySearch (collection 2061550)
- **Gaps:** Not every town recorded diligently from 1639; recording quality varies by town and clerk. Plymouth Colony records before 1691 require a separate search.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptisms, marriages, and burial records — the primary vital source for many families

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church and kept the most complete records throughout the period. Quaker meetings, Anglican churches, and some Baptist congregations appear by the 1670s-1680s.
- **Record types:** Membership admission lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — name-indexed with images
  - FamilySearch digitized volume 007612045: Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700, 121 images — **full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed** (accessible via fulltext_search but not name search)
  - New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston — manuscript church records and published compilations
- **Language:** English
- **Note:** Church membership admission was a formal event separate from baptism, and the admission date can appear years after arrival in a community — both series (admissions and baptisms) should be searched.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790 — well after the target period of 1620-1700. No federal census records apply to this period.
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** No formal periodic census existed during this period. Tax lists and militia musters functioned as partial population enumerations.
- **State/provincial census:** None for the 1620-1700 period.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting records and proprietors' records serve as partial enumerations — see the town meeting volumes below.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions
- **Date range:** County probate courts began in the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — name-indexed with images. Original records at county probate courts and the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Testate or intestate:** If an ancestor left a will, search the will series; if they died without one, search the administration series. The probate collection covers both.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial governments granted land; county registries of deeds recorded transfers from the 1630s onward
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, proprietors' records, town allotments
- **Date range:** County deed records begin in the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (held at county level, not town or state). FamilySearch has microfilmed many county deed books but the tool did not return a specific indexed collection for colonial-era deeds — consult the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific county name.
- **Town meeting and proprietors' records:** FamilySearch digitized volume 007612044 covers Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698, 188 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be reviewed image by image)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675-1676); earlier Pequot War (1636-1637); various militia musters throughout the period
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colonial military service records, pension records (pensions postdate this period)
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial military records. The FamilySearch collection Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some colonial-era military records, but its primary holdings for this period are limited.
- **Note:** No federal military pension or draft records apply to this pre-federal period. Bounty land records also postdate this era.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Many 17th-century burying grounds survive in Massachusetts towns (e.g., King's Chapel Burying Ground, Boston, 1630; Granary Burying Ground, Boston, 1660; Plymouth Burial Hill)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has broad Massachusetts coverage including colonial-era stones. However, many 17th-century stones are weathered or missing.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this period; most burials are documented through surviving headstones, transcription projects, and town records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in Massachusetts was Publick Occurrences (1690, single issue) and the Boston News-Letter (1704). No newspapers survive for most of the 1620-1700 target period.
- **Access:** Not applicable as a primary source for 1620-1700.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston was the primary port of entry for the Great Migration. Plymouth received the Mayflower passengers (1620) and subsequent ships.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial arrivals, though formal manifests as required later did not exist. Published ship lists and reconstructed passenger records from the Great Migration era are the primary finding aids.
- **Where held:** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series (https://www.nehgs.org) documents every known settler who arrived 1620-1643, reconstructed from multiple colonial sources — the single most important finding aid for this period. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) begins in 1820 and does NOT cover colonial arrivals.
- **Note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) for the colonial period were not uniformly kept. The Great Migration series and published works such as Banks's "Planters of the Commonwealth" reconstruct arrivals from church, court, and land records.
  - Content note: For the colonial period, family groups are reconstructed from multiple sources — children as young as infants traveled with parents, and siblings may appear in church, land, or probate records rather than passenger lists.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rate lists (property/poll tax), colony tax lists
- **Date range:** Tax lists begin in the 1630s at the town and colony level
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); some published in local histories. No specific FamilySearch indexed collection was returned for colonial-era tax records.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census records and can place a man in a town in a given year.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Town meeting records document who held office, who owned property, who was responsible for roads, and who received poor relief — naming ordinary people not found elsewhere. Volume 007612044 (FamilySearch, 1620-1698, browse-only) is the digitized example.
- **Court records:** The Massachusetts General Court and county courts handled civil suits, criminal cases, and community disputes. The Massachusetts Archives holds the original colony court records from the 1620s onward.
- **Published local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories often reprint early records and carry biographical sketches of founding families. These are a major finding aid for this period.
- **The "Great Migration" study series (NEHGS):** Encyclopedic, multi-volume series covering every known settler 1620-1643 with source citations. Essential first stop.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (collection 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection 1678901); digitized volumes 007612044 (town meeting/proprietors' records, browse-only) and 007612045 (Suffolk Congregational admissions, full-text searchable) | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection and additional Massachusetts record sets | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records including colonial burying grounds | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Federal records (limited applicability to 1620-1700 colonial period) | Free/Fee |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` tool returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts, 1620-1700 (totalResults: 2); both are detailed above. This appears to be the complete set for this query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward, colonial military records | In-person; some records available via microfilm |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript church records; published genealogies | In-person; some records online via AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| County registries of deeds | Colonial-era deed books from the 1630s, in remarkably complete runs | In-person or county website |
| County probate courts | Colonial probate files, wills, administrations from the 1630s | In-person or via FamilySearch collection 1678901 |
| Individual town clerk offices | Original town vital records from 1639 | In-person or via FamilySearch collection 2061550 |
| Plymouth Colony records | Published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records | Published in print; NEHGS and Massachusetts Archives |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial-era land deed books (beyond what FamilySearch has microfilmed at the county level — the specific county-level deed collections were not returned in this survey; consult the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific county)
- Most town meeting minutes beyond the two volumes returned (007612044 is browse-only and covers only one batch of records)
- Colonial tax lists and rate books (held at Massachusetts Archives and in town records; not returned as an indexed online collection)
- Congregational church disciplinary records (excommunications, admonishments) for most churches outside Suffolk County in this period
- Many local and county histories (WorldCat and NEHGS catalog are the finding aids; physical copies at NEHGS and state libraries)

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed several frontier Massachusetts towns and their records. No tool result named a specific record set destroyed; the Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS are the repositories to consult for confirmation of any individual town's record survival.
- No other specific record losses were returned by tool results for this period.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Great Migration series (NEHGS):** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series documents every known settler who arrived 1620-1643, reconstructed from church, court, land, and probate records. These often survive when town records are sparse and predate or supplement civil registration. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Browse-only volumes require patience:** FamilySearch volume 007612044 (town meeting/proprietors' records, 1620-1698) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be reviewed image by image. Volume 007612045 (Suffolk Congregational admissions/baptisms, 1630-1700) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed.
- **County probate and deed records begin in the 1630s:** These survive in remarkably complete runs and name family members through land transactions, wills, inventories, and guardianship appointments — essential for reconstructing family relationships when vital records are sparse.
- **Efficient research sequence:** (1) Search the Great Migration series for your ancestor's name; (2) identify the specific town; (3) search FamilySearch collection 2061550 (town vitals) and 1921657 (church records); (4) search FamilySearch collection 1678901 (probate); (5) consult county deed books; (6) check the Massachusetts Archives for court and colony records.

## Oklahoma Territory, 1889–1907: Key Records & Repositories

Oklahoma's Land Run era covers two jurisdictions: the **Unassigned Lands** (April 22, 1889 – May 2, 1890, with no civil government) and then **Oklahoma Territory** until statehood in November 1907.

### 🏛️ Federal Land Records (Most Important Starting Point)
- **General Land Office (GLO) homestead case files** — Every Land Run filer left a case file. Search via:
  - FamilySearch collection **1541872** ("Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907")
  - **glorecords.blm.gov** (free, online)
  - Original files at **NARA Washington** and **NARA Fort Worth**

### 📋 Census Records
- The **1890 US Census was largely destroyed** (nationally), but the **Oklahoma Territory Special Census (1890) survived** — held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)** in Oklahoma City. This is one of the only early census snapshots of Land Run families.

### 📝 Vital & County Records
- FamilySearch has indexed **county marriages from 1890** and **mission/church records from 1820**
- Territorial **court and probate records** → NARA Fort Worth & Oklahoma State Archives

### 🌿 Indian Territory (Eastern Oklahoma)
- The eastern half was legally **Indian Territory**, a separate jurisdiction until 1907
- Key records: **Dawes Commission rolls** and **tribal enrollment records** rather than county records
- **Indian censuses and rolls** are on FamilySearch

### 🏛️ Key Repositories
| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS), Oklahoma City | 1890 territorial census, state archives |
| NARA Fort Worth | Territorial court/probate, land records |
| NARA Washington | GLO homestead case files |
| FamilySearch | Land, marriage, Indian rolls, church records |
| glorecords.blm.gov | BLM land patents, free online |

### ⚠️ Important Cautions
1. **Eastern Oklahoma ≠ Oklahoma Territory** — if your family was in the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, or Seminole nations, you're in Indian Territory and need Dawes/tribal records, not county records.
