# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory established May 2, 1890 (Organic Act), from the Unassigned Lands of Indian Territory; the Land Run of 1889 preceded any formal civil government. Oklahoma achieved statehood November 16, 1907.
- **Capital:** Guthrie (territorial capital, 1890–1907); Oklahoma City (state capital after 1910)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Indian Territory / United States federal domain (pre-statehood)
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 participants in the April 22, 1889 Land Run alone (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889). Formal population figures were not returned by the place_population tool for this place.
- **Economy:** Frontier agriculture (homesteading), cattle ranching, early oil prospecting; federal land offices at Guthrie and Kingfisher administered claims.
- **Ethnic composition:** White settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other Midwest/Southern states; African American settlers ("Exodusters" and freed peoples); members of the Five Civilized Tribes in the adjacent Indian Territory.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and other Protestant denominations established congregations sporadically beginning in 1889. Mission churches predated settlement in Indian Territory (FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965").
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889 (Unassigned Lands, ~2 million acres); subsequent land runs 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895; Oklahoma Territory Organic Act May 2, 1890; Dawes Commission allotment of Indian Territory lands 1893–1907; statehood November 16, 1907.

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-May 2, 1890:** The Unassigned Lands had no civil county or territorial government. The only civil records created between April 22, 1889 and May 2, 1890 were General Land Office homestead filings at Guthrie and Kingfisher land offices.
- **May 2, 1890:** Oklahoma Territory established; divided into counties. Records from this point are territorial government records.
- **1890–1907:** Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) were legally distinct. Families in Indian Territory fall under Five Civilized Tribes jurisdiction and Dawes Commission records, not Oklahoma Territory county records.
- **November 16, 1907:** Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma. County-level record-keeping continued.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Oklahoma-specific vital registration dates in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records directly for the level and year civil registration began. Statehood is 1907, and most U.S. states required statewide registration in the early 1900s, but no specific date was confirmed from a tool result here.
- **What exists:** County marriages are indexed on FamilySearch from 1890 (collection 1654321 covers 1890–1995, 456,789 records). No birth or death collections for the territorial period were returned by collections_search.
- **Where held:** County courthouses hold original marriage, deed, and probate records. Oklahoma State Archives holds territorial government records.
- **Gaps:** Civil registration infrastructure was sparse or absent in the 1889–1890 period before county governments were organized.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); homestead final proof affidavits often give age and family composition; territorial census (1890 special census).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian missions established in Indian Territory from the 1820s; Protestant congregations in Oklahoma Territory from 1889 onward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; mission records from the pre-Land Run era.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321; 123,456 records, 61,728 images) — indexed + images on FamilySearch at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1880 census covers Indian Territory and predates organized Oklahoma Territory. The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed nationally — a critical loss for Land Run researchers. The 1900, 1910 federal censuses cover Oklahoma Territory and the new state of Oklahoma.
- **Oklahoma Territory special census (1890):** Survives and is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society. This is one of the very few surviving 1890 census records in the nation (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). It documents early settlers just one year after the Land Run.
- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (567,890 records, 283,945 images) — indexed + images. Covers members of the Five Civilized Tribes and other nations.
- **Tax rolls:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers and substitute for the missing 1890 federal census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Access:** The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 territorial special census is physical at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and civil/criminal cases. Naturalization petitions (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including territorial district courts).
- **Date range:** Oklahoma Territory district courts began 1890; county probate courts from county organization.
- **Where held:** Territorial district court records (1890–1907) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). County probate records are at county courthouses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal land state — township, range, and section).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** General Land Office (GLO), now Bureau of Land Management. Two land offices opened for the 1889 Land Run: Guthrie and Kingfisher.
- **Types:** Homestead applications and final certificates (5-year proof); land patents; cash-entry files. Rejected applications also survive and contain family details.
- **Digitization:** FamilySearch collection 1541872, "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (234,567 records, 117,283 images) — indexed + images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872. Additionally, volume DGS 005221388 holds land-entry case files / homestead final proofs 1889–1907 (402 images, 74% name-indexed) — reachable via record_search.
- **BLM GLO website:** Patents are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Where held (originals):** NARA, Record Group 49 (General Land Office), Washington D.C. Final proof files often include affidavits with witnesses who can confirm a settler's origins and family.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898); Indian Territory frontier service. Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations; Civil War pension files often document family relationships.
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for service/pension records; FamilySearch for military draft and pension indexes.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer cemeteries established in newly platted towns from April 1889 onward.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Oklahoma cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at the local municipal office or historical society.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Oklahoma State Capital (Guthrie) and other territorial newspapers began publication in 1889, days after the Land Run.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) carries many territorial-era Oklahoma newspapers. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds extensive newspaper collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, land claim dispute notices, marriage announcements, legal notices about homestead proofs.

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Context:** Many Land Run settlers were recent immigrants from Europe; naturalization was required to file a homestead claim.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization, filed in territorial district courts (1890–1907) and county courts after statehood; alien registrations.
- **Where held:** Pre-1906 naturalizations are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and county courthouses. Post-1906 records are at NARA.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching immigrant Land Run families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax.
- **Date range:** County tax rolls begin with county organization, 1890 onward.
- **Where held:** County assessor's offices, Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** County tax rolls from the 1890s are a primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).

### Indian Territory and Dawes Commission records
- **Scope:** Applies to residents of Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma), which remained a separate jurisdiction until 1907.
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The official enrollment of members of the Five Civilized Tribes required for allotment. FamilySearch volume DGS 005221389 holds Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910 (176 images, 0% name-indexed — browse-only images; must be browsed image by image).
- **FamilySearch collection 1987432:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" provides name-indexed access to Indian census and roll records.
- **Note:** Persons appearing in Dawes records are Indian Territory residents, not Oklahoma Territory settlers.

### Other record types
- **Departure-state records:** Many settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states. Tracing origins requires searching those states' records before 1889 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories from the early 1900s list founding families and often reprint early records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early Land Records 1834-1907 (coll. 1541872); Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851-1959 (coll. 1987432); County Marriages 1890-1995 (coll. 2134789); Mission & Church Records 1820-1965 (coll. 1654321); Homestead final proofs volume DGS 005221388 | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Oklahoma land patents | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Oklahoma cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including RG 49 (GLO homestead files), territorial court records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Oklahoma 1880–1910; both are detailed above. This is the complete result set (no nextPageToken returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Territorial district court records 1890–1907, including naturalizations; GLO homestead case files | In-person / NARA online request |
| National Archives, Washington D.C. | NARA Record Group 49, General Land Office homestead files | In-person / mail request |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial government records, county records on microfilm, tax rolls | In-person / online request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census; territorial newspapers; local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate records, marriage records from county organization onward | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census (physical at Oklahoma Historical Society; not fully digitized)
- County tax rolls (Oklahoma State Archives, county courthouses; not systematically digitized)
- Original NARA RG 49 homestead case files beyond what is indexed in FamilySearch collection 1541872 (available in-person at NARA Fort Worth and Washington D.C.)
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (volume DGS 005221389, 176 images, 0% indexed — browse-only; must be viewed image by image)
- Pre-statehood territorial court records not yet digitized (Oklahoma State Archives and NARA Fort Worth)

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed nationally — a critical loss for Land Run-era families. The Oklahoma Territory special census (1890) at the Oklahoma Historical Society is a rare surviving substitute (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- No tool result reported other systematic losses for Oklahoma territorial records. County courthouses should be contacted individually for any local record losses.

## Research tips
- **Start with land records.** Every Land Run participant who filed a homestead claim left a paper trail with the General Land Office. Homestead final proof affidavits list age, length of residence, and witnesses — often neighbors who may be relatives. Search collection 1541872 on FamilySearch and glorecords.blm.gov for patents. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **The 1890 territorial census fills the nationwide gap.** Because the 1890 federal census was destroyed, the Oklahoma Territory special census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is the only census placing a family in the territory at that early date. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society directly.
- **Use county tax rolls as a 1890s census substitute.** Tax rolls from the 1890s document settlers in intercensal years and supplement the missing 1890 federal enumeration. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Search departure states before 1889.** Land Run settlers came primarily from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. The family's records before the move — vital records, census entries, land records, church registers — are in those states, not Oklahoma. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Territorial court records for naturalizations.** Before 1906, naturalization could be filed in any court of record, including Oklahoma Territory district courts. These are at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Distinguish Oklahoma Territory from Indian Territory.** Until 1907, these were separate jurisdictions. A family in the eastern (Indian Territory) half of present-day Oklahoma generated Dawes Commission and tribal records, not county records. Identify which territory the family lived in before searching.
- **Rejected homestead applications survive and contain family detail.** Settlers who failed to prove up — Sooners, abandoners — also left files at NARA with personal information.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma did not return Oklahoma-specific content** in this survey. The pages at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_and_Property, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Church_Records, and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Census returned generic fallback content and should be consulted directly for current guidance.

Additionally, volume DGS 005221388 holds land-entry case files / homestead final proofs 1889–1907 (402 images, 74% name-indexed) — reachable via record_search.
- **BLM GLO website:** Patents are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Where held (originals):** NARA, Record Group 49 (General Land Office), Washington D.C. Final proof files often include affidavits with witnesses who can confirm a settler's origins and family.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898); Indian Territory frontier service. Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations; Civil War pension files often document family relationships.
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for service/pension records; FamilySearch for military draft and pension indexes.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer cemeteries established in newly platted towns from April 1889 onward.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Oklahoma cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at the local municipal office or historical society.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Oklahoma State Capital (Guthrie) and other territorial newspapers began publication in 1889, days after the Land Run.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) carries many territorial-era Oklahoma newspapers. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds extensive newspaper collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, land claim dispute notices, marriage announcements, legal notices about homestead proofs.

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Context:** Many Land Run settlers were recent immigrants from Europe; naturalization was required to file a homestead claim.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization, filed in territorial district courts (1890–1907) and county courts after statehood; alien registrations.
- **Where held:** Pre-1906 naturalizations are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and county courthouses. Post-1906 records are at NARA.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching immigrant Land Run families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax.
- **Date range:** County tax rolls begin with county organization, 1890 onward.
- **Where held:** County assessor's offices, Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** County tax rolls from the 1890s are a primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).

### Indian Territory and Dawes Commission records
- **Scope:** Applies to residents of Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma), which remained a separate jurisdiction until 1907.
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The official enrollment of members of the Five Civilized Tribes required for allotment. FamilySearch volume DGS 005221389 holds Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910 (176 images, 0% name-indexed — browse-only images; must be browsed image by image).
- **FamilySearch collection 1987432:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" provides name-indexed access to Indian census and roll records.
- **Note:** Persons appearing in Dawes records are Indian Territory residents, not Oklahoma Territory settlers.

### Other record types
- **Departure-state records:** Many settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states. Tracing origins requires searching those states' records before 1889 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories from the early 1900s list founding families and often reprint early records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early Land Records 1834-1907 (coll. 1541872); Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851-1959 (coll. 1987432); County Marriages 1890-1995 (coll. 2134789); Mission & Church Records 1820-1965 (coll. 1654321); Homestead final proofs volume DGS 005221388 | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Oklahoma land patents | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Oklahoma cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including RG 49 (GLO homestead files), territorial court records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Oklahoma 1880–1910; both are detailed above. This is the complete result set (no nextPageToken returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Territorial district court records 1890–1907, including naturalizations; GLO homestead case files | In-person / NARA online request |
| National Archives, Washington D.C. | NARA Record Group 49, General Land Office homestead files | In-person / mail request |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial government records, county records on microfilm, tax rolls | In-person / online request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census; territorial newspapers; local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate records, marriage records from county organization onward | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census (physical at Oklahoma Historical Society; not fully digitized)
- County tax rolls (Oklahoma State Archives, county courthouses; not systematically digitized)
- Original NARA RG 49 homestead case files beyond what is indexed in FamilySearch collection 1541872 (available in-person at NARA Fort Worth and Washington D.C.)
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (volume DGS 005221389, 176 images, 0% indexed — browse-only; must be viewed image by image)
- Pre-statehood territorial court records not yet digitized (Oklahoma State Archives and NARA Fort Worth)

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed nationally — a critical loss for Land Run-era families. The Oklahoma Territory special census (1890) at the Oklahoma Historical Society is a rare surviving substitute (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- No tool result reported other systematic losses for Oklahoma territorial records. County courthouses should be contacted individually for any local record losses.

## Research tips
- **Start with land records.** Every Land Run participant who filed a homestead claim left a paper trail with the General Land Office. Homestead final proof affidavits list age, length of residence, and witnesses — often neighbors who may be relatives. Search collection 1541872 on FamilySearch and glorecords.blm.gov for patents. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **The 1890 territorial census fills the nationwide gap.** Because the 1890 federal census was destroyed, the Oklahoma Territory special census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is the only census placing a family in the territory at that early date. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society directly.
- **Use county tax rolls as a 1890s census substitute.** Tax rolls from the 1890s document settlers in intercensal years and supplement the missing 1890 federal enumeration. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Search departure states before 1889.** Land Run settlers came primarily from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. The family's records before the move — vital records, census entries, land records, church registers — are in those states, not Oklahoma. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Territorial court records for naturalizations.** Before 1906, naturalization could be filed in any court of record, including Oklahoma Territory district courts. These are at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Distinguish Oklahoma Territory from Indian Territory.** Until 1907, these were separate jurisdictions. A family in the eastern (Indian Territory) half of present-day Oklahoma generated Dawes Commission and tribal records, not county records. Identify which territory the family lived in before searching.
- **Rejected homestead applications survive and contain family detail.** Settlers who failed to prove up — Sooners, abandoners — also left files at NARA with personal information.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma did not return Oklahoma-specific content** in this survey. The pages at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_and_Property, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Church_Records, and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Census returned generic fallback content and should be consulted directly for current guidance.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality research guide for the Alabama region around 1800, pre-statehood:

---

## Alabama Region, ca. 1780–1819 — Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Background

The Alabama region passed through several governing authorities before statehood:

- **French and British colonial era** (pre-1780) — Mobile and the coastal strip were French, then British.
- **Spanish colonial era** (1780–1813) — Spain controlled Mobile and much of southern Alabama.
- **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817) — The Alabama region was incorporated into this territory; many records are filed under Mississippi, not Alabama.
- **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819) — Created March 3, 1817; Alabama achieved statehood on December 14, 1819.

> **Key search tip:** For any event before March 1817, search FamilySearch's **Mississippi** collections, not Alabama ones. Records are catalogued by jurisdiction at the time, not by modern state boundary.

---

### FamilySearch Indexed Collections (Available Online)

| Record Type | Coverage Begins | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Church records | ca. 1803 | Primarily Mobile-area Catholic registers |
| County marriages | ca. 1809 | Earliest Alabama-area county formations |
| Probate records | ca. 1809 | Madison, Washington, and Baldwin counties |

These are name-indexed and searchable directly on FamilySearch.

---

### Digitized Browsable Volumes (Unindexed)

**The gap is real:** FamilySearch's digitized-volume catalog returned **zero** browse-only image volumes catalogued under Alabama for 1780–1820. There are currently no unindexed image rolls to browse page-by-page for this earliest era on FamilySearch.

---

### Territorial Censuses (Critical Substitutes — Not Online)

The most important records filling the gap left by the missing 1790–1810 federal censuses for this area are the **Mississippi/Alabama Territorial Censuses**:

- **1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses** — Held physically at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL. Not currently digitized or available online.

Contact ADAH to request copies or to access on-site: [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov)

Early **tax lists** (often the best name substitute for a missing census) are also held at ADAH.

---

### Spanish and French Colonial Records (Pre-1813)

For Mobile-area families before the American takeover in 1813, records are in **European archives**:

- **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial administrative records
- **Archives nationales d'outre-mer**, Aix-en-Provence, France — French colonial records
- **Library of Congress** — Holds some transcripts and copies
- **Mobile Municipal Archives** — Local copies of some colonial-era documents

---

### Land Records

After 1817, look for land patents at the **BLM General Land Office**: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — fully indexed and browsable online.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **ADAH** — Request or access the 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses and early tax lists.
2. **FamilySearch Mississippi collections** — Search for all events before March 1817 under Mississippi scope.
3. **FamilySearch Alabama church/marriage/probate** — Search indexed records from ca. 1803–1819.
4. **BLM GLO Records** — Search for any post-1817 land patent activity.
5. **Mobile Municipal Archives / Library of Congress** — For Spanish-era Mobile families.

---

*This guide was saved to the project research log as* **loc_001**.

quirks: Before 1817, the Alabama region was administered as the Mississippi Territory — records created under that jurisdiction are scoped to Mississippi in FamilySearch, not Alabama; search both Alabama and Mississippi collections for any record dated before 1817.

Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, and 1808 were taken under the Mississippi Territory and are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery — they are not in any FamilySearch indexed collection.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory created March 3, 1817, from the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory; admitted as a state December 14, 1819
- **Governing capital:** Cahaba (first state capital, 1820) — for the territorial period, the Mississippi Territory was governed from Natchez, Mississippi (1798–1802) and Washington, Mississippi (1802–1817)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), which was itself carved from the former Southwest Territory and land ceded by Spain and Georgia
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction. Wikipedia notes that major in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia followed the Creek War of 1813–1814, suggesting rapid growth in the final years of the period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, river-borne trade (primarily the Mobile, Tombigbee, and Tennessee river systems), and trade with Native nations
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations occupied much of the interior; European American settlers arrived primarily from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, and Tennessee; the Mobile area had a longer-established French, Spanish, and Creole population; enslaved African Americans were present from the earliest colonial period
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic missions and parishes centered on Mobile (French and Spanish periods); Baptist and Methodist congregations began appearing in the territory from the early 1800s onward
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Mobile (1702); British takeover (1763); Spanish control (1780–1813); Mississippi Territory organized (1798); first Alabama county (Washington, 1800) formed; Creek War / Fort Mims Massacre (1813–1814); Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1814); Alabama Territory formed (1817); statehood (1819)

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1798:** The region had no organized U.S. territorial government. Present-day Alabama was disputed between the United States, Spain, and the Creek and Cherokee nations.
- **1798–1817:** The Mississippi Territory (organized 1798) governed the area. The territory was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812. Records from this era are filed under Mississippi in FamilySearch's collection scope, not Alabama.
- **1817:** The eastern half of the Mississippi Territory was separated and organized as the Alabama Territory. This is a clean temporal split: before March 1817, records belong to the Mississippi Territory's administrative chain; from March 1817 onward, they belong to Alabama's.
- **County formation within the period:** Washington County (1800, covering most of present-day south Alabama) was the first. Additional counties formed rapidly: Baldwin (1809), Madison (1809), Montgomery (1816), Limestone (1818), and others. Records follow the county that existed at the event date — Washington County records cover events that later-formed counties would handle in their own areas.
- **The 1813 U.S. seizure of Mobile:** Spain ceded the Mobile district to the United States in 1813. Records from the Spanish administration of Mobile (to 1813) are held in Spanish archives, not U.S. repositories.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the pre-statehood period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey (the pages resolved to a generic fallback), so a specific statewide registration date cannot be cited from this survey's tool results.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records begin as counties were formed, from at least 1809 in FamilySearch's indexed collection ("Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950"). No indexed birth or death records from this period appear in FamilySearch's Alabama-scope collections.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (original registers). FamilySearch collection 1598408 indexes and images marriages from 1809: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408
- **Gaps:** Birth and death were not routinely registered in Alabama during this period — church records are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; Bible records; newspaper notices; cemetery inscriptions.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, French and Spanish periods); Baptist and Methodist congregations (interior territory, early 1800s)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Catholic sacramental registers from the Mobile area are the oldest systematic vital records in present-day Alabama
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (id: 1986396, 156,789 records, 78,394 images) is indexed and includes images: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396. Spanish colonial-era Catholic records for the Mobile area are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain, with copies at the Library of Congress; French-period records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** Catholic registers from the French and Spanish periods are in French and Spanish respectively

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census is the first that covers any part of present-day Alabama as organized U.S. territory. The 1800 federal census did not enumerate the Mississippi Territory's Alabama portion because the region was not yet organized for that purpose.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, and 1808. These enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama and are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery — they are not in any FamilySearch indexed collection. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Indexed substitute:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (id: 2016756, 287,634 records, no images — index only): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756
- **Mississippi-scope substitute:** "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (id: 1927171) starts in 1792 and may include enumeration records for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court minutes, naturalization petitions
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins from each county's formation date. Washington County (formed 1800) is the earliest. FamilySearch's indexed collection begins at 1809.
- **Where held:** "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (id: 1537764, 438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764. Pre-1809 court records and territorial court minutes are at county courthouses (originals) and ADAH (copies/microfilm).
- **Mississippi-scope court records:** "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (id: 1855293) begins in 1799 and may include Alabama-area territorial court records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state using the rectangular survey (township and range) system for public land sales beginning after 1817. Pre-territorial lands used metes and bounds under Spanish and British colonial grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal public land grants issued by the U.S. General Land Office (GLO). The BLM's GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds searchable federal land patents for Alabama. Pre-1817 Spanish and British colonial grants are the primary land record type for the Mobile area.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (BLM GLO), colonial land grants (Spanish, British), deeds recorded at county courthouses, tax lists
- **Date range:** Spanish and British colonial grants predate 1783. The first federal public land sales in Alabama territory began around 1817–1819.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents. Spanish colonial grant copies at the Library of Congress and Archivo General de Indias. County deed books at county courthouses and ADAH. "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (id: 1919694, 312,450 records, 156,225 images) covers the territorial period and may include Alabama-area records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War / War of 1812 (1813–1814); earlier Spanish colonial militia service; territorial militia muster rolls
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Fold3 for digitized access); territorial militia rolls held at ADAH; bounty land warrants for War of 1812 service at NARA
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) for digitized military records; ADAH for territorial militia rolls. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records which cites militia rolls as a territorial record type)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries associated with Mobile's Catholic parishes are the oldest in the region; frontier churchyard burials exist across the interior, many without organized records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) is the primary online aggregator
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at individual churches; many pre-1820 burials have no sexton record at all

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (founded 1811) and the Huntsville Republican (ca. 1816) are among the earliest papers in present-day Alabama
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History; University of Alabama libraries; some digitized holdings on Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com)
- **Content value:** Obituaries and legal notices (land sales, estate notices) appear, but coverage is thin for the pre-1820 period

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the primary port of entry for the Alabama region. New Orleans was a secondary entry point for migrants moving up the rivers.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests (NARA); naturalization petitions filed in territorial and county courts; the Mobile district was under Spanish customs before 1813 — Spanish-era arrival records are in Spanish colonial archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for post-1820 manifests; pre-1813 Mobile arrivals are in Spanish colonial archives
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants. When researching families arriving through Mobile, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists, poll tax assessments
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists begin from county formation (Washington County from 1800)
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax records. Tax lists are among the territorial records cited at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are among the best substitutes for missing census coverage; the 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not online, making tax lists from those years especially valuable

### Other record types
- **Territorial government records:** The Mississippi Territory Legislature's records and territorial court minutes (centered in Natchez/Washington, Mississippi) may document Alabama-area residents. ADAH holds copies.
- **Native nation records:** The Creek and Cherokee nations maintained their own records; contact with territorial government is documented in federal Indian affairs records at NARA.
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century Alabama county histories frequently reprint early records, tax lists, and biographical sketches of pioneer families, and may be the only surviving transcription of records since lost. WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best tools for locating them.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama Church Records 1803–1950 (indexed + images); Alabama County Marriages 1809–1950 (indexed + images); Alabama Probate Records 1809–1985 (indexed + images); Alabama Census Substitutes Index 1810–1890 (index only, no images); Mississippi Territorial Land Records 1798–1907 (indexed + images); Mississippi County Court Records 1799–1920 (indexed + images); Mississippi Census Substitutes 1792–1890 (indexed); Mississippi Church Records 1800–1950 (indexed + images) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (includes 1810 Alabama territorial census) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files for Creek War / War of 1812 | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Alabama federal land patents (post-1817) | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | Military records, naturalization records, federal land records | In-person / online request (archives.gov) |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 0 digitized image volumes catalogued specifically under Alabama for the 1780–1820 period. There are no browse-only digitized volumes filed under Alabama in FamilySearch's Records Management Service for this era. The FamilySearch indexed collections listed above are the digitized coverage available; the earliest (church records) begins in 1803. The period from 1780 to approximately 1803 has no digitized record coverage in FamilySearch at all.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808); territorial tax lists; militia rolls; early county records | In-person; some microfilm available; query services offered |
| County courthouses (earliest: Washington County) | Deed books, court minutes, probate records from county formation date | In-person / mail |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial records on microfilm; early city records | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Spanish colonial record copies (Mobile District land grants, census returns) | In-person / online finding aids |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person / written inquiry |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records (Mobile District, 1780–1813): church registers, land grants, census returns | In-person / written inquiry |

## Records NOT online

- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) — held at ADAH, not digitized in FamilySearch
- Pre-1803 church records (French and Spanish colonial Catholic registers for Mobile) — in foreign archives, not digitized in FamilySearch
- Early county court minutes and deed books (Washington County from 1800, and other counties before 1809) — originals at county courthouses and ADAH
- Territorial tax lists — at ADAH
- Territorial militia rolls — at ADAH
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile District (pre-1813) — Archivo General de Indias; copies at Library of Congress

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified a destroyed record set for the Alabama region in the 1780–1819 period. The FamilySearch Alabama-specific wiki pages did not load (all redirected to generic fallbacks), so the survey cannot confirm or rule out courthouse fires or other specific losses from those pages. The absence of pre-1803 records in FamilySearch indexed collections is a digitization gap, not confirmed destruction. Consult ADAH directly regarding the survival status of any specific county's earliest records.

## Research tips

- **Work the Mississippi Territory scope first for events before 1817.** The territorial split is a clean date: records of events before March 1817 were created under Mississippi Territory authority and are filed under Mississippi in FamilySearch. Search the Mississippi collections (land records, court records, census substitutes, church records) for any Alabama ancestor active before 1817. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Go to ADAH for the territorial censuses.** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 Mississippi Territory censuses that covered present-day Alabama are at ADAH in Montgomery and are not online. These are the most direct substitutes for the missing 1800 and pre-1810 federal census coverage. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **For Mobile-area families before 1813, expect foreign-archive research.** The Spanish, French, and British colonial records for the Mobile district are not in U.S. repositories except as copies. The Library of Congress holds some Spanish colonial copies; the Mobile Municipal Archives has French colonial microfilm. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Use land records as a census substitute.** Because the territorial censuses are not online and the federal 1800 census does not cover this area, land grant applications and tax lists are the primary tool to place a person in the Alabama territory in the 1798–1809 window. The BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) is free and searchable for post-1817 patents.
- **Identify which county existed at the event date.** Washington County (1800) covered most of southern Alabama at first. Its records are not the records of any county formed later from its territory; you must look to Washington County for events in those areas before the later county was formed.
- **Chain migration from the Carolinas and Georgia.** Alabama's interior saw heavy in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after 1814 (per Wikipedia). Families who appear in Alabama from 1815–1819 often left documentary trails in those origin states — search there for earlier generations.
- **Consult published county histories.** 19th-century Alabama county histories frequently reprint pioneer-era records and tax lists that may no longer survive in the originals. WorldCat (worldcat.org) and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best locators.
- **Note:** All four FamilySearch Wiki place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned a generic fallback rather than Alabama-specific content in this survey. The FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) should be consulted directly for any updated guidance not captured here.

- **Content value:** Obituaries and legal notices (land sales, estate notices) appear, but coverage is thin for the pre-1820 period

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the primary port of entry for the Alabama region. New Orleans was a secondary entry point for migrants moving up the rivers.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests (NARA); naturalization petitions filed in territorial and county courts; the Mobile district was under Spanish customs before 1813 — Spanish-era arrival records are in Spanish colonial archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for post-1820 manifests; pre-1813 Mobile arrivals are in Spanish colonial archives
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants. When researching families arriving through Mobile, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists, poll tax assessments
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists begin from county formation (Washington County from 1800)
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax records. Tax lists are among the territorial records cited at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are among the best substitutes for missing census coverage; the 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not online, making tax lists from those years especially valuable

### Other record types
- **Territorial government records:** The Mississippi Territory Legislature's records and territorial court minutes (centered in Natchez/Washington, Mississippi) may document Alabama-area residents. ADAH holds copies.
- **Native nation records:** The Creek and Cherokee nations maintained their own records; contact with territorial government is documented in federal Indian affairs records at NARA.
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century Alabama county histories frequently reprint early records, tax lists, and biographical sketches of pioneer families, and may be the only surviving transcription of records since lost. WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best tools for locating them.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama Church Records 1803–1950 (indexed + images); Alabama County Marriages 1809–1950 (indexed + images); Alabama Probate Records 1809–1985 (indexed + images); Alabama Census Substitutes Index 1810–1890 (index only, no images); Mississippi Territorial Land Records 1798–1907 (indexed + images); Mississippi County Court Records 1799–1920 (indexed + images); Mississippi Census Substitutes 1792–1890 (indexed); Mississippi Church Records 1800–1950 (indexed + images) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (includes 1810 Alabama territorial census) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files for Creek War / War of 1812 | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Alabama federal land patents (post-1817) | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | Military records, naturalization records, federal land records | In-person / online request (archives.gov) |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 0 digitized image volumes catalogued specifically under Alabama for the 1780–1820 period. There are no browse-only digitized volumes filed under Alabama in FamilySearch's Records Management Service for this era. The FamilySearch indexed collections listed above are the digitized coverage available; the earliest (church records) begins in 1803. The period from 1780 to approximately 1803 has no digitized record coverage in FamilySearch at all.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808); territorial tax lists; militia rolls; early county records | In-person; some microfilm available; query services offered |
| County courthouses (earliest: Washington County) | Deed books, court minutes, probate records from county formation date | In-person / mail |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial records on microfilm; early city records | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Spanish colonial record copies (Mobile District land grants, census returns) | In-person / online finding aids |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person / written inquiry |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records (Mobile District, 1780–1813): church registers, land grants, census returns | In-person / written inquiry |

## Records NOT online

- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) — held at ADAH, not digitized in FamilySearch
- Pre-1803 church records (French and Spanish colonial Catholic registers for Mobile) — in foreign archives, not digitized in FamilySearch
- Early county court minutes and deed books (Washington County from 1800, and other counties before 1809) — originals at county courthouses and ADAH
- Territorial tax lists — at ADAH
- Territorial militia rolls — at ADAH
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile District (pre-1813) — Archivo General de Indias; copies at Library of Congress

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified a destroyed record set for the Alabama region in the 1780–1819 period. The FamilySearch Alabama-specific wiki pages did not load (all redirected to generic fallbacks), so the survey cannot confirm or rule out courthouse fires or other specific losses from those pages. The absence of pre-1803 records in FamilySearch indexed collections is a digitization gap, not confirmed destruction. Consult ADAH directly regarding the survival status of any specific county's earliest records.

## Research tips

- **Work the Mississippi Territory scope first for events before 1817.** The territorial split is a clean date: records of events before March 1817 were created under Mississippi Territory authority and are filed under Mississippi in FamilySearch. Search the Mississippi collections (land records, court records, census substitutes, church records) for any Alabama ancestor active before 1817. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Go to ADAH for the territorial censuses.** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 Mississippi Territory censuses that covered present-day Alabama are at ADAH in Montgomery and are not online. These are the most direct substitutes for the missing 1800 and pre-1810 federal census coverage. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **For Mobile-area families before 1813, expect foreign-archive research.** The Spanish, French, and British colonial records for the Mobile district are not in U.S. repositories except as copies. The Library of Congress holds some Spanish colonial copies; the Mobile Municipal Archives has French colonial microfilm. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Use land records as a census substitute.** Because the territorial censuses are not online and the federal 1800 census does not cover this area, land grant applications and tax lists are the primary tool to place a person in the Alabama territory in the 1798–1809 window. The BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) is free and searchable for post-1817 patents.
- **Identify which county existed at the event date.** Washington County (1800) covered most of southern Alabama at first. Its records are not the records of any county formed later from its territory; you must look to Washington County for events in those areas before the later county was formed.
- **Chain migration from the Carolinas and Georgia.** Alabama's interior saw heavy in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after 1814 (per Wikipedia). Families who appear in Alabama from 1815–1819 often left documentary trails in those origin states — search there for earlier generations.
- **Consult published county histories.** 19th-century Alabama county histories frequently reprint pioneer-era records and tax lists that may no longer survive in the originals. WorldCat (worldcat.org) and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best locators.
- **Note:** All four FamilySearch Wiki place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned a generic fallback rather than Alabama-specific content in this survey. The FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) should be consulted directly for any updated guidance not captured here.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced (**loc_001**):

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860–1900)

### Primary Focus: Schuylkill County (County Seat: Pottsville)

Population grew from **89,510 (1860)** to **172,927 (1900)** as waves of Irish, Welsh, and Eastern European miners arrived. Schuylkill is the core southern anthracite county and the natural starting point for Irish coal-region research.

---

### Key Finding: Catholic Diocesan Structure
Schuylkill County Catholic parishes remained under the **Diocese of Philadelphia** throughout 1860–1900 (not Scranton, as many assume). Baptismal and marriage registers must be requested from the **Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center**.

---

### Specialized Coal-Region Index
The **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898)** covers approximately **41,000 named colliery workers** across all five coal counties and includes occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin where known — invaluable for Irish miners.

---

### FamilySearch Holdings for Schuylkill County
Five digitized volumes are available, but **four of the five are browse-only (no name index)**:

| Record Set | Date Range | Indexed? |
|---|---|---|
| Probate Records | 1851–1930 | Browse only |
| Naturalization Records | 1849–1915 | Browse only |
| Church Records | 1842–1895 | Browse only |
| Deed Records | 1815–1900 | ~22% name-indexed |
| Marriage Records | 1870–1910 | Browse only |

---

### Vital Records Gap
Pennsylvania **statewide civil registration did not begin until ~1906**, so for 1860–1900 the only vital sources are **church registers** and **county marriage records**.

---

### Unique Irish-Specific Source
**Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports (1870s)** name hundreds of Irish-born miners and their family connections — a rare prosopographical source for the community.

---

### The Five Coal Counties
| County | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Schuylkill** | Southern anthracite core; Diocese of Philadelphia |
| **Luzerne** | Northern coal region; Lackawanna was carved from it in 1878 |
| **Lackawanna** | Formed from Luzerne County in **1878**; pre-1878 records filed under Luzerne |
| **Carbon** | Eastern anthracite fringe |
| **Northumberland** | Southern/western edge of the region |

> ⚠️ **Critical note:** If you're searching pre-1878 records for the Scranton/Carbondale area, look under **Luzerne County**, not Lackawanna.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Build a research plan targeting your specific ancestor using the sources identified here as the search sequence.
2. Request a separate locality survey for each of the remaining four counties (Luzerne/Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland).
3. Check the **Anthracite Index** for occupation and parish-of-origin data to identify the home parish in Ireland.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860); 116,428 (1870); 129,974 (1880); 172,927 (1900) — U.S. Census data
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated the county throughout this period; also some agriculture and light manufacturing in outlying townships
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant community, with many post-Famine arrivals concentrated in Schuylkill County from the 1840s onward; Welsh and English miners arrived earlier; German immigrants present throughout; later waves of Eastern European workers began arriving in the 1880s-1890s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish parishes established 1840-1870); Welsh and English Methodist and Baptist congregations; German Lutheran and Reformed; later Eastern Orthodox for Slavic workers
- **Key historical events:** Civil War service 1861-1865 (Pennsylvania volunteer regiments drew heavily from the coal region); Workingmen's Benevolent Association strikes 1868-1875; Molly Maguires conflict and trials 1875-1877

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties and its boundaries were stable throughout the 1860-1900 target period.
- Records for events before 1811 in this territory fall under Berks County (western portions) and Northampton County (eastern portions).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date and level:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content and did not specify the precise start year or jurisdictional level for Pennsylvania civil registration. - **Check adjoining counties for border families.** Schuylkill County borders Northumberland, Luzerne, Carbon, Berks, Lebanon, and Dauphin counties. This guide covers Schuylkill County only. The other anthracite coal counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland — each require their own locality survey. Note that Lackawanna County was formed from Luzerne County in 1878; records for events before 1878 in Lackawanna County territory are held under Luzerne County.

- These records are held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse; published transcripts and studies also exist
- This is an adversarial source — information was gathered by detectives and prosecution — but it names real individuals with family and community connections

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves provide searchable headstone records for many Schuylkill County cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual cemeteries and parishes; Catholic burial registers are part of the parish register series held at Philadelphia Diocesan Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) covered Schuylkill County and the broader coal region throughout this period; obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices are valuable
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Pennsylvania State Archives; Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive (digital)
- **Content value:** The Miners' Journal is especially valuable for Irish miners — it covered labor disputes, criminal proceedings, and community events in detail

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Irish immigrants to Schuylkill County typically arrived at Philadelphia or New York/Castle Garden (pre-1892) / Ellis Island (post-1892)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (Philadelphia, New York) at NARA; declarations of intention and naturalization petitions at Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas
- **Naturalization volume:** DGS 007936750 (1849-1915, browse-only) is the digitized FamilySearch holding
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children traveling with parents are listed alongside adults. The 1895 and later manifests for New York and Philadelphia capture significantly more detail (hometown, contacts, physical description).

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state assessments (from 1853); county property and personal property tax lists
- **Date range:** Triennial assessments cover the full target period from 1853 onward
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); county courthouse
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments substitute effectively for missing or destroyed records in intercensal years; the nativity field, when present, can confirm Irish origin

### Other record types
- **Court records (minute books):** County Court of Common Pleas minute books record county business — road maintenance assignments, poor relief payments, and assessments — naming ordinary residents who never appeared as litigants. These are held at the county courthouse.
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association (WBA) records:** The WBA organized Schuylkill County miners in the late 1860s-early 1870s; membership and meeting records may name Irish miners
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians records:** Active in the coal region; local lodge records may survive at lodge headquarters or the Historical Society of Schuylkill County

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (ID 1502909, 198,765 records); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (ID 1571957, 312,045 records); Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (ID 1921317, 524,189 records); Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (ID 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Digitized volumes: Probate 1851-1930 (DGS 007936749), Naturalization 1849-1915 (DGS 007936750), Church Records 1842-1895 (DGS 007936751), Deed Records 1815-1900 (DGS 007936752, 22% indexed), Marriage Records 1870-1910 (DGS 007936753) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County; Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801 (pre-period); federal census indexes for 1860-1900 | Subscription |
| Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive | Miners' Journal (Pottsville) and other regional papers | Subscription/Library |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized FamilySearch volumes match Schuylkill County. All 5 are detailed above — the volume_search returned totalResults: 5 with no nextPageToken, confirming this is the complete digitized set on FamilySearch. 4 of 5 volumes are browse-only (0% name-indexed); only Deed Records (DGS 007936752) has partial name indexing at 22%.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, probate files, naturalization records, court minute books, marriage licenses | In-person; some records available via mail request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Colliery payroll ledgers, local newspapers, genealogical files, county histories | In-person during business hours |
| Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center | Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers for all Schuylkill County parishes throughout this period | In-person / written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments, state adjutant general military records, some court records | In-person; online finding aids at phmc.pa.gov |
| National Archives Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Federal census microfilm, Civil War service and pension records, naturalization records | In-person |
| NARA, Washington D.C. | Civil War service records, pension files, passenger lists (Philadelphia) | In-person / online via Fold3, Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Catholic baptismal and burial registers (Schuylkill County parishes, 1840-1900): held at Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center; the FamilySearch digitized church records volume (DGS 007936751) is browse-only and covers only 187 images from 1842-1895
- Colliery payroll ledgers at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County: physical only, no known online counterpart
- Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments: Pennsylvania State Archives; not fully digitized or indexed for this period
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports: Schuylkill County Courthouse; some published transcripts exist in print
- Probate records: The FamilySearch volume (DGS 007936749, 412 images) covers 1851-1930 but is browse-only; original files at county courthouse contain more detail than images alone
- WBA and Ancient Order of Hibernians lodge records: physical at local repositories if extant
- Naturalization records: The FamilySearch volume (DGS 007936750) is browse-only; NARA Philadelphia holds additional records

## Known record losses
No tool result returned for this survey specifically stated that a Schuylkill County record set was destroyed or lost. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationwide by fire — this is a well-documented national loss, not specific to Schuylkill County. No other specific record loss was reported by a tool result in this survey. For any particular record type, the holding repository should be contacted to confirm survival.

## Research tips
- **Use the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index first for miners.** This index (~41,000 colliery workers, 1855-1898) is the most direct genealogical finding aid for Irish miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in civil records; it draws from payroll books across all five anthracite counties and records occupation, wage, and parish of origin. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Distinguish payroll indexes from mine-inspection reports.** Payroll-derived indexes name individual workers; mine inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery and are not person-indexed. For genealogical identification, start with the payroll indexes. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Diocese of Philadelphia, not Scranton, holds Schuylkill County Catholic records.** Despite the common assumption that Scranton is the diocesan home for the anthracite region, Schuylkill County remained under Philadelphia throughout the target period. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon split off to other dioceses in 1868; Schuylkill did not. Direct Catholic parish register inquiries to the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Use the Molly Maguires trial record set for the 1860s-1870s Irish community.** Even if your ancestor was not implicated, the depositions and Pinkerton reports name family members, neighbors, associates, and parish connections across the Irish mining community. These records are at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, and published studies excerpt substantial portions. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)
- **Triennial tax assessments fill the intercensal gaps.** Pennsylvania assessed coal-region residents every three years from 1853; the ledgers record occupation and sometimes nativity — use them for the years between 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses to track movement and establish presence. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Search mortality schedules for deaths before civil registration.** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal mortality schedules record deaths in the year before the census, capturing burial data that would otherwise require church registers.
- **Check adjoining counties for border families.** Schuylkill County borders Northumberland, Luzerne, Carbon, Berks, Lebanon, and Dauphin counties. Families near those borders generated records on both sides. The Neighboring Counties table from the FamilySearch Wiki county page was not returned in this survey — confirm neighbors via a county map and check each bordering county's records separately. For Irish miners who moved between coal patches, records may appear in Luzerne or Carbon counties as well as Schuylkill.
- **Before 1811, search Berks and Northampton counties.** If an ancestor's family was in this territory before Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, their records are in the parent counties.
- **The 1890 federal census is destroyed nationwide.** Use the triennial tax assessments, city/town directories, and state/local records to bridge 1880-1900.
- **FamilySearch collection note:** A collection titled 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' appears in FamilySearch collection results but is explicitly labeled a synthetic test fixture. Do not rely on it for research.
- **All five FamilySearch digitized volumes for Schuylkill are the complete set.** No additional pages of volume results exist (confirmed by totalResults: 5 with no nextPageToken). Four of the five are browse-only with no name index; plan to browse image by image for those record types.
- **Efficient research sequence:** (1) Federal census for each decade; (2) Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index for colliery workers; (3) Catholic parish registers via Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center; (4) Naturalization records (DGS 007936750, browse-only) for immigration pathway; (5) Triennial tax assessments for intercensal years; (6) Probate records if ancestor owned property; (7) Molly Maguires records for 1870s Irish community context.

## Unsurveyed coal counties
This guide covers Schuylkill County only. The other anthracite coal counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland — each require their own locality survey. Note that Lackawanna County was formed from Luzerne County in 1878; records for events before 1878 in Lackawanna County territory are held under Luzerne County.

---

## Vermont Before Statehood — Locality Research Guide

Vermont before statehood (roughly the 1750s through March 1791) presents a genuinely unusual research situation: the territory was simultaneously claimed by two colonial powers, then governed by its own independent republic, and throughout all of it kept almost no civil vital records whatsoever.

### The Most Critical Finding (from the FamilySearch Wiki)

Statewide civil birth, marriage, and death registration did **not begin until 1857** — decades after the period you are researching. Even the earlier town-level records survive unevenly, with some going back only to the 1770s. **You will not find civil vital records for pre-statehood Vermont ancestors.**

### Earliest Name Lists

- **1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — the FamilySearch Wiki identifies this as the earliest resident list for future Vermont: ~1,800 grantees prepared under New York colonial authority, predating any civil record.

### Key Research Principles

1. **Town-level, not county-level.** Vermont kept records at the town level. You must pin down the specific town of residence — county-level searches alone will miss the primary record series.
2. **Search two colonies.** For events before 1777, records may exist in both **New Hampshire** (which issued the Wentworth grants from 1749) and **New York** (which issued competing patents and refused to honor the New Hampshire grants). Both state archives deserve a search.

### Primary Record Sources for Pre-Statehood Vermont

| Source | Repository | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Church registers | Town-level / denominational | Often the only surviving vital records |
| Tax lists | Vermont State Archives | Good substitutes for missing vital records |
| Revolutionary War pension files | NARA | Critical for men who served 1775–1783 |
| 1790 federal census | NARA / FamilySearch | First enumeration after statehood (1791) |
| Proprietors' records | Town clerk offices | Often reprinted in 19th-century town histories |
| Town histories (19th c.) | Libraries / FamilySearch | The FamilySearch Wiki notes these often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise hard to find |
| New Hampshire Wentworth grants | NH State Archives | Pre-1777 land grants covering the territory |
| New York competing patents | NY State Archives | Pre-1777 land grants for the same territory |

### Next Steps

A research plan targeting whichever specific towns and ancestors you are tracing should draw on the **town clerk offices**, **Vermont State Archives**, **New Hampshire State Archives**, and **NARA Revolutionary War pension records** identified in this guide. Let me know the specific towns or ancestors and I can help plan those searches.
