Vermont declared independence as the Vermont Republic on January 15, 1777, and maintained its own government, land office, and courts until statehood on March 4, 1791 — records from 1777–1791 may be held under the Vermont Republic's authority rather than any U.S. federal or colonial system.

Nineteenth-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access and may be the only surviving transcription of early records.

The collections_search, volume_search, and catalog_search tools were not available in this environment — the FamilySearch Catalog should be searched directly by town name to identify microfilmed or digitized Vermont collections.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted as the 14th U.S. state on March 4, 1791. Before that, the territory existed first as the New Hampshire Grants (ca. 1749–1777) and then as the independent Vermont Republic (1777–1791).
- **Administrative center:** Windsor and then Montpelier served successive roles; in the Vermont Republic era, the legislature was itinerant.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Claimed by New Hampshire (which issued grants from 1749 under Governor Benning Wentworth) and simultaneously by New York (which issued competing patents and refused to honor the NH grants). Neither fully administered the territory.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by place_population for this period. Vermont participated in the first federal census of 1790 (one year before statehood), which is the earliest enumeration available.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and small-scale commercial farming, timber, potash production, and early frontier settlement.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent settlers moving north from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire); some Scottish and Irish settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Primarily Congregational in the early settled towns; Baptist and other dissenting Protestant groups were also present. Specific congregation data for this period was not returned by the tools.
- **Key historical events:** The New Hampshire Grants land dispute (1749–1777); formation of the Green Mountain Boys militia (1770s) under Ethan Allen to resist New York authority; Vermont's Declaration of Independence (January 15, 1777); the Revolutionary War, in which Vermont forces participated independently; Vermont Constitution of 1777 (the first to prohibit adult slavery in North America); statehood March 4, 1791.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1777, the territory had no settled boundaries recognized by all parties. New Hampshire issued grants east of the Connecticut River. New York claimed the same territory and issued competing patents.
- The Vermont Republic declared its boundaries in 1777 and maintained them through statehood.
- Vermont's boundaries were essentially stable from 1777 onward.
- **Research consequence:** For events before 1777, check colonial New Hampshire records (Governor's Council records, New Hampshire State Archives) and colonial New York records (New York State Archives, New York Colonial Documents series) in addition to any Vermont-territory sources. The two systems produced overlapping and conflicting claims — a family may appear in both.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in 1857, per the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). This is entirely after the pre-statehood period. There was no civil vital registration — at any level — during the 1750–1791 window.
- **Town clerk records:** Some Vermont town clerks recorded births, marriages, and deaths from the 1770s onward. The FamilySearch Wiki states these survive unevenly and researchers should consult town clerk offices directly. These are held at the town level, not the county level.
- **What exists:** No statewide or county-level civil records. Surviving records are town-by-town and inconsistent.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; some may have been microfilmed by FamilySearch (check the FamilySearch Catalog by town name — the catalog_search tool was not available in this survey).
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly notes that pre-1857 town records survive unevenly. Many towns will have nothing for the 1770s–1780s.

The FamilySearch Wiki notes only that pre-1857 town vital records survive unevenly — this reflects inconsistent record-keeping rather than a documented destruction event. Researchers should not assume records do not exist without checking the holding repository directly.

## Research tips
- **Start with the town, not the county.** Vermont's record-keeping system is town-centric. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) instructs researchers to consult town clerk offices directly for pre-1857 records. Always identify the specific town of residence before searching.
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the earliest systematic name list.** It enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants and predates any Vermont civil registration, per the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). If your ancestor held land in the New Hampshire Grants territory, this schedule may name them.
- **Search New Hampshire AND New York records for pre-1777 events.** Because both colonies claimed Vermont territory and issued competing grants, a single family transaction could appear in either archive.
- **Town histories are a primary substitute.** The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) explicitly identifies 19th-century Vermont town histories (1860–1900) as reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise hard to access. Search WorldCat, Google Books, and the Internet Archive for town history titles.
- **The 1790 federal census is the earliest household enumeration.** Vermont appears in it even though formal statehood came in March 1791. This is the baseline for identifying who was present at the close of the pre-statehood period.
- **Church records fill the vital records gap.** With no civil registration before 1857, church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the primary source for life events. Search the FamilySearch Catalog by town name for microfilmed church records.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are rich.** Pension applications at NARA often include depositions naming family members, places of birth, and migration history — far more narrative detail than a service record alone. Available indexed on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and some through Ancestry.
- **Tax lists bridge the 1777–1790 gap before the first census.** Annual tax records at the town level can place a person in a specific Vermont town in the years between the Vermont Republic's formation and the 1790 federal census.
- **Vermont-specific topical FamilySearch Wiki pages were not found.** Attempts to retrieve Vermont_Vital_Records, Vermont_Land_and_Property, Vermont_Church_Records, Vermont_Census, Vermont_Probate_Records, and Vermont_Naming_Customs all redirected to a generic page. The researcher should check the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy for any updates to those pages.
